It is hard to find that person. There is a detective who tries to catch the bad person. People like reading her books because they can try to find the answer, too. Reading these books is like playing a game. The most well-known characters in her books are Miss Marple and Hercule Poirot. Miss Marple is an old English lady, and she talks to everyone. People do not think she is smart, but she always finds the bad person. She uses logic to find out who is guilty of the murder. Hercule Poirot is a strange man, a private detective from Belgium who lives in London. He likes to find out who did the murder by thinking about all the evidence. The stories of Poirot and Miss Marple were made into many TV shows and movies. Christie also wrote plays. One of them is called The Mousetrap, and it started over 60 years ago. It remains the world's longest-running play. Christie was born in Torquay in Devon, England. She did not go to school. She had lessons from her mother at home. Her mother thought children should not learn to read until they were eight years old. But Christie learned how to read by herself when she was four. She read many books, so she learned to become a good writer. She later became a very good pianist and singer, too. She was married twice; she had a daughter called Rosalind Hicks. She worked in a hospital and in a pharmacy during World War I. She also wrote romance novels and plays. They were very successful too. In 1971, she was honoured by the Queen with the title Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire. Christie died on 12 January 1976 at age 85 from natural causes at her Winterbrook House in the north of Cholsey parish, adjoining Wallingford in Oxfordshire (formerly part of Berkshire). She is buried in the nearby churchyard of St Mary's, Cholsey. The Guinness Book of World Records ranks Christie as the best-selling novelist ever. Her novels have sold about 4 billion copies. Her works are the world's most-widely published books after those of William Shakespeare and the Bible. Her books have been translated into at least 103 languages. Christie's best-selling novel is And Then There Were None. It has sold 100 million copies. It is the world's best-selling mystery novel.

Sir Arthur Charles Clarke (Minehead, Somerset, 6 December 1917 – Colombo, Sri Lanka, 19 March 2008) was a British writer and inventor. He was most famous for his science fiction novel 2001: A Space Odyssey, and for working with director Stanley Kubrick on the movie of the same name. Clarke and Isaac Asimov were probably the two best-known science fiction writers of their day. Some of Clarke's novels include Childhood's End, A Fall of Moondust, The Songs of Distant Earth, The Sands of Mars, and Meeting with Medusa. He also wrote many short stories, and several serious works on science. Clarke served in the Royal Air Force as a radar instructor and technician from 1941 to 1946. He proposed a satellite communication system in 1945 which won him the Franklin Institute Gold Medal in 1963. He was the chairman of the British Interplanetary Society from 1947 to 1950 and again from 1951 to 1953. Clarke emigrated to Sri Lanka in 1956 largely to pursue his interest in scuba diving; That year, he discovered the underwater ruins of the ancient Koneswaram temple in Trincomalee. He lived in Sri Lanka until his death. He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 1998, and was awarded Sri Lanka's highest civil honour, Sri Lankabhimanya, in 2005. Clarke died from heart and respiratory failure at the age of 90.

Arthur Conan Doyle (22 May 1859 – 7 July 1930) was a British doctor and author. He is well known because he wrote short stories about the detective Sherlock Holmes. He also wrote science fiction and historical stories. He became an agnostic by the time he left school. He studied medicine at Edinburgh University from 1876 to 1881. He wrote short stories in his spare time. In 1882, he started working as a doctor in Southsea. He carried on writing short stories while he waited for patients. His first Sherlock Holmes story that was published was A Study in Scarlet. Doyle's great gifts as a writer were story-telling and character. He created really memorable characters. Holmes' gift for deduction has been copied many times in fiction. The character was probably based on a doctor called Joseph Bell. Holmes himself and Watson were balanced by the evil genius Moriarty, one of the great villains in fiction. After A Study in Scarlet came The Sign of the Four, The Valley of Fear and The Hound of the Baskervilles. The other Holmes stories were published in the Strand Magazine. They were later collected together in five volumes, starting with The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes. Conan Doyle also wrote The Lost World, published in 1912. In it, Professor Challenger and his companions travel to find a large plateau in South America where dinosaurs still live. Their children were: Mary Louise, Arthur Alleyne Kingsley (with Louise), Jean Lena Annette, Denis Percy Stewart, and Adrian Malcolm (with Jean). Doyle's wife Louisa died in 1906. After the death of his son Kingsley just before the end of the First World War, and the deaths of his brother Innes, his two brothers-in-law and his two nephews shortly after the war, Doyle sank into depression. He found solace supporting spiritualism and its attempts to find proof of existence beyond the grave. He was a member of the renowned supernatural organisation The Ghost Club.

Roald Dahl (13 September 1916 – 23 November 1990) was a Welsh and English novelist, poet, screenwriter, short-story writer and wartime fighter pilot. He was best known for his children's novels and his children books. Dahl was born on 13 September 1916 in Llandaff, Cardiff, Wales to Norwegian parents. He was educated in England, Llandaff Cathedral School, and then worked in Africa for the Shell Oil Company. In the Second World War, he was an RAF fighter pilot. It was after an air-crash and "a monumental bash on the head" that he began to write. The crash was the subject of his first published story, "Shot Down Over Libya". He wrote Matilda and The Twits. He wanted to become an adult book writer but ended up as a children's book writer. He had a tragic life since his father and oldest sister both died when he was young. Roald Dahl said that the key to his success rested in sympathising with children and realising that to children, parents and school teachers are the enemy. Dahl wrote many famous children's stories and adult horror stories. Many of his books and stories have been made into films and television shows all over the world. Among his most popular books are Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, James and the Giant Peach, Matilda, The Witches, The BFG, and Kiss Kiss. Many of his children's books have pictures drawn by Quentin Blake. Dahl was married to Patricia Neal from 1953 until they divorced in 1983. They had four daughters (one of whom died before them) and a son. Dahl was married to Felicity Crosland from 1983 until his death. He lived in Great Missenden, Buckinghamshire. He died on 23 November 1990 in Oxford, from myelodysplastic syndrome, aged 74. Model Sophie Dahl is his granddaughter. There is a Roald Dahl Museum and Story Centre in Great Missenden.

Robert Lee Frost (March 26, 1874 – January 29, 1963) was an American poet. He is well known for his realistic writing of rural life and his use of American informal (slang) speech. His poems were often set in rural life in New England in the early twentieth century, and used these settings to look at complex social and philosophical themes. Frost has often been quoted by other people. He was honored often during his lifetime, receiving four Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry. Robert Frost was born in San Francisco, California, to journalist William Prescott Frost, Jr., and Isabelle Moodie. Frost's father was a teacher, and later an editor of the San Francisco Evening Bulletin (later the San Francisco Examiner), and an unsuccessful candidate for city tax collector. After his death on May 5, 1885 the family moved across the country to Lawrence, Massachusetts. Frost graduated from Lawrence High School in 1892. Frost's mother joined the Swedenborgian Church and had him baptized in there, but he left the church as an adult. Although he would be famous for writing about rural life, Frost grew up in the city, and published his first poem in his high school's magazine. He attended Dartmouth College for two months, long enough to be accepted into the Theta Delta Chi fraternity. Frost returned home to teach and to work at different jobs. In 1894, Frost sold his first poem, "My Butterfly: An Elegy", for fifteen dollars. It was published in the November 8, 1894, edition of the New York Independent. Proud of this accomplishment, he proposed marriage to Elinor Miriam White. She waited, wanting to finish college before they married. Frost then went on a trip to the Great Dismal Swamp in Virginia. After returning he proposed again to Elinor. Because she had then graduated, she agreed. They got married on 19th December 1896. He attended liberal arts studies at Harvard for two years, but left to support his growing family. Shortly before dying, Robert's grandfather purchased a farm for Robert and Elinor in Derry, New Hampshire; and Robert worked the farm for nine years, while writing early in the mornings and producing many of the poems that would later become famous. His farming was unsuccessful and he returned to education as an English teacher at New Hampshire's Pinkerton Academy from 1906 to 1911, then at the New Hampshire Normal School (now Plymouth State University) in Plymouth, New Hampshire. In 1912, Frost sailed with his family to Great Britain, living first in Glasgow before settling in Beaconsfield outside London. His first book of poetry, A Boy's Will, was published the next year. In England, he made some important friends, including Edward Thomas (a member of the group known as the Dymock Poets), T.E. Hulme, and Ezra Pound. Surrounded by his peers, Frost wrote some of his best work while in England. After World War I began, Frost returned to America in 1915 and bought a farm in New Hampshire, where he started a career of writing, teaching, and lecturing. This family homestead was the Frosts' summer home until 1938, and is used today as The Frost Place, a museum and poetry conference site. During the years 1916–20, 1923–24, and 1927–1938, Frost taught English at Amherst College in Massachusetts, notably encouraging his students to account for the sounds of the human voice in their writing. For forty-two years – from 1921 to 1963 - Frost spent almost every summer and fall teaching at the Bread Loaf School of English of Middlebury College, at its mountain campus at Ripton, Vermont. The college now owns and maintains his former Ripton farmstead as a national historic site near the Bread Loaf campus. In 1921 Frost accepted a fellowship teaching post at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, where he resided until 1927; while there he was awarded a lifetime appointment at the University as a Fellow in Letters. The Robert Frost Ann Arbor home is now situated at The Henry Ford Museum in Dearborn, Michigan. Frost returned to Amherst in 1927. In 1940 he bought a 5 acre plot in South Miami, Florida, naming it Pencil Pines; he spent his winters there for the rest of his life. Harvard's 1965 alumni directory says Frost received an honorary degree there. Although he never graduated from college, Frost received over 40 honorary degrees, including ones from Princeton, Oxford and Cambridge universities; and was the only person to receive two honorary degrees from Dartmouth College. During his lifetime, the Robert Frost Middle School in Fairfax, Virginia, and the main library of Amherst College were named after him. Frost was 86 when he spoke and performed a reading of his poetry at the inauguration of President John F. Kennedy on January 20, 1961. He died in Boston two years later, on Jan. 29, 1963, of complications from prostate surgery. He was buried at the Old Bennington Cemetery in Bennington, Vermont. His epitaph quotes a line from one of his poems: "I had a lover's quarrel with the world." Frost's poems are analyzed in the Anthology of Modern American Poetry (Oxford University Press) where it is mentioned that behind a sometimes charmingly familiar and rural front, Frost's poetry frequently presents hopeless and hostile undertones which often are either unseen or unanalyzed. One of the original collections of Frost materials is found in the Special Collections department of the Jones Library in Amherst, Massachusetts. The collection consists of approximately twelve thousand items, including original manuscript poems and letters, correspondence, and photographs, as well as audio and visual recordings.

Aldous Leonard Huxley (26 July 1894 22 November 1963) was an English writer, and one of the most prominent members of the famous Huxley family. He wrote a number of novels, on various themes. Most of his books are about modern society, the effects of modern science and, later, on mysticism and psychedelic drugs like LSD. Huxley is probably best known for his book Brave New World. In the book, which was written in 1932, he writes about a world in the far future, where the whole social hierarchy is based on genetic traits, and not on the personal effort of individual people to improve themselves. Adonis and the Alphabet (U.S. title: Tomorrow and Tomorrow and Tomorrow) (1956) Moksha: Writings on Psychedelics and the Visionary Experience 1931–63 (1977) The Human Situation: Lectures at Santa Barbara, 1959 (1977) Pride and Prejudice (Collaboration. 1940) Jane Eyre (Collaboration with John Houseman. 1944) An Encyclopedia of Pacifism (editor, 1937)

Joseph Rudyard Kipling (30 December 1865 – 18 January 1936) was an English writer and poet. Kipling was born in Bombay, India. He wrote children's fiction, like Kim, The Jungle Book and Puck of Pook's Hill. He also wrote the well-known poems, If — and Gunga Din, and many short stories set in India. He was awarded the 1907 Nobel Prize in Literature. He spent part of his life living and writing in New England with his American wife but returned to England to live in Sussex. Kipling died of a perforated duodenal ulcer in Fitzrovia, London in 1936 and is buried in Westminster Abbey, London.

Astrid Anna Emilia Lindgren (born Astrid Anna Emilia Ericsson; November 14, 1907 – January 28, 2002) was a famous Swedish writer. She wrote many books for children. She had a son named Lars and a daughter named Karin. Astrid Lindgren grew up in Näs, near Vimmerby, Småland, and many of her books are based on her family and childhood memories. However, Pippi Longstocking, her most famous character, was invented for her daughter Karin, who was, at the time, ill and had to stay in the bed. Lindgren was the daughter of Samuel August Ericsson and Hanna Johnsson. She had two sisters. Her brother, Gunnar Ericsson, was a member of the Swedish parliament. She finished the school and took a job with a local newspaper in Vimmerby. When she became pregnant with the chief editor's child in 1926, he proposed marriage. She did not accept, and moved to Stockholm, learning to become a typist and stenographer. There she gave birth to her son Lars in Copenhagen and left him with another family to care for him. Although poorly paid, she saved whatever she could and travelled as often as possible to Copenhagen to be with Lars; often just over a weekend, spending most of her time on the train back and forth. Eventually, she managed to bring Lars home, leaving him in the care of her parents until she could afford to raise him in Stockholm. In 1931 she married her boss, Sture Lindgren (1898-1952). Three years later, in 1934, Lindgren gave birth to her second child, Karin, who later became a translator. The family moved in 1941 to an apartment on Dalagatan, with a view over Vasaparken, where Astrid lived until her death. Astrid Lindgren died in 2002, at the age of 94. In 1976, they had a scandal in Sweden when Lindgren's had to pay taxes 102% of her income. This is known as the "Pomperipossa effect" from a story, which she published in Expressen on 3 March 1976. Astrid Lindgren was well known both for her support for children's and animal rights, and for her opposition to corporal punishment. In 1994, she received the Right Livelihood Award (also known as the Alternative Nobel Prize), "...For her commitment to justice, non-violence and understanding of minorities as well as her love and caring for nature." The Pippi Longstocking series (Pippi Långstrump) The Six Bullerby Children (Barnen i Bullerbyn) Mio, my Mio (also known as Mio, my Son) (Mio, min Mio) The Brothers Lionheart (Bröderna Lejonhjärta) Ronia the Robber's Daughter (Ronja rövardotter)

Henri René Albert Guy de Maupassant (; 5 August 1850 – 6 July 1893) was a French writer. He is best known for his short stories. He wrote about three hundred of them in a little more than ten years. He also wrote six novels, three travel books, a book of poems, a few plays, and about two hundred newspaper articles. Maupassant was one of the writers who helped to develop the modern short story, both in France and in other countries. Critics have sometimes seen him as a skilled but simple writer. However, his clear and easy style came from strict training and careful work. Modern studies have shown how much thought and care he put into his writing. Maupassant was born in Normandy, in northern France, and he loved the region all his life. Many of his stories take place there, among farmers, fishermen, and people from small towns. Other stories take place in Paris, where he worked for eight years as a clerk in government offices. A third group of stories is about the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871, in which he served as a young soldier. His most famous story, "Boule de suif" ("Ball of Fat"), is about this war. It was published in 1880 and made him famous very quickly. The novelist Gustave Flaubert had been the closest friend of Maupassant's uncle. For about seven years, Flaubert taught the young Maupassant how to write. He taught him to work slowly and to look carefully at the world before writing about it. Flaubert died in May 1880, only a few weeks after the success of "Boule de suif". After this, Maupassant became one of the best-paid writers in France. He wrote for the newspapers Le Gaulois and Gil Blas. His novels Une vie (1883), Bel-Ami (1885), and Pierre et Jean (1888) were very successful. Maupassant's stories are short, clear, and carefully built. They often end with a surprise. They show people through their actions, without long explanations. Many of the stories are sad or cruel because Maupassant had a dark view of human life. He also wrote strange stories about fear and madness, such as "Le Horla" (1887). Maupassant's life was short. He caught syphilis when he was a young man, and the disease slowly damaged his brain. In January 1892, he tried to kill himself. He spent the last eighteen months of his life in a clinic in Paris. He died there in July 1893, at the age of 42. His books are still widely read, especially in schools, and many of his stories have been made into films. Guy de Maupassant was born on 5 August 1850 at the Château de Miromesnil, a large country house near Dieppe, in Normandy. His parents had rented the house in September 1849. The baby was registered under the names Henry René Albert Guy. His father, Gustave de Maupassant, and his mother, Laure Le Poittevin, were both born in 1821. They came from the rich middle class of Normandy. During the French Revolution, the family had quietly stopped using the noble "de" before its name. In 1846, Gustave went to court and won the right to use it again. Gustave was an easy-going man who liked painting and city life. He had little success in business. Laure was an intelligent woman who loved books. Her brother, Alfred Le Poittevin, had been the closest friend of the young Gustave Flaubert. Alfred died in 1848. Because of this old friendship, Flaubert later treated Laure's son almost like a son of his own. Some early biographers even said that Flaubert was Guy's real father. There is no evidence for this story. Guy's younger brother, Hervé, was born in May 1856. From 1859, the family had money problems. Gustave had to take a job in a bank and later in a Paris company that bought and sold shares. About a year later, Laure left her husband. She went to live with her two sons at Étretat, a small fishing village on the Normandy coast. In 1863, the couple were legally separated. Divorce was not legal in France at that time. Laure had money of her own from land and houses, so the boys lived comfortably. Their house at Étretat was called Les Verguies. It had orchards and gardens, and the sea was at the end of the road. Little is known for certain about Maupassant's childhood. Biographers have often said that the separation of his parents hurt him deeply. They point to his story "Garçon, un bock!" ("Waiter, a Beer!"). In the story, a boy of thirteen sees a violent argument between his father and mother, and the experience ruins his whole life. However, this character is very different from Maupassant himself, who was full of energy and enjoyed life. What is certain is that the boy loved the sea, the cliffs, and the free life of the village. He went sailing and climbed the cliffs. From an early age, he liked the company of the sons of fishermen and rope-makers. He joined them in their games and trips. In this way, he learned how the farmers of Normandy spoke. He later used this way of speaking in many of his stories. His mother gave him his first lessons. She loved him but also expected much from him. She often suffered from depression and worried about her health. Marie-Claire Bancquart describes her as an unhappy wife who wanted to keep her two sons close to herself and loved them in an anxious way. Maupassant remained closer to his mother than to anyone else for the rest of his life. In 1859–1860, Guy spent a year at the lycée impérial Napoléon in Paris, now the lycée Henri-IV. In 1863, when he was thirteen, he was sent to a Catholic boarding school at Yvetot, a small town between Étretat and Rouen. His mother chose this school even though there was a good state school at Le Havre, twenty miles away. At first, he was a quiet pupil. A letter from May 1864 shows him working for school prizes in Latin, the only foreign language that he ever knew well. In the same letter, he asked for a rowing boat. However, he soon came to hate the school. In a letter to a cousin, he called it a gloomy monastery. He complained about the smell of the priests' clothes, which seemed to him to hang over the whole town. He wrote sad poems about missing home, and his mother kept them. In 1868, the school expelled him. The reason was a poem in which he made fun of the religious life of the school. He never forgave it. In an article of 1885, he described schools of this kind as places of "moral torture". A strong dislike of priests appears many times in his work. One example is the abbé Tolbiac in Une vie. He finished his studies at the lycée of Rouen, the main city of Normandy. There he made an important friend. Louis Bouilhet, a poet and the oldest friend of Flaubert, lived in Rouen. Maupassant later said that, when he was eighteen, he heard a teacher read some lines by Bouilhet during a school walk. He bought a book of Bouilhet's poems that same evening and read almost nothing else for a month. Then he found the courage to knock at the poet's door. Bouilhet read the young man's poems and gave him advice. Through him, Guy also became closer to Flaubert. He had known Flaubert since childhood but had until then approached him only "with timid respect". Bouilhet died on 18 July 1869, nine days before Maupassant passed the baccalauréat, the French school-leaving examination. Flaubert wrote that he had "buried a part of himself". From then on, Flaubert alone guided the young man. Passing the baccalauréat was an important success at that time. Only about two per cent of young men in France received this diploma. During one of these summer holidays at Étretat, Maupassant helped to save the English poet Algernon Charles Swinburne, who had got into trouble while swimming. The grateful poet invited him to lunch. Swinburne and his friend George Powell lived in a small house full of strange objects. One of them was a dried human hand. Maupassant never forgot it. He later used the idea in two stories about a hand that kills, "La Main d'écorché" (1875) and "La Main" (1883). At Étretat, he also met the painter Gustave Courbet. In the autumn of 1869, he went to Paris to study law. He lived in the same building as his father. On 16 July 1870, France declared war on Prussia. Maupassant was almost twenty and was called into the army at once. Because he was an educated young man, he was not sent to a fighting regiment. He passed an examination at Vincennes and was placed in the army supply service, the Intendance, as a clerk with the second division at Rouen. The war went very badly for France. Within six months, the French armies were defeated, the Empire of Napoleon III fell, and the two sides agreed to stop fighting. Maupassant was part of the retreat of the defeated army. He marched for days among tired and disordered soldiers. His feet were bleeding, and he slept outside in the forest of Les Andelys. Once, while carrying orders to the front, he was almost taken prisoner. Rouen surrendered to the Germans without a fight on 6 December 1870. Maupassant was then at Le Havre, which the Germans never occupied. Paris surrendered on 28 January 1871, and the first peace agreement was signed the next month. France lost two provinces to Germany. In the spring of 1871, the workers of Paris rose against the new French government. The government defeated them with great violence. The war was the most important event of Maupassant's youth. It showed him death and destruction on a scale that he would probably never have seen otherwise. After the war, he no longer respected the generals and politicians who had led France to disaster. However, he admired the courage of ordinary people. He used his memories of the war in many stories, among them "Boule de suif", "Mademoiselle Fifi", "Deux amis", "Le Père Milon", "La Mère Sauvage", "Un duel", "Le Lit 29", and "Les Prisonniers". Antonia Fonyi has collected fifteen of his war stories in one volume. In the autumn of 1871, his father paid for another man to take his place in the army, and Guy left military service. Gustave could give his son only 600 francs a year. Like his father, Guy had to find a job. In March 1872, friends with important connections helped him to begin work at the Ministry of the Navy and Colonies in Paris. He was officially appointed in October, but at first he still received no pay. From February 1873, he received 125 francs a month, or 1,500 francs a year. A year later, he was given a regular job. This was about the same pay as a junior clerk or an ordinary worker received. His letters from these years often show his worries about money. He carefully listed his expenses for each month. By the end of 1878, he earned 2,000 francs a year. However, he could not stand the officials above him. In February 1879, after trying for a long time, he moved to the Ministry of Public Instruction. He later said little about his office work. He only said that it was boring and took all his time. However, life in the ministries gave him material for many stories. He wrote about small officials, their routines, and the little men who had power over them. France had about seven hundred thousand minor officials at the time. These were often lonely years. On 6 October 1875, he wrote to his mother that December frightened him. He called it "the black month, the sinister month, the deep month, the midnight of the year". Sport gave him a way to escape. He walked, swam, fenced, hunted and, above all, rowed. On Sundays, he went to villages along the river Seine near Paris: Bezons, Bougival, Chatou, Croissy, and the floating café called La Grenouillère. With four friends, he formed a group of rowers, or canotiers. They shared boats, cheap rooms, and girlfriends, and they enjoyed rough jokes. These friends came from the same middle class as Maupassant. Later, all of them entered respectable careers. With his friend Robert Pinchon, Maupassant also wrote a very rude play, À la feuille de rose, maison turque. The friends performed it privately in 1875 and 1877. Flaubert thought it was very funny. Flaubert did not approve of all Maupassant's way of life. In August 1878, he told his pupil that he was wasting his time rowing and chasing girls on the banks of the Seine. "You were born to write poetry: write it!" he told him. These years of freedom had a terrible result. In a letter to Pinchon dated 2 March 1877, Maupassant said, almost with pride, that he had caught syphilis. At that time, people did not understand how dangerous the disease could become after many years, and there was no cure. It killed at least 30,000 people each year in France. Maupassant was probably treated with mercury around 1876–1877, but this treatment did not remove the infection. For the rest of his life, he suffered from headaches, problems with his eyes, hair loss, and stomach trouble. Later, he began to see things that were not really there. Doctors did not understand these problems, and neither did Maupassant. In one letter from these years, he wrote that his eyes were red and swollen. He said that the fear of becoming blind tortured him all the time. On some days, he added, he felt such horror of life that he wanted to die. From March 1880, his eyes became a serious problem. They grew worse every year and were followed by violent headaches. After 1877, Maupassant never mentioned syphilis again in his letters. During these same years, Maupassant was learning how to write. Flaubert lived for most of the year at Croisset, near Rouen, but spent the winters in Paris. Maupassant visited him there on Sunday afternoons, at his apartment in the rue Murillo. He also sometimes visited Croisset on Saturdays or Sundays. Flaubert read everything that the young man wrote and corrected it. Maupassant later explained their relationship simply. Flaubert, whom he saw from time to time, had "conceived an affection" for him. Maupassant described Flaubert's teaching in 1887, in the essay that opens his novel Pierre et Jean. Flaubert told him that talent, in the words of Chateaubriand, is only "a long patience". A writer, Flaubert said, must look at something for a long time until he sees something in it that nobody else has seen before. Every object, even a fire or a tree in a field, has a part that has not yet been explored. The writer must find this part and describe it with the one right word. Maupassant also said that Flaubert's method was not only to look carefully at things but also to understand what was behind them. Through Flaubert, Maupassant met many of the most important writers of the time. They included Émile Zola, Alphonse Daudet, Edmond de Goncourt, and the Russian novelist Ivan Turgenev, who lived in Paris. Turgenev later helped Maupassant to have his work published in Russia. During one of Flaubert's Sunday meetings in the winter of 1875–1876, the young American writer Henry James met Maupassant. James remembered him telling a fantastic story that could not be repeated in print. Maupassant's first story, "La Main d'écorché" ("The Flayed Hand"), appeared in 1875 under the name Joseph Prunier. For several years, publishers ignored him or paid him very little. Sometimes they did not pay him at all. He signed some of his early work "Guy de Valmont". Valmont was the name of a village in Normandy that some of his ancestors had added to the family name. Under this name, he published a poem called "Au bord de l'eau" ("At the Water's Edge"), which Flaubert had sent to a review. He also wrote a short play in verse, Histoire du vieux temps. It was performed in February 1879 at the Théâtre Déjazet. At the end of the 1870s, Maupassant often visited the house that Zola had bought at Médan, a village on the Seine. Zola had bought it with the money from his novel L'Assommoir. Zola and five younger writers decided to publish a book of stories together about the war of 1870. The other writers were Joris-Karl Huysmans, Henry Céard, Léon Hennique, Paul Alexis, and Maupassant. They called the book Les Soirées de Médan ("The Evenings at Médan"). Maupassant wrote his story in 1879. Its title, "Boule de suif", is the nickname of its heroine, a plump prostitute from Rouen. The name means "ball of fat". Flaubert read the story before it was published. Early in 1880, he wrote to Maupassant that it was a masterpiece, "the work of a master". He said that the idea was original, the story was well built from beginning to end, and the style was excellent. During the same winter, Maupassant had a serious problem. His poem "Au bord de l'eau" had been printed again under the title "Une fille" ("A Girl") in a small review at Étampes, a town near Paris. The local prosecutor, the official who brings people to court, noticed it. Maupassant was threatened with a trial because the poem was considered indecent. He feared that he would lose his job at the ministry. Flaubert, who had himself been tried for Madame Bovary in 1857, wrote a long open letter in Maupassant's defence. Le Gaulois published the letter. The case was dropped. In April, Maupassant's first book, Des vers ("Verses"), was published. He dedicated it to Flaubert. Flaubert wrote that the dedication had made him cry. Les Soirées de Médan appeared on 17 April 1880. Many critics were angry because the book did not show the war in a heroic way. However, almost everyone agreed that "Boule de suif" was by far the best story in the book. At almost thirty years old, Maupassant suddenly became famous. Three weeks later, on Saturday 8 May 1880, he received a telegram. Flaubert had suffered a stroke and was dying. Maupassant hurried to Croisset. He stayed beside the body, and on 11 May he walked at the head of the funeral procession. He later wrote that Flaubert had taken with him "the keenest love I shall ever have for a man". After Flaubert's death, Maupassant asked the ministry for three months of leave with pay. He then asked for more leave with half pay, and finally for leave without pay. He never returned to the office. From June 1880, he earned his living only by writing. From May 1880, Maupassant had a contract with Le Gaulois. He had to write one article or story each week. The contract brought him 6,000 francs a year and lasted until 1888. From December 1881, he also wrote regularly for Gil Blas, sometimes under the name Maufrigneuse. He received similar terms from other newspapers. At the ministry, his salary had been only 2,400 francs a year. Now he earned money quickly. Most of his newspaper pieces were chroniques, essays of about 2,500 words. In them, he gave his opinions on many subjects: politics, science, women, war, hunting, and country life. The stories that he wrote for newspapers were later collected in books. In May 1881, his first collection of stories, La Maison Tellier, was published. The title story is about the women of a small-town brothel. They close the house for one day to go to a first communion in the country. Maupassant told his mother that he thought the story was at least as good as "Boule de suif". The book was dedicated to Turgenev. Turgenev gave a copy to Leo Tolstoy, who did not like it. However, Turgenev then made Tolstoy read Une vie, and Tolstoy became an admirer of Maupassant. Other collections followed quickly: Mademoiselle Fifi (1882), Contes de la bécasse and Clair de lune (1883), and Miss Harriet, Les Sœurs Rondoli, and Yvette (1884). Maupassant also began to travel. He visited Corsica in 1880 and Algeria in 1881 as a reporter for Le Gaulois. His articles about North Africa later became his first travel book, Au soleil ("In the Sun", 1884). He had started his first novel, Une vie ("A Life"), in 1877–1878, with Flaubert's encouragement. He did not finish it until 1883, after many delays and much rewriting. Gil Blas paid him 8,000 francs for the right to publish the novel in parts. He received another 2,000 francs for the Russian translation. The book appeared in April 1883 and sold 25,000 copies within a few months. Hachette, the company that controlled the bookshops in railway stations, refused to sell the novel there because people thought it was improper. Newspapers made fun of the decision. A deputy asked a question about it in Parliament, and Hachette changed its decision. Tolstoy later called Une vie an admirable novel. He said that it was not only Maupassant's best novel but perhaps the best French novel since Victor Hugo's Les Misérables. His new wealth allowed Maupassant to live as he wanted. In 1883, he built a house at Étretat. His neighbour, Hermine Lecomte du Noüy, suggested the name La Guillette, meaning "Guy's house". There he swam far out to sea, walked, and gave parties for summer visitors. He also rented a fine apartment in Paris and, during winter, houses at Cannes on the Mediterranean coast. He could not bear cold weather, and the sun helped his health. In 1883, he employed a Belgian servant, François Tassart, who remained with him until the end of his life. Tassart later wrote a book of memories about Maupassant. By the middle of the 1880s, Maupassant earned about 35,000 francs a year. This was more than ten times his old salary. He worked with strict discipline. He never accepted invitations to lunch because he wanted to keep the whole day for writing. Nobody, not even his father, was allowed into his house in the morning. He refused interviews and, for a long time, did not allow newspapers to publish his photograph. He liked to say that he wrote only for money and that he was a "merchant of prose". Bel-Ami, his second novel, appeared in 1885, first in Gil Blas and then as a book. It tells the story of Georges Duroy, a poor former soldier who becomes rich and powerful in the world of Paris newspapers, mainly through his relationships with women. In the same year, Maupassant travelled through Italy and Sicily with friends. Maupassant never married and never officially recognised any children. In 1903, ten years after his death, a Paris newspaper reported that a woman named Joséphine Litzelmann had had three children by him. They were born in 1883, 1884, and 1887. The biographer Armand Lanoux accepted this story. Christopher Lloyd points out that no proof has survived, so the question is still open. Maupassant now entered the world of rich society. There he became friends with several educated women, such as the countess Potocka and Madame Straus. He kept the details of these friendships very private. One woman, Clémence Brun, known as Clem, worked for him for several years without pay as a secretary when his eyes began to fail. After 1885, Maupassant wrote fewer short works and more long ones. Between 1885 and 1890, he published five novels, two travel books, and nine collections of stories. Mont-Oriol appeared in Gil Blas from December 1886 to February 1887 and then as a book. It is a novel about love and money in a spa town, and it makes fun of the people who visit such places. The collection Le Horla (1887) contains his most famous story of fear. Pierre et Jean, a short novel about two brothers in Le Havre, appeared in La Nouvelle Revue in December 1887 and as a book in January 1888. It begins with the essay "Le Roman" ("The Novel"), in which Maupassant explains his ideas about fiction. Fort comme la mort (1889) and Notre cœur (1890) are novels about love among the rich people of Paris. His second travel book, Sur l'eau ("On the Water", 1888), describes a journey by boat along the Mediterranean coast. It is the most personal of all his books. A third travel book, La Vie errante ("The Wandering Life", 1890), tells about his travels in Italy, Sicily, and North Africa. Edward D. Sullivan has noted that Maupassant's creative power began to weaken after Pierre et Jean. He published relatively little new work in 1888, and much of what appeared in 1888 and 1889 was older material published again. During the summers of 1885 and 1886, he went for treatment at Châtel-Guyon, a spa town in the mountains of the Auvergne. The town later became the setting of Mont-Oriol. He also bought a sailing boat and named it Bel-Ami after his novel. A second, larger yacht, Bel-Ami II, replaced it in 1888. With two sailors as crew, he travelled along the coasts of Provence and Italy. Sur l'eau grew out of these journeys. In February 1887, Maupassant joined other artists and writers in signing a public protest against the building of the Eiffel Tower. He hated the tower. At the beginning of La Vie errante, he wrote that he had left Paris to escape from it. On 8 July 1887, he went up in a balloon called Le Horla, which Captain Jovis had built. The balloon left Paris in the evening. The passengers ate cold chicken and drank champagne while the sun went down. The next morning, the balloon came down at Heist, on the coast of Belgium. Maupassant described the flight in an article called "De Paris à Heyst". His health continued to get worse. His eyes hurt, and sometimes he could not read. He took ether for the pain and employed a secretary who read to him and wrote for him. He saw many doctors and tried treatments at spas and cold showers, but nothing made him better. He travelled constantly. He went to Italy and Tunisia in the autumn of 1889 and to Algeria in the autumn of 1890. Problems in his family added to his own difficulties. His father's bad investments had lost 80,000 francs by 1882. From that time, Guy gave money to both of his parents. His brother Hervé had married and had a daughter, but he could not keep a job. He lived on money from his mother and brother. In 1887, Hervé had already been sent for the first time to an asylum, a hospital for people with serious mental illness. By February 1888, he was behaving violently towards his family. Guy wrote to him that for ten years he had done nothing but suffer because of him and care for him. He said that he was now trying to save Hervé's life. In August 1889, after another violent crisis, Guy had Hervé taken to the asylum at Bron, near Lyon. He wrote to his father that all the money from his new novel would go to Hervé's illness and to their mother. Hervé died there in November 1889. He was 33, had lost his mind, and could no longer move. The family said that he had suffered from sunstroke. In fact, both brothers almost certainly had the same disease, syphilis, which was slowly damaging their brains. In 1891, Maupassant could still work a little. His play Musotte, which he adapted with Jacques Normand from his story "L'Enfant", was performed at the Gymnase theatre in Paris in March 1891. It was a success. That summer, he tried treatments at Luchon, Divonne, and Champel, near Geneva. In December, he wrote his will. He was also trying to write a new novel, L'Angélus, but he never finished it. From the end of 1890, he could no longer write anything longer than short notes. In January 1891, he told his doctor and friend Henri Cazalis: "I assure you that I am losing my mind. I am becoming mad." In December, he wrote to him again: "I am absolutely lost... Death is imminent and I am mad. Farewell, my friend, you will see me no more." During the night of 1 to 2 January 1892, at Cannes, Maupassant cut his throat with a paper knife. His servant François and the sailors of his yacht saved his life. On 7 January 1892, he was taken to Paris and placed in the private clinic of Dr Blanche at Passy. He lived there for eighteen months. The newspapers reported on his illness, and his slow death became something like a public show. His strong body continued to live, but his mind was badly damaged. He could not sleep. He talked without stopping and had strange beliefs. In the spring of 1893, he could sometimes walk in the garden. He pushed small sticks into the ground and said that little Maupassants would grow there the next year. In March 1893, the Comédie-Française performed his play La Paix du ménage. Some people in the audience wondered whether the writer was still alive. In June 1893, Maupassant began to have violent fits. On 28 June, he fell into a coma. He died on 6 July 1893, late in the morning, at the age of 42. The funeral took place on 8 July at the church of Saint-Pierre-de-Chaillot in Paris. Neither his father nor his mother attended. His mother lived at Nice and said that she was too tired to travel. Maupassant had asked to be buried directly in the earth without a coffin. The authorities did not allow this. His body was placed in three coffins, one of pine, one of zinc, and one of oak. Zola, the publisher Paul Ollendorff, and the family's lawyer walked beside the coffin. Maupassant was buried in the Montparnasse Cemetery. Zola spoke at the grave. He said that Maupassant had become famous overnight and that nobody had even argued about his value. People had understood him, Zola said, "because he was clarity, simplicity and strength". Zola ended by saying that Maupassant's work would live. He said that future readers would love him for the song of love that he had sung to life. His parents and his brother's widow argued about what he had left. The yacht and La Guillette were sold. His mother lived for another ten years. She always denied that her sons had died from syphilis. Two unfinished novels, L'Angélus and L'Âme étrangère, were published after Maupassant's death. Maupassant published about three hundred stories in newspapers and reviews. In a complete edition, they fill more than 2,600 pages. Most of them are short, usually no more than 3,000 words, because they had to fit into one issue of a daily newspaper. In the Pléiade edition, only about forty stories are longer than ten pages. A usual story is six or seven pages long, or about 2,000 words. About ten stories are much longer, with more than 8,000 words. These longer stories, called nouvelles in French, are among his best works. "Boule de suif" itself has about 13,000 words. Maupassant put only about seventy per cent of his stories into the fifteen collections published during his lifetime. He left out nearly a hundred stories. Later editors published them again in many different groups. Early critics grouped the stories by subject. There were stories about Normandy farmers, Paris clerks and shopkeepers, war, love, madness, fear, and many other subjects. The index of one complete edition lists 79 themes. Together, they show a dangerous and cruel world: divorce, duels, madness, incest, drunkenness, abandoned women, and murdered children. His characters come from every social class. They include farmers and politicians, rich women and prostitutes, nuns and priests, servants, soldiers and sailors, nobles, criminals, and people with mental illness. A French handbook published in 1992 divides his world into six parts: the provinces, Paris, fear, women, nature, and the "elsewhere" of travel and dreams. Maupassant gave a voice to people whom literature had often ignored. Some of his stories about incest, rape, and abortion can still shock readers. Two worlds appear in most of Maupassant's stories. The first is Normandy, the country of his childhood. Here live the farmers, servants, fishermen, and small landowners of stories such as "Le Papa de Simon", "La Ficelle", "Aux champs", "Le Petit Fût", and "Toine". Maupassant knew their way of life very well. He also wrote their way of speaking with care and affection. "Le Papa de Simon" (1879) tells the story of a boy without a father who finds one in a kind blacksmith. It is the earliest example of Maupassant's mature art. It is a gentle story, written in a style close to that of Alphonse Daudet, but it already shows Maupassant's gift for choosing the right words. The Normandy farmers in his later stories are harder people. They are often greedy, clever in a dishonest way, and cruel. Their tragedies may begin over only a few francs. The second world is Paris. Its characters include small clerks in government ministries, shopkeepers, women who work on the streets, and young men who row on the Seine on Sundays. Maupassant had spent eight years working in a ministry. Stories such as "L'Héritage", "En famille", and "Promenade" show the dull and unfree life of the minor official. Sometimes they also show his quiet courage. His novels are also set in places that he knew well: the country houses of Normandy, the newspapers of Paris, and spa towns. Later, after he became rich, the drawing rooms of Paris society and the villas of the Riviera also entered his work. Maupassant did not invent the modern French short story. Prosper Mérimée had written realistic and violent stories fifty years earlier. The fantastic stories of E. T. A. Hoffmann and Edgar Allan Poe had also been translated into French. Turgenev was perhaps the writer who influenced Maupassant most strongly. From the Russian writer, Maupassant learned how to create a place and a mood with only a few carefully chosen details. He also learned how to show the sadness of ordinary lives. One thing that makes Maupassant different from many writers of his time is his clear story line. His stories are short and easy to follow. They are full of feeling, but the writer usually keeps his distance from the characters. They are modern, but they also continue the old tradition of the tale. The British scholar Trevor Harris has shown how important repetition is in Maupassant's work. The same kinds of people, images, and situations return from one story to another, like reflections in a hall of mirrors. His newspaper articles also help readers to understand his fiction. One of the most striking things about Maupassant's stories is the way they are told. More than 160 of them are presented as stories told aloud, or sometimes written down, by a character. In about half of these stories, a narrator inside the story tells something to a group of listeners: friends after dinner, hunters around a fire, or travellers in a train. This form of storytelling is very old. It can be found in the Decameron and the Thousand and One Nights. It allows Maupassant to keep some distance from the story. It also lets him describe events that he could not have seen himself. Other stories are told through letters or a diary, as in "Le Horla". The critic W. M. Landers wrote that a short story must waste nothing. Everything in it must work towards one main point. In Maupassant's stories, this point is often a crisis, an event that suddenly changes a person's life. The reader often learns the full truth only at the end, and the ending can be a surprise. The critic André Vial compared these endings to the crack of a whip. The most famous example is "La Parure" ("The Necklace", 1884). Mathilde Loisel is the pretty wife of a poor clerk. She borrows a diamond necklace from a rich friend so that she can wear it to a ball. She loses the necklace. Mathilde and her husband buy another one like it and spend ten years working hard to pay for it. At the end, Mathilde learns that the necklace she lost was false. It was worth no more than 500 francs. The story is built so carefully that the cruel ending seems natural rather than a simple trick. Its first sentence recalls Flaubert's Madame Bovary. Like Emma Bovary, Mathilde is a woman destroyed by her dreams of wealth and luxury. Maupassant often leaves the most important things unsaid. The reader must understand them from small clues in the story. He gives no moral lesson and does not spend many pages explaining the feelings of his characters. However, his art is not only about saying little. The Swedish scholar Hans Färnlöf has shown that Maupassant sometimes repeats and develops an idea at length. This makes the reader feel the full importance of one moment in a person's life. In this view, the short story is not simply a small novel. It is a complete telling of one important moment. "Boule de suif" is the story that made Maupassant famous, and it is still his best-known work. The first nine pages describe the French defeat and the German occupation of Rouen. The story shows tired soldiers who look almost like bandits, officers who think too highly of themselves, and townspeople who are eager to please the German soldiers and return to business. Only after this does the main character appear. Ten travellers leave Rouen in a coach for Dieppe. They hope to continue to Le Havre, which the Germans have not occupied. The group has three rich couples, two nuns, a loud democrat named Cornudet, and a prostitute called Boule de suif. Several characters were based partly on real people. Boule de suif herself is often said to have been based on Adrienne Legay, a prostitute from Rouen who really had that nickname and died in 1892. The businessman Carré-Lamadon recalls Pouyer-Quertier, a mayor of Rouen. Parts of Cornudet's character may come from Maupassant's uncle, Charles Cord'homme, who is said to have told him the story. At first, the rich travellers refuse to speak to Boule de suif. Later, when they become hungry, they eat her food. At an inn in Tôtes, on the road to Dieppe, a Prussian officer stops the coach. He says that he will allow the travellers to leave only if Boule de suif spends the night with him. She refuses because she loves her country. The other travellers want to continue their journey. For two days, they put pressure on her until she finally agrees. The next morning, they reject her again. She cries in the coach while Cornudet whistles the Marseillaise. On a first reading, most readers feel pity for Boule de suif and anger towards her false companions. On a second reading, they may notice that Maupassant also shows her faults and gives some real good qualities to the other travellers. The story can also be read as having a wider meaning. It is about war between countries and between social classes. It is also about people who help an occupying army and those who resist it. After 1940, "Boule de suif" became a model for many French stories and films about the German occupation during the Second World War. Another famous war story, "Deux amis" ("Two Friends", 1883), tells of two friends in Paris during the Prussian siege. They go fishing outside the city walls and are shot by the Prussians. The linguist A. J. Greimas, a specialist in the study of signs, wrote a whole book about this story of only a few pages. He studied it sentence by sentence. Two of Maupassant's fifteen collections can show the different kinds of stories that he wrote. Les Sœurs Rondoli was published in July 1884, during the most productive period of his life. It brings together stories first published in newspapers between 1882 and 1884. The book contains many different kinds of stories. There are strange stories about death, such as "Lui ?" and "Suicides", and cruel or comic stories about Normandy, such as "Le Petit Fût". There are comic stories about sex, such as "Les Sœurs Rondoli" and "La Patronne", sharp pictures of society, such as "Mon oncle Sosthène" and "Le Parapluie", and an adventure in a distant country, "Châli". Marie-Claire Bancquart notes that in all these stories Maupassant keeps only the details that are useful. He uses few unnecessary details and little dialogue. Le Rosier de Madame Husson appeared in 1888. The title story takes place at Gisors, a small town in Normandy. A respectable woman wants to reward a pure and good life with a crown of roses and some money. Some villages gave this prize to a "rose girl", or rosière. She cannot find a girl who seems pure enough, so the prize is given to a simple young man named Isidore. He becomes the town's "rose boy", or rosier. Isidore uses the money to get drunk, and after that he never stops drinking. For Louis Forestier, the story makes fun of the awkward and false ways in which people try to appear good. Benjamin Britten later made a comic opera from the story. From 1875 onward, the fear of becoming mad appears again and again in Maupassant's stories. Maupassant believed in science and progress. For two years, he attended the lessons of the doctor Jean-Martin Charcot at the Salpêtrière hospital in Paris. Doctors there studied illnesses of the nervous system. Marie-Claire Bancquart has argued against the old idea that Maupassant's fantastic stories were simply caused by his own illness. In her view, these stories use the new ideas about the mind that existed in his time. Madness was no longer seen only as a sudden break. It could also be seen as a slow change in a person's mind and character. Nafissa Schasch calls Maupassant's fantastic world "dark" (ténébreux). She argues that it comes from the darker side of a person divided between opposite feelings. In stories such as "La Peur", "Lui?", "La Main", "Qui sait?", and "Le Horla", Maupassant shows the fear caused by things that science cannot yet explain. Even these stories take place in a clearly described real world and follow a clear order of events. "Le Horla" is his best-known story of this kind. Maupassant wrote two versions, one in 1886 and another in 1887. Only the second version appeared in a book, as the title story of a collection. A man who lives alone in a house near Rouen begins to believe that an invisible being drinks his water at night. Then the being begins to control his will. An invisible hand picks a rose, opens doors, and turns the pages of a book. The man gives the creature the name "the Horla". One day, he sees its shape because it stands between him and his mirror and hides his reflection. In the first version, the man tells his story to a doctor, and other people have seen some of the events. The second version is three times longer and is written as a diary. There is no outside witness. Because of this, the reader cannot decide whether the narrator is mad or whether the invisible being is real. At the end, the narrator sets fire to his house and thinks about suicide. Suicide is a common ending in Maupassant's stories. Maupassant published six novels between 1883 and 1890. He also left two more unfinished when he stopped writing in 1891. All six novels first appeared in parts in newspapers. Critics generally received them well, and they sold well. For readers of his own time, these books showed that Maupassant was more than a writer of short pieces for newspapers. Compared with the novels of Balzac, Dickens, or Zola, Maupassant's novels are short. They also became shorter with time. All six together are shorter than Victor Hugo's Les Misérables. Two of them are still widely read: Bel-Ami and Pierre et Jean. Une vie is also still well known. The American scholar Edward D. Sullivan published the first full study of Maupassant's novels in 1954. He followed Maupassant's long search for the best way to build a novel. Sullivan calls the first three books "novels by addition". They are built by adding one event after another. Pierre et Jean is a "novel by extension", because it develops one main situation. The last two are "novels by introspection", because they study the thoughts and feelings of their characters. The French scholar Francis Marcoin has called the six novels "six journeys into the blue". In each novel, there is a moment when a character dreams of escaping into the blue sky or sea, away from a life that has become like a prison. Maupassant first told Flaubert about his plan for a novel in a letter dated 10 December 1877. The subtitle of Une vie is L'humble vérité, or "the humble truth". Jeanne is the daughter of a Norman baron. She leaves her convent school at the age of seventeen, full of dreams. Her father wants her to be "happy, good, upright and tender". She marries a handsome neighbour, Julien de Lamare. He soon shows himself to be mean and unfaithful. He first has an affair with Jeanne's maid and later with one of Jeanne's friends. Jeanne then gives all her love to her son, Paul. He grows up and ruins her financially. At the end, Jeanne is old and poor. She lives in a small house with her former maid Rosalie. In the last sentence of the novel, Rosalie tells Jeanne that life is never as good or as bad as people think. In French: "la vie, voyez-vous, ça n'est jamais si bon ni si mauvais qu'on croit". The novel treats time in a special way. The two years described in chapters VII to X are full of events and conversations. Later chapters pass over many long and empty years in only a few pages. The same small events also return again and again. The first chapter shows Jeanne free and leaving the convent. The last shows her sitting still, shut inside a time that seems to have stopped. The novel also shows how girls of that period were taught to believe in happiness but were not taught how to fight against difficulties or how to suffer. Critics have often compared Une vie with Madame Bovary. Both novels tell the story of a woman's hopes for marriage and how those hopes fail. Bel-Ami is Maupassant's longest novel. It also gives one of his widest pictures of French society. The book has a strong main character, and Maupassant wanted it to stand beside the great novels of Balzac, Stendhal, Flaubert, and Zola. The novel begins when Georges Duroy leaves a cheap restaurant with the change from a five-franc coin in his pocket. Duroy is the son of Norman innkeepers and a former soldier in Algeria. He is poor and hungry in Paris. An old friend finds him a job at a newspaper. Duroy cannot write well, but he is handsome, and women help him. First there is the intelligent Madeleine Forestier, whom he marries after her husband dies. Then there is the gentle Clotilde de Marelle and the wife of the newspaper owner. Finally, Duroy runs away with the owner's young daughter, Suzanne, and marries her. Clotilde's small daughter Laurine gives him the nickname "Bel-Ami", or "handsome friend", and everyone begins to use it. Many famous novels about ambitious young men, from Stendhal's Le Rouge et le noir to Balzac's Illusions perdues, end with the young man's failure. Bel-Ami ends with Duroy's success, in a splendid wedding at the Madeleine church. The novel also makes fun of the Paris newspaper world, politics, and the money made from French colonies in North Africa. Duroy's newspaper articles about Algeria are similar to the letters that Maupassant himself sent from Algeria in 1881. Jean-Marie Sapet has shown that Maupassant also reused parts of his own newspaper articles in the novel. Many readers in 1885 believed that some characters were based on real people. They saw the journalist Aurélien Scholl behind Jacques Rival and the poet Théodore de Banville behind Norbert de Varenne. For these readers, a novel about current news also became a novel about real people hidden behind false names. Mont-Oriol takes place in a spa town in the Auvergne. A banker builds a new bathing resort on the land of a farmer. The novel combines a love story with criticism of the people who try to make money from the new spa, its advertising, and its doctors. Christiane, the banker's wife, is loved by a young man. He leaves her after she becomes pregnant. Critics have often given little attention to this novel. Pierre et Jean is much shorter than Maupassant's other five novels. It is a close study of jealousy inside one family in Le Havre. Jean, the younger son, receives a large inheritance from an old family friend. His brother Pierre, who is a doctor, slowly understands that Jean must really be the son of this friend. He also understands that their mother once had a lover. Jean receives both the money and the woman he wants to marry. Pierre cannot accept the family secret and leaves as a doctor on a ship. Maupassant said that this short book was a true novel because it studies the human mind in great depth. Sullivan calls it a small masterpiece, almost without a fault. He connects it with the question of uncertain fatherhood, which appears often in Maupassant's work. Pierre's disgust with the small world of Le Havre has reminded some critics of Roquentin, the main character of Jean-Paul Sartre's La Nausée. Sartre's novel was published fifty years later and is also set in a town similar to Le Havre. Pierre et Jean begins with the essay "Le Roman", in which Maupassant explains his ideas about fiction (see below). Maupassant's last two novels take place among the rich people of Paris who have little need to work. In Fort comme la mort ("Strong as Death"), the famous painter Olivier Bertin has loved the countess de Guilleroy for many years. When her daughter Annette grows up, Bertin falls in love with the young woman because she looks like her mother when she was young. Bertin cannot accept that he is growing old. He is knocked down by a bus in the street and dies. In Notre cœur ("Our Heart"), André Mariolle loves Michèle de Burne, a beautiful woman who welcomes artists into her salon but cannot truly love anyone. Mariolle finds comfort with a simple servant girl named Élisabeth. The novel ends with a promise, "Je t'aimerai comme ici", which has one meaning for Mariolle and another for Michèle. Christopher Lloyd finds the love problems in these two novels somewhat tiring. However, he notes that their close study of jealousy points forward to Marcel Proust and his story of Swann and Odette. These last novels also contain many artists. Notre cœur includes the musician Massival and the sculptor Prédolé. Fort comme la mort has the painter Bertin. Joseph-Marc Bailbé has studied these characters. He concludes that, for Maupassant, a true artist must first be a person who feels the world strongly through the senses. When Maupassant stopped writing, he left about fifty pages of L'Angélus. The novel is set in Normandy during the terrible winter of 1870. In the story, Prussian soldiers badly treat a pregnant woman on Christmas night. She later gives birth in a stable. The last pages that Maupassant wrote contain a curse against God, whom he calls "the eternal murderer". A second unfinished novel, L'Âme étrangère, also survives in only a few pages. Maupassant began his career as a poet. However, his poems are much less admired than his stories, and he knew this himself. His only book of poetry, Des vers (1880), contains poems from his youth, including "Au bord de l'eau" and "Vénus rustique". His plays are also little read today. His short play in verse, Histoire du vieux temps, was performed in 1879. Musotte (1891) was adapted from one of his stories. La Paix du ménage was performed in 1893, when Maupassant was already living in the clinic. Successful plays could make a great deal of money, but Maupassant's plays were not among his best works. His three travel books are more important. Au soleil (1884), Sur l'eau (1888), and La Vie errante (1890) were made from articles that had first appeared in newspapers. Maupassant carefully changed these articles into longer and more thoughtful books. Sur l'eau is the most personal of all his writings. It describes a journey on his yacht, but it is really a book of thoughts about life, death, society, and himself. It contains his famous statement that he had desired everything and enjoyed nothing. In these books, Maupassant also gives his views on French rule in North Africa. He thought that it was unjust and badly managed. He did not believe that it would give a better life to the Arab and Berber peoples, although he admired the courage of the settlers and soldiers. His newspaper articles, or chroniques, number about two hundred and fill several volumes. Maupassant was a very good observer of the society around him, but his opinions were often one-sided. In "La Lysistrata moderne" (1880), for example, he repeated the ideas of Arthur Schopenhauer and other men about the supposed weakness of women's minds. In "Adieu mystères" (1881), he supported science against belief in magic and mystery. However, in "Un miracle" (1886), he attacked Pasteur's new treatment for rabies. Maupassant wrongly said that rabies did not exist in human beings. A later study of 6,000 patients showed that Pasteur was right. Maupassant wrote nothing about the art of the short story. However, he wrote quite a lot about the novel. His most important text on this subject is "Le Roman", the essay placed at the beginning of Pierre et Jean in 1888. In this essay, he says that a realist writer does not simply copy reality. The writer chooses a small number of important details and puts them together in such a way that the reader can feel the deeper and hidden meaning of events. Every person sees the world through his or her own senses and character. Because of this, Maupassant writes that "great artists are those who impose their particular illusion on humanity". He therefore says that talented realists should really be called "illusionists", because they create an illusion of reality. He preferred novels that show what people are like through their actions instead of explaining their thoughts at great length. In the same essay, he also described what Flaubert had taught him: patience, careful observation, and the search for the one word that fits exactly. In an article of 1883, Maupassant had already written that the novelist is not a moral teacher. The writer's task is not to correct people. It is only to observe and describe them. In another essay, "L'Évolution du roman au XIXe siècle" (1889), Maupassant rejected popular adventure writers such as Eugène Sue and Alexandre Dumas as simple entertainers. He was more interested in novels that describe the life and habits of society. Above all, he admired Flaubert's Madame Bovary, which he saw as a model of exact observation and careful style. Sullivan says that one main idea guides Maupassant's writing: the writer shows things but does not explain them. Maupassant's own style follows this rule. He uses as few words as possible. His novels are short, and his descriptions are brief. The scholar John Raymond Dugan has shown that Maupassant's descriptions are never only pictures. They are usually seen through the eyes of a character, and they always help the story. Maupassant also keeps himself out of his fiction. His narrators and characters do not speak for him. Readers who want to know what he really thought have to study each story carefully. Alain Quesnel notes that Maupassant's method often depends on suggestion. Love scenes are told in only a few words, and portraits are drawn with only a few details. For example, the reader learns little about the appearance of Georges Duroy except that he has a moustache. Maupassant did not believe in God. Critics have often described him as a follower of Schopenhauer, the German philosopher who taught that life is full of suffering and that the desire to live can itself become a trap. Schopenhauer's ideas became better known in France in 1880 through Jean Bourdeau's translation of his Pensées, maximes et fragments. In 1884, Maupassant wrote to a young admirer that he did not have "an ounce of poetry" in him. He said that he looked at everything without interest and was deeply bored for two-thirds of his time. Everything, he added, was only boredom, farce, and misery. This dark view appears throughout his work. His families are often broken by unfaithful husbands and wives and by lies. His marriages are usually unhappy. Children are abandoned by their fathers, and the child without a father appears again and again, from "Le Papa de Simon" to Pierre et Jean and Musotte. His farmers are often hard and greedy. His clerks are weak and afraid. His rich people are vain and idle. Death, madness, and suicide appear at the end of many stories. However, his view of life is not completely dark. Many pages in his work show a strong physical joy in nature: the sea, rivers, sunlight, and the smell of the woods. Thérèse and Fabrice Thumerel call this his pantheism, the idea that nature itself has something sacred in it. For Maupassant, nature is like a temple, and people enter it through their senses. He kept Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du mal beside his bed. In a letter of January 1881, he wrote that he loved the bodies of women in the same way that he loved grass, rivers, and the sea. He liked to present himself as a kind of primitive being, closer to animals than to civilised people. His cold and bored manner was also partly a way of protecting himself from people who were too curious about him. In some of his newspaper articles, Maupassant wrote that women were less intelligent than men and were too strongly guided by feelings. His fiction often gives a different picture. Women are frequently among the strongest and most sympathetic characters. Boule de suif is one example. Another is the old farm woman in "La Mère Sauvage", who burns four Prussian soldiers alive to take revenge for the death of her son. Maupassant was especially interested in the difficult situations in which women could become trapped: unhappy marriages, unwanted pregnancies, poverty, and the false goodness of "respectable" people. Money is another major subject in his work. Maupassant knew what it was like to count every franc, and he never forgot the experience. In the France of his time, poor people could easily lose everything they had. Many of his stories show the small but serious tragedies caused by poverty. Maupassant himself was very good at business. He knew the value of his writing and made his publishers pay well for it. Unlike Victor Hugo or Tolstoy, he never wanted to become a reformer or a prophet. He observed the suffering of poor people in France and Africa with calm sympathy, but he did not try to change society. He refused to belong to any political party or group. He wrote that the one thing people hate in both religion and politics is true independence of mind. Maupassant also watched social position very closely. He laughed at titles and decorations, but he was fascinated by the ways in which people could rise or fall in society. His picture of the Paris newspaper world in Bel-Ami, and of government offices in many of his stories, gives one of the clearest pictures of French society under the Third Republic. Maupassant's readers and friends sincerely mourned his death. Some other writers were less kind. Edmond de Goncourt attacked the large amount of money Maupassant had earned and what he saw as his lack of taste, even in the days after the funeral. At least five writers of his time, including Zola, put unkind pictures of Maupassant into their novels. Other critics admired his work. In the 1890s, Ferdinand Brunetière understood that Maupassant's clear and simple style was the result of real art. Anatole France praised the strength and shortness of his style. In 1897, a bust of Maupassant by Raoul Verlet was placed in the Parc Monceau in Paris. For a long time, serious French critics saw Maupassant as a very good storyteller and a useful writer for schoolchildren, but not as a great artist like Flaubert. The American scholar Artine Artinian studied French criticism of Maupassant from 1880 to 1940. He asked 147 writers what they thought of him. Most French writers, including André Gide and Paul Valéry, saw him mainly as a very skilful craftsman. Foreign novelists such as Thomas Mann admired him more. Gide called Maupassant "a remarkable and impeccable workman of letters", or a perfect craftsman. The words can be read as praise, but they can also suggest that Maupassant was only a craftsman and not a great artist. In 1966, the critic Paul Ignotus described the problem in another way. He thought that only Tolstoy was better than Maupassant at understanding people and making readers see them clearly. Yet other writers never treated Maupassant as a master. This view began to change in the 1950s. André Vial's study Guy de Maupassant et l'art du roman (1954) showed how much careful art was hidden behind Maupassant's simple style. Hundreds of studies followed in many countries. Today Maupassant is one of the most widely read French classic writers. A survey by the Ministry of Culture in 1999 placed him among the ten favourite writers of French readers between the ages of fifteen and twenty. In 2012, Le Figaro reported that Maupassant had been the best-selling classic French author from 2004 to 2011. He was ahead of Molière, Camus, and Hugo, with 3.8 million copies sold. Many of these books were bought for schools.

Arthur Miller (October 17, 1915 – February 10, 2005) was an American playwright. His best known plays are All My Sons, Death of a Salesman and The Crucible. He wrote for the movie The Misfits while married to Marilyn Monroe. She acted in this movie. Arthur Miller's family was a rich Jewish family from New York City. During the Great Depression in the 1930s, his family's business was forced to close down and they lost all their money. Because Miller wanted to go to university, he had to work in a warehouse. He studied economics and history at the University of Michigan as well as working for the school newspaper which helped him learn how to write plays. He married Mary Slaughterhouse in 1940. In Miller’s childhood, his family had money issues. That influenced his writings. He often includes the theme of financial problems which is a result of everything he had seen as a child. Another thing that influenced him a lot was Greek literature. Miller once said that he liked to read Greek literature for ideas to write about. The readers are able to see it in his writing style and the element he uses in his writing. In 1936 his very first play, No Villain, was produced and gained a huge success. The play won him a Hopwood Award and people started to get to know him. In 1944, Miller had his first play in the theater on Broadway in New York City, called The Man Who Had All the Luck. Not many people liked it so this play was stopped after one week. However, three years later, his play All My Sons became very popular. This play won the Pulitzer Prize for drama. In 1949, he wrote Death of a Salesman, a story about the American Dream, it addresses the loss of identity and a man who's unable to accept change within himself and society. In 1953, he wrote The Crucible, a story about the Salem Witch Trials. He wrote this because of the McCarthyism of the 1950s, the fear that communism would take over America. A few years later, Miller was blamed for being a communist himself. He had to answer questions from the House Un-American Activities Committee, a group that Senator Joseph McCarthy made. Miller was an atheist. In 1956, Miller divorced Mary Slaughterhouse so he could marry the actress Marilyn Monroe. During this marriage, he wrote for the movie The Misfits. Monroe acted in this movie. After five years of marriage, Monroe divorced him. The following year, Miller married again. The photographer Inge Morath was his third wife, and they were together until she died in 2002. They had two children. His son, Daniel, was born with Down syndrome. Miller put him in a hospital and did not want to see him again. His daughter, Rebecca, who married actor Daniel Day-Lewis, asked Miller several times to contact his hospitalised son. In 1964, Miller produced the play After The Fall that talks about the marriage with Marilyn Monroe. Later on, during the mid 1990s, he wrote three new plays, including The Ride Down Mt. Morgan, The Last Yankee and Broken Glasses. On February 10, 2005, Miller died of heart disease. He was 89. Miller's ideas influence the society a lot.
