For example, the way of writing has changed a lot. He often writes about the experience of being human in a very raw but very loving way. He once said that “Maybe all one can do is hope to end up with the right regrets” which later on has a huge impact on people. Another influence on society is that the way people write stage plays have changed a lot. People tend to focus on characters more than anything else. Miller believes that “the theater is so endlessly fascinating because it's so accidental (happens by chance). It's so much like life.” It reflects on his writing because he likes to write more on the bonds between individual and society rather than only character.

Vladimir Nabokov (April 22, 1899 – July 2, 1977) was a Russian-American writer. He wrote his first books in Russian, and after he moved to the United States, he wrote in English. His most famous book is Lolita, but others have also become famous, such as Pnin, Pale Fire, and Ada or Ardor. Nabokov was born in Saint Petersburg, Russia, the first of five children. In 1919, he and his family went to Europe. In 1945, he became an American citizen. He died in Montreux, Switzerland. Nabokov's father was a lawyer and politician. As a child, Vladimir learned Russian, English, and French. After the October Revolution, the family moved a few times, but settled in Berlin in 1920. Two years later, his father was shot and killed by mistake, because he had blocked the person the gunman was trying to murder. His mother and sister moved to Prague, but Vladimir stayed in Berlin. He wrote for other Russians who had left Russia to live there. He met Véra Slonin, a woman from a Jewish-Russian family, in 1923. They married in 1925. In 1934, they had their only child, Dmitri. In 1937, Nabokov started to look for another job. He left for France that year, and his family followed. They all fled to America in 1940, except his brother Sergei, who died in a Nazi concentration camp. Nabokov was an expert on butterflies. As a child he had read books by entomologist Maria Sibylla Merian which he found in the attic of his family's country home in Vyra. During the 1940s, he was a research fellow in zoology. He organized the butterfly collection of the Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard University. His specialty was the tribe Polyommatini of the family Lycaenidae. The genus Nabokovia was named after him in honor of this work, as were a number of butterfly and moth species (e.g. many species in the genera Madeleinea and Pseudolucia have names alluding to Nabokov or names from his novels). In 1967, Nabokov commented: "The pleasures and rewards of literary inspiration are nothing beside the rapture of discovering a new organ under the microscope or an undescribed species on a mountainside in Iran or Peru. It is not improbable that had there been no revolution in Russia, I would have devoted myself entirely to lepidopterology and never written any novels at all".

Joanne Rowling, ( "rolling"; born 31 July 1965), writing under the pen names J. K. Rowling and Robert Galbraith, is a British writer. She wrote the Harry Potter books. She only uses the name J. K. Rowling for her books: the "K" stands for "Kathleen", which was the first name of her grandmother. Rowling was born 31 July 1965 at Chipping Sodbury Cottage Hospital in Chipping Sodbury, Yate, Gloucesterhire England. She grew up in Tutshill, Gloucestershire, and went to school at Wyedean Comprehensive. She earned a degree in French and Classics at the University of Exeter. She worked at Amnesty International in London in 1990. The original idea for Harry Potter came to her on a train that was delayed for four hours in 1990. She moved to Portugal to teach English in the same year. She married Jorge Arantes in October 1992. They had her first child, Jessica in 1993. The marriage ended in divorce and Rowling moved to Edinburgh, Scotland. Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (British version) (American version: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone) was first published in the United Kingdom in 1997. She married Dr. Neil Murray in 2001. She had a second child, David, in 2003, and a third, Mackenzie, in January 2005. Rowling claims to have been inspired by Christianity. Rowling has received strong criticism for her outspoken public views on matters around transgender people, which she started to talk about in 2020. Rowling has won many awards for the Harry Potter series of books and has earned over $1 billion. The last book of the series, Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows, was released on 21 July 2007. Due to the popularity of the books, Rowling has become very wealthy. The books have sold over 500 million copies. Rowling has written many books about the magic in Harry's world, such as 'Quidditch Through the Ages' and 'Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them'. Additionally, she has written other books targeting adults, the first of which is called The Casual Vacancy. The Cuckoo's Calling was published in April 2013, under the pen name Robert Galbraith, and its sequel, called The Silkworm, followed in June 2014. In 2016, people made an eighth book inspired by Harry Potter. This book was called Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. The book was the script for a play. J K Rowling's novels feature a teenage boy named Harry Potter who grows up in a normal world with his aunt, uncle and cousin Dudley. When he is eleven years old, he discovers that he is a wizard and attends a magical academy called Hogwarts school of witchcraft and wizardry, where Albus Dumbledore is headmaster. Harry discovers his past about a dark wizard and with the help from his best friends Ronald Weasley and Hermione Granger, he attempts to destroy the darkest wizard of all time, Voldemort, once and for all. He go's through a series of challenges with his friends, but in the end they defeat the darkest wizard. Akinwande Oluwole "Wole" Babatunde Soyinka (Yoruba: Akinwándé Oluwo̩lé Babátúndé S̩óyinká; born 13 July 1934) is a Nigerian playwright and poet. He was awarded the 1986 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first African to be honored in that category.

Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, essayist, poet and travel writer. He was born on 13 November 1850 and died on 3 December 1894. His parents were Thomas Stevenson, and Margaret Isabella Balfour. He spent much of his childhood sick in bed with lung trouble. He studied law in Edinburgh University, but later turned his interest to writing. Some of his best known works are Treasure Island, Kidnapped and Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll. He is the subject of several literature classes, especially his book KIDNAPPED for children aged 12 to 13 across the globe. The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886)

Walter "Walt" Whitman (May 31, 1819 – March 26, 1892) was an American poet, essayist and journalist. He was an important American poet of the 19th century. His most famous collection of poems is Leaves of Grass, which was first published in 1855 with his own money. The work was an attempt at reaching out to the common person. Whitman kept adding to this book right up until he died of pneumonia, in 1892. It was controversial because readers thought it was obscene. It included some sexuality. Whitman was either bisexual or homosexual. However, there is disagreement about whether Whitman had actual sexual experiences with men. Whitman was deeply influenced by deism. He denied any one faith was more important than another, and embraced all religions equally. Whitman first tried writing in many different popular genres. In 1850, he began writing Leaves of Grass, a collection of poetry which he would continue working on until his death. Whitman wanted to write an epic that was clearly American, using free verse. At the end of June 1855, Whitman surprised his brothers with the first copies of Leaves of Grass. His brother George "didn't think it worth reading". Whitman paid for the publication of the first version of Leaves of Grass himself and had it printed at a local print shop. A total of 795 copies were printed. The first page was an image of Whitman, but he doesn't write his name until 500 lines into the body of the text. Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote a kind five-page letter to Whitman and praised the book to friends. The first edition of Leaves of Grass was very popular, but was some people didn't like the "obscene" or offensive parts of the poetry. In the months after the first edition of Leaves of Grass, people became more upset about the sexual themes. Because of this, the publisher almost did not release the second edition. In 1856, 20 new poems were added. Different versions of Leaves of Grass continued to be published throughout the rest of Whitman's life. Many famous writers like Amos Bronson Alcott and Henry David Thoreau liked the work enough to visit Whitman.

Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde (16 October 1854 – 30 November 1900) was an Irish writer, poet and playwright. He wrote The Picture of Dorian Gray, and the plays Salomé, The Importance of Being Earnest, An Ideal Husband, and Lady Windermere's Fan. Wilde was bisexual. He had a wife and two children. He had an affair with a younger man named Lord Alfred Douglas. This affair ruined his life. Wilde was born in Ireland in 1854. He went to school at Trinity College in Dublin. Then he went to the Magdalen College (part of Oxford University.) In London, he worked as a journalist for four years. He was very well known in his time. This was because he dressed well and was very good at conversation. He was also well known because he wrote a novel called The Picture of Dorian Gray. He also wrote plays. In 1891, he wrote a play called Salomé. He wrote it in French while living in Paris. No one could perform it in England, because there were characters from the Bible in it. This did not discourage him. He then wrote four comedic plays in the early 1890s. He was one of the most successful playwrights of the time. His masterpiece was the play called The Importance of Being Earnest. When he was very famous, he sued his lover's father for libel (lying about someone in print). There were many trials. In the end, the court sentenced Wilde to two years of work in Reading Gaol (jail). The crime was gross indecency (sexual contact with other men). After he went to prison, his wife went to Switzerland with their children. She changed their last names to Holland. While he was in prison, he wrote a long letter called De Profundis. De Profundis was about his experiences during the trials. It was very sad compared to his earlier work. When he got out of prison, he went to France. He never went back to the British Isles. In France, he wrote The Ballad of Reading Gaol, which was a poem about prison. It was his last work. In Paris, he lived in a hotel. He did not have very much money, or very many friends. He died of cerebral meningitis (swelling in his brain) in Paris. He was forty-six. Before he died, he said, "My wallpaper and I are fighting a duel to the death. One of us has got to go".p546 Wilde was in a romantic relationship with Lord Alfred Douglas. Douglas was the son of the Marquess of Queensberry. Queensberry argued a lot with his son. He spoke to Wilde and Douglas several times about their relationship. In June of 1894, Queensberry visited Wilde with no warning. Queensberry threatened to beat up Wilde if he saw Wilde with his son in a restaurant again. The Marquess of Queensberry left Wilde a calling card on February 18, 1895. On the card he wrote: "For Oscar Wilde, posing as a sodomite". Sodomy (men having sex with other men) was a crime. This note accused Wilde of having committed a crime. Because of this, Wilde sued him for libel (lying about someone else in print). His friends thought this was a bad idea, but Douglas encouraged him. In the trial, Queensberry only had to prove that Wilde had posed as a sodomite. But he also presented evidence that suggested Wilde had committed sexual acts with male prostitues. On the advice of his lawyer, Wilde withdrew his case. The court decided Queensberry was not guilty. They thought Queensberry was telling the truth when he wrote that Wilde was posing as a sodomite. Because of the Libel Act of 1843, Wilde had to pay Queensberry's lawyers. After this, Wilde was declared bankrupt. Wilde left court. The government wanted to arrest him for sodomy and gross indecency. His friends told him to try to flee to France, but his mother said he should stay in England. The government put him in prison before his trial. Douglas visited him daily, until Wilde told him to go to Paris to avoid punishment. Wilde's trial began on April 26, 1895. He pled not guilty. During the trial, he spoke about "the love that dare not speak its name". He described it as strong love between an older and a younger man. He said it was misunderstood and that it was the reason he was on trial. Saying these things was not helpful, because it convinced the jury that he had sex with men. The jury could not decide what to do. His lawyer got the court to agree on a bail. Reverend Stewart Headlam paid his bail, so he could leave prison. Wilde went into hiding at his friends' house. The lawyer for the government wanted to give up the case, but many people knew about it. Another government lawyer thought it was too well known to give up.p435 Wilde went to court again. The court sentenced him to (made him do) two years of work in prison. They also sentenced another man, named Alfred Taylor. The judge thought it was not harsh enough, but it was illegal to keep him in prison for longer. Wilde tried to respond to the judge, but others in the courtroom yelled "Shame", so that no one could hear him. I have the simplest tastes. I am always satisfied with the best. A thing is not necessarily true because a man dies for it. Consistency is the last refuge of the unimaginative. A poet can survive everything but a misprint. We have really everything in common with America nowadays, except, of course, language. On George Bernard Shaw: An excellent man: he has no enemies, and none of his friends like him. Hard work is simply the refuge of people who have nothing whatever to do. Life imitates art far more than art imitates Life. Anybody can make history. Only a great man can write it. Truth, in the matters of religion, is simply the opinion that has survived. The one duty we owe to history is to rewrite it. I can resist everything except temptation. (Lord Darlington in Lady Windermere's Fan) Life is far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it. (Lord Darlington in Lady Windermere's Fan) We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars. (Lord Darlington in Lady Windermere's Fan) What a pity that in life we only get our lessons when they are of no use to us. (Lady Windermere) In this world there are only two tragedies. One is not getting what one wants, and the other is getting it. (Mr Dumby) Experience is the name everyone gives to their mistakes. (Mr Dumby) The English country gentleman galloping after a fox—the unspeakable in full pursuit of the uneatable. (Lord Illingworth) Children love their parents. Eventually they come to judge them. Rarely do they forgive them. (Mrs. Arbuthnot) To love oneself is the beginning of a lifelong romance.

Adeline Virginia Woolf (;; 25 January 1882 28 March 1941) was an English modernist writer, essayist and feminist. She was born into a well-known family in London. Her father, Leslie Stephen, was a Victorian scholar. Her mother, born in India, was a favourite model of the Preraphaelite artists. Her sister, Vanessa Bell, was a painter. She had two brothers; one of them, Thoby, died in 1906. Her mother died when she was thirteen and four years later her half-sister Stella died. In these times Virginia started to have her psychological, or mental problems. She had bipolar disorder in the time when few people knew this illness and most thought she was strange. After the death of her mother, Leslie Stephen was not able to keep good relations in the family. Virginia and her sister Vanessa were sexually abused by their half-brothers George and Gerald. It affected Virginia for the rest of her life. In their childhood, all the Stephens children wrote diaries, but only Virginia kept it for her whole life (and after her death, lots of them were published). It was important for her when she was sexually abused, because there was no one with whom she could talk about it. In the diary, she could write everything. After her father's death, Virginia and her brothers and sister moved to Bloomsbury, London and there they became members of the famous group of artists called Bloomsbury Group. Here Virginia met writer Leonard Woolf (1880-1969), whom she was married to from 1912 until her death. Together, they moved to Richmond, where they opened a publishing office called Hogarth House Press, which later published all of Virginia's novels and essays. She was bisexual. When she was a teenager, she fell in love with Violet Dickinson and she wrote her lots of love letters. Violet probably never loved her back. Later, Virginia had a sexual relationship with Vita Sackville-West, a writer and a poet. Their letters, which have been published, show how deeply they were in love. Her most famous novels are Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse. She completed Mrs Dalloway in 1925. It is about a day in the life of an English woman called Clarissa Dalloway. Clarissa is throwing a party and she spends the entire day preparing. The story can appear stupid, but it is not so important in the book. What's more important are the feelings, the colours, or the mood of the story. To the Lighthouse was published in 1927 for the first time. It is about a family of Ramsays and its friends. These people are altogether spending a summer in Ramsay's house on an island. The youngest of the Ramsays' children, James, wants to go to the lighthouse, but they can't go there because of bad weather. In the next part of the book, James is ten years older and his father is taking him to the lighthouse, although he doesn't want to go there anymore. Virginia Woolf is also an author of these novels: Jacob's Room (1923), Orlando (1928) and The Waves (1931). She was a feminist and she wrote a few essays about women's position in the society, for example The Room of One's Own and Three Guineas. On 28 March 1941, Woolf drowned herself by filling her overcoat pockets with stones and walking into the River Ouse near her home. Her body was not found until 18 April. Her husband buried her cremated remains beneath an elm tree in the garden of Monk's House, their home in Rodmell, Sussex. In 1998, American writer Michael Cunningham wrote a novel in which she appeared, called The Hours (a winner of the Pulitzer award), which is best known because of the same named movie, in which the role of Virginia was played by actress Nicole Kidman. Kidman won an Oscar for her performance. Rather better known is Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf, in which her name is used as a catch-phrase by the lead couple. This was a play, and then a film starring Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton. The film won five Academy Awards.

William Butler Yeats (13 June 1865 – 28 January 1939) was an Irish poet, dramatist and mystic. He was born in Dublin, Ireland on 13 June 1865. He spent most of his time in Sligo and some time in London. Yeats' early poetry drew heavily on myth and legend. His later work had more to do with contemporary issues. One of his famous poems is called "Leda and the Swan". With Lady Gregory and others, he was one of the people who founded the Irish Literary Theatre and the Abbey Theatre. He was also interested in Hermeticism and Theosophy. He was a member of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. Yeats won the Nobel Prize in literature in 1923. He died in Menton, France on 28 January 1939.

Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o (; born James Ngugi; 5 January 1938 – 28 May 2025) was a Kenyan author and academic. He was called "East Africa's leading novelist". Ngũgĩ started writing in English, but later wrote mostly in Gikuyu. He wrote many novels, plays, short stories, and essays. His work were many different things. He wrote literary and social criticism, to children's books. He was the founder and editor of the Gikuyu-language journal Mũtĩiri. His short story The Upright Revolution: Or Why Humans Walk Upright has been translated into 100 languages. Ngũgĩ was a professor at the University of California, Irvine, Northwestern University, Yale University, and New York University. Ngũgĩ has often said to be a possible candidate for the Nobel Prize in Literature. He won the 2001 International Nonino Prize in Italy. In 2016, he won the Park Kyong-ni Prize. His children are also popular authors, including Mũkoma wa Ngũgĩ and Wanjiku wa Ngũgĩ. In March 2021, his work, The Perfect Nine, became the first work written in an indigenous African language to be longlisted for the International Booker Prize, with Ngũgĩ becoming the first nominee as both the author and translator of the book. Ngũgĩ died on 28 May 2025 at a hospital in Buford, Georgia at the age of 87. John Maxwell Coetzee (born 9 February 1940) is a South African-Australian novelist, essayist, linguist, literacy critic, activist and translator. He won the 2003 Nobel Prize in Literature. He has won the Booker Prize twice for The Life and Times of Michael K (1983) and Disgrace (1999). He writes his works in English, Afrikaans and Dutch. He moved to Australia in 2002 and became a citizen in 2006. Coetzee was born in Cape Town to Afrikaner parents. He studied at the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Cape Town. He lives in Adelaide, South Australia with his partner Dorothy Driver. He was married to Philippa Jubber from 1963 to 1980. They had two children, son Nicholas (died 1989) and daughter Gisela.

Nadine Gordimer (20 November 1923 – 13 July 2014) was a South African writer, political activist and recipient of the 1991 Nobel Prize in Literature. She was known as a woman "who through her magnificent epic writing has – in the words of Alfred Nobel – been of very great benefit to humanity". She was of Jewish descent. Gordimer's writing helped abolishing apartheid in South Africa. She was active in the anti-apartheid movement, joining the African National Congress during the days when the organization was banned. Later on she was also active in HIV/AIDS causes. Gordimer was one of 20 Nobel Laureates who signed the "Stockholm memorandum" at the 3rd Nobel Laureate Symposium on Global Sustainability in Stockholm, Sweden on 18 May 2011. Gordimer was born near Springs, a small town outside of Johannesburg on 20 November 1923. Gordimer died on 13 July 2014 at the age of 90.

Pearl S. Buck (June 26, 1892March 6, 1973) was an American writer. She lived in China for over 20 of 40 years and wrote about the country. Her book The Good Earth was a bestseller in 1931 and 1932. The book won a Pulitzer Prize in 1932. She won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Literature for a trilogy of novels about a Chinese farm family and biographies about her missionary parents. When she returned to the United States, she became active in charitable and political causes. Buck was born in Hillsboro, West Virginia. The letter "S" in her name, "Pearl S. Buck", stands for "Sydenstricker" because her father was named Absalom Sydenstricker. He was a Christian Presbyterian missionary to China, so Buck went to China a little while after she was born. She lived in China until 1934. Buck learned both Chinese and English. Her mother taught her English, and a tutor taught her Chinese language. When she lived in China, the Boxer Rebellion, in 1900-1901, changed her life and her family's life. Chinese friends stopped being their friends, and people from Europe and America came less to China to visit. In the early 1900s, Buck went to America to attend college. She went to Randolph-Macon Woman's College in Lynchburg, Virginia. She finished college in 1914. She then became a Presbyterian missionary like her father and returned to China. She left the missionary life in 1933, after the Fundamentalist-Modernist Controversy, where Fundamentalists (people who thought the Christian Bible should be taught as it was and that ideas such as Darwinism were wrong) and Modernists (people who thought Darwinism was okay) in the Presbyterian church did not like each other. Buck went back to China in 1914. She married a missionary named John Lossing Buck in 1917. In 1920, they had a daughter. She was named Carol. Carol had Phenylketonuria, a disorder that can cause mental retardation. Buck was not just a missionary in China. She did other work too. Buck and her family lived in Nanjing from 1920 to 1933. There is a college called Nanjing University in the city. That was where Buck's family lived. Pearl taught English Literature in two different colleges which would later become part of Nanjing University. Those colleges were the University of Nanjing and the National Central University. Buck's mother died in 1921 of a disease called sprue. Pearl went back to America in 1924 and got a Masters Degree from Cornell University in 1924. Pearl's family went back to China in 1925. Something called the Nanjing Incident, where soldiers of two armies fighting for the control of China attacked Nanjing, happened in 1927. Pearl had to hide from the soldiers. Pearl nearly died. American Navy ships rescued her. Pearl's family moved back to China a year after the Nanjing Incident happened. Then she started to write. She wrote because she needed money to support her family. In 1929, Pearl and her family went back to America to get Carol medical care. In America, her first book was published. It was called East Wind: West Wind. It was accepted for publication by a man named Richard Walsh, with whom Buck would later live after she left her husband. She went back to Nanjing later in 1929, and then she started to write The Good Earth. She finished the book in less than one year. After the Fundamentalist-Modernist Controversy, Pearl quit her job as missionary and moved back to America for good. She left her husband and he stayed in China. Buck divorced her husband in 1935. Richard Walsh helped her with the divorce, and she lived with him in Pennsylvania until he died in 1960. Buck died on March 6, 1973 of lung cancer in Danby, Vermont. She designed her tombstone. It had her birth name on it in Chinese. Pearl wrote many books and short stories about her political views and what she saw in her life. She wrote about women's rights, immigration, adoption, war, missionary work, and Asian life. Pearl did not like how adoption worked in America. The adoption companies in 1949 thought Asian children and children with mixed races were not able to be adopted. Pearl did not like that. Pearl created Welcome House, which was the first adoption company that had adoption internationally (between two different countries) and interracially (between races). However, some Asian kids were not able to be adopted. This led Pearl to create the Pearl S. Buck Foundation in 1964 to help those kids. It was later renamed Pearl S. Buck International. A year later she opened the Opportunity House (first called the Opportunity Center and Orphanage) in South Korea. Offices of the Opportunity House were later opened in Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines. She made Opportunity house to help Asian kids who were not able to live like other children. Her books were reviewed a lot. She got many positive reviews. One person said she had "beautiful prose" (prose is how a person writes something) but also said her style makes reading her books hard sometime. Some people like how Pearl's books made Americans understand more how Chinese people lived. The books Pearl wrote made Americans like China more and also made Americans like Japan less. In 1983 (ten years after Pearl died), the United States Postal Service made a postage stamp with Pearl on it. It was part of the 5 cent Great Americans Series. In 1999, the National Women's History Project made Pearl Buck an Honoree of the Women's History Month. The Good Earth was Buck's most popular book. It was a bestseller in 1931 and 1932. In 1932, Buck won the Pulitzer Prize for The Good Earth. She wrote many other books and short stories. She wrote biographies (a biography is a story about the life of someone) about her parents. In 1938, she won the Nobel Prize in Literature for her biographies and her trilogy.

Washington Irving was an American writer. He was born in New York City on April 3, 1783. He began his literary career writing humorous newspaper sketches. He edited magazines. He went to Europe on family matters as a young man. He remained there for 17 years. He served as the United States ambassador to Spain from 1842 to 1846. He wrote biographies. He regarded his 5-volume life of George Washington as his masterpiece. He died in his home, Sunnyside, in Tarrytown, New York on November 28, 1859. Irving and his contemporary James Fenimore Cooper were America's first internationally acclaimed authors. Irving encouraged American authors and supported stronger copyright laws. He is best known today for two short stories: "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow". They have been adapted to the stage, to television, and to animated and live-action movies. The Chicago community area Irving Park is named after him. The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. (1819-20)

Jaroslav Hašek (; 1883–1923) was a Czech writer, humorist, satirist, journalist, and bohemian. He first believed in anarchy, but then he became a communist. He was also a commissar of the Red Army against the Czechoslovak Legion. He is known for the novel The Fate of the Good Soldier Švejk during the World War. This novel was an unfinished collection stories about a soldier in World War I. It was a satire about how unskilled authority figures can be. The novel has been translated into 58 languages. It is the most translated novel in Czech literature. At first, Hašek only wrote stories about travel. He published these in magazines. He wrote most of his works while in Prague pubs. His writings were based on his own experiences. However, in some cases, we do not know if some of what he wrote was true or poetic hyperbole. In his life, he wrote about 1,200 short stories. Most of his short prose is found throughout many different magazines and newspapers. Almost all of his stories have been found and printed into books. Some of his work may be lost, such as "The History of the Ox." There are also many works that Hašek probably wrote, but is not confirmed. His most famous text by far is the humorous novel The Fate of the Good Soldier Švejk during the World War. It has been translated into 58 languages. It has also been made into a movie or play. The novel is in four parts. Each part has a name: "In the Background (1921)", "At the Front (1922)", "Famous Spanking (1922)" and "Unfinished Continuation of the Famous Spanking" (1923). Hašek did not finish writing the book. Over time, the novel became very popular. Some of Hašek's works have also been made into theatre performances.

Thomas Stearns Eliot OM (26 September 1888 – 4 January 1965) was an American-born British poet. He was one of the most important poets of the 20th century. He also wrote plays and some important essays about literature. He was born in St. Louis, Missouri, then went to college at Harvard. He spent most of his adult life in London, England. He became a British citizen in 1928. One famous book he wrote was written for children and is called The Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats. The songs in the Andrew Lloyd Webber musical Cats are based on poems in it. He also wrote "The Waste Land", a very mysterious, complicated poem that helped start a new style called Modernism. His friend, Ezra Pound, another Modern poet, helped him finish it. His poem "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" and his play Murder in the Cathedral (about Thomas Becket) are also well known. Eliot was married two times. He worked at a bank in England and later as the head editor of a famous publishing company in London that is now called Faber and Faber. In 1948, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature. He died of emphysema in London.

William Faulkner (born William Cuthbert Falkner), (September 25, 1897–July 6, 1962) was an American author. One of the most influential writers of the twentieth century, he was awarded the 1949 Nobel Prize in Literature. His reputation is based on his novels, novellas, and short stories. However, he was also a published poet and also was a screenwriter. He is now deemed among the greatest American writers of all time. Faulkner received the 1949 Nobel Prize for Literature for "his powerful and artistically unique contribution to the modern American novel." He donated a portion of his Nobel winnings "to establish a fund to support and encourage new fiction writers," eventually resulting in the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction. He donated another portion to a local Oxford bank to establish an account to provide scholarship funds to help educate African-American education majors at nearby Rust College in Holly Springs, Mississippi. Faulkner won two Pulitzer Prizes for what are considered as his "minor" novels: his 1954 novel A Fable, which took the Pulitzer in 1955, and the 1962 novel, The Reivers, which was posthumously awarded the Pulitzer in 1963. He also won two National Book Awards, first for his Collected Stories in 1951 and once again for his novel A Fable in 1955. In 1946, Faulkner was one of three finalists for the first Ellery Queen Mystery Magazine Award. He came in second to Manly Wade Wellman. The PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction has its name, in part, as a tribute to Faulkner, because he was one of the main inspirations of Mary Lee Settle, a founder of the PEN/Faulkner Foundation; Faulkner was an inspiration because he used his 1949 Nobel Prize money to fund awards for younger writers. In 1987, the United States Postal Service issued a 22 cent postage stamp in his honor. If I Forget Thee Jerusalem (The Wild Palms/Old Man) (1939) Go Down, Moses (1942). Episodic novel made up of rewritten previous published short stories. "Tomorrow" (1940). Filmed in 1972, starring Robert Duvall. "My Grandmother Millard and General Bedford Forrest and the Battle of Harrykin Creek" (1943) Helen, a Courtship and Mississippi Poems (1981).

Kenneth Elton Kesey (September 17, 1935 – November 10, 2001) was an American writer best known for his novel One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. He was born in La Junta, Colorado and moved to Springfield, Oregon in 1946.

Guillaume Apollinaire (; 26 August 1880 – 9 November 1918) was a French poet, writer, and art critic. His real name was Wilhelm Albert Włodzimierz Apolinary Kostrowicki. He was born in Rome, Italy. His mother came from a Polish family. He did not become a French citizen until 1916. He is seen as one of the most important French poets of the early 20th century. Apollinaire wrote two famous books of poetry. The first was Alcools (1913). Its poems were printed without punctuation, such as commas and full stops. The second was Calligrammes (1918). Some of its poems use words to make pictures on the page. Apollinaire was a close friend of the painter Pablo Picasso. He was also a strong supporter of Cubism, which was then a new style of painting. In 1912, he gave the name Orphism to another art movement. In 1917, he made the word surréalisme, which means "surrealism". Some people who study art history also say that he helped make the word "Cubism" popular. His play Les Mamelles de Tirésias appeared in 1917. He called it a "surrealist drama". Francis Poulenc later made it into an opera, first performed in 1947. Apollinaire fought as a French soldier in the First World War. In March 1916, a piece of an exploding shell went through his helmet and wounded him in the head. He later returned to his busy life as a writer, but he never became fully healthy again. He died in Paris on 9 November 1918. This was two days before the Armistice, which stopped the fighting. He died during the Spanish flu, a serious influenza pandemic that spread around the world in 1918. He was 38 years old. After his death, young writers such as André Breton and Louis Aragon saw Apollinaire as a guide. In 1924, they used his word "surrealism" as the name of their own movement. Today, his work is studied in many schools. Poems such as "Le Pont Mirabeau" and "Zone" are among the best-known poems in the French language. "Guillaume Apollinaire" was a pen name, or a name that a writer uses for his work. The poet made it from his real names. "Guillaume" is the French form of "Wilhelm", his first name. "Apollinaire" was another of his given names. It was also the first name of his Polish grandfather. When he was young, his mother and his friends called him "Wilhelm" or "Kostro". The name "Guillaume Apollinaire" was first printed on 10 August 1901. He used it under an article in a small weekly paper that made fun of people and events. In March 1902, an important Paris magazine called La Revue blanche printed his story "L'Hérésiarque" under the new name. In 1903, he wrote to a young Englishwoman whom he loved. He told her that she could now write to him under the name "Guillaume Apollinaire". The name "Apollinaire" also made people think of the Greek god Apollo, the god of poetry and light. Apollinaire liked this connection very much. Apollinaire was born in Rome at the end of August 1880. His official date of birth was 26 August, but some writers believe that he was born one day earlier. A few days later, a midwife reported his birth at the town hall. A midwife is a woman who helps mothers when they give birth. She used the false name "Guglielmo Alberto Dulcigni" and said that the baby's parents were unknown. The child was baptized at the church of San Vito on 29 September. On 2 November, his mother told a notary that he was her son. A notary is a public officer who records legal facts and prepares official papers. She gave the child her own family name. His full name then became Guglielmo Alberto Wladimiro Alessandro Apollinare de Kostrowitzky. His mother, Angelica de Kostrowitzky, was 22 years old. Her father, Michel Apollinaire Kostrowicki, was a Polish nobleman, and her mother, Julie Floriani, was Italian. The family had left Poland after the failed January Uprising of 1863. At that time, Russia ruled the part of Poland where they had lived. Two of Michel's brothers were sent to Siberia, and the family lost its lands near Navahrudak. Michel moved to Rome. There he became a chamberlain at the court of Pope Pius IX. A chamberlain was an officer who served a ruler or an important religious leader. Angelica grew up in a strict convent school in Rome. French was the language used there every day. However, she was proud and did not like to obey rules. As a young woman, she lived alone among the rich people of Rome. People at the time called her a "kept woman". This meant that rich lovers gave her money and paid for her way of life. Apollinaire never officially knew who his father was. The man most often named as his father is Francesco Flugi d'Aspermont. He was an Italian army officer from an old noble family of Swiss origin. He was about 44 years old when he met Angelica at her first ball. She ran away with him. For several years, they travelled through Italy and southern France, but they never married. Flugi d'Aspermont left the family around 1884 or 1885, when Guillaume was still a young child. Apollinaire probably knew who his father was. One of his friends said that, around 1900, Apollinaire showed him a photograph of an Italian officer and said, "This is my father". However, he never told the public the truth. He sometimes joked that his father was a cardinal or even the Pope. The missing father became an important subject in his poetry. His poems often speak about people who do not know where they belong and about travellers who move from one place to another. In June 1882, Angelica had another son, Albert. His birth was also reported under a false name. Writers do not agree about whether Albert and Guillaume had the same father. Guillaume and Albert remained close throughout their lives. Albert later worked in a bank and moved to Mexico. Apollinaire's first picture-poem, "Lettre-Océan" (1914), was written as a letter to his brother far away. In March 1887, Angelica moved with her two sons to Monaco, a small country beside France on the Mediterranean Sea. She now called herself "Olga" and spent much of her time at the casino in Monte Carlo. In October of the same year, Wilhelm entered the Collège Saint-Charles. It was a Catholic boarding school, where pupils lived as well as studied. Wilhelm was a very good pupil. He won many school prizes and was a deeply religious child. For a time, he even thought about becoming a priest. At Saint-Charles, he made friends who remained close to him for the rest of his life. They included René Dupuy, who later became a writer under the name René Dalize, and Louis de Gonzague Frick, who later became a poet. In 1889, his mother took the two boys on a short visit to Paris. They saw the World's Fair and the new Eiffel Tower. The Collège Saint-Charles closed in 1895. In 1896, Wilhelm entered the Collège Stanislas in Cannes. In May, the school sent him away because he had brought in a forbidden book. In October 1896, he entered the lycée, or high school, in Nice. There he made another lifelong friend, Ange Toussaint Luca. Wilhelm read a very large number of books. He read ancient Greek and Latin writers and the great French novels. He also read forbidden books, old stories and legends, and anarchist newspapers. Anarchists were against government and political authority. In July 1897, he passed the written part of the baccalauréat, the French examination taken at the end of high school. However, he never received the full diploma and left school without it. He never studied at a university. Even so, his friends later said that he seemed to know everything. He educated himself by reading in libraries. This wide and unusual knowledge appears throughout his poetry. In 1899, Angelica left Monaco with her two sons and her companion, Jules Weil, a businessman whom she had known since her years in Monaco. After short stays in Aix-les-Bains and Lyon, they arrived in Paris in April. In the middle of July, Angelica left the two boys in Stavelot, a small town in the Walloon part of Belgium, among the Ardennes hills. She went to try her luck at the casino in nearby Spa. She was not allowed into the gaming rooms, and she and Weil soon moved on to Ostend, leaving the boys behind. Wilhelm spent a happy summer in Stavelot. He walked across the high moors called the Fagnes, listened to the Walloon language spoken by the villagers, and fell in love with Maria Dubois, the daughter of a café owner. He wrote his first real love poems for her. He also learned enough Walloon to use it in his writing for many years. It gave him material for a short story called "Que vlo-ve ?", which means "What do you want?" in Walloon. He also used it in a chapter of Le Poète assassiné and in a war poem written in 1914. However, the boys soon had no money left. On 5 October 1899, following their mother's orders, they quietly left their guesthouse at dawn without paying the bill. They then took the train back to Paris. The angry owner of the guesthouse went to the police, but the case was closed without punishment in January 1900. This small and shameful event stayed in Apollinaire's memory. Throughout his life, he remained a poor man among rich friends, a foreigner without proper papers, and someone who could be forced to leave at any time. In Paris, he was officially recorded as a foreigner of Russian nationality under the name "Guillaume Kostrowitzky". This paper was his only identity document until 1916. The family settled in Paris, and Wilhelm began looking for work. Because he was a foreigner and did not have a diploma, he could not work in the French public administration. He took several small jobs. In the spring of 1900, he secretly wrote parts of a newspaper serial called Que faire ? ("What to Do?"). A serial is a story published in separate parts. It appeared in the daily newspaper Le Matin under the name of another man, the lawyer Henry Esnard. He earned a diploma in shorthand, a system used for writing very quickly. From July 1900, he worked as a secretary in a small financial office. In his free time, he read rare books at the Bibliothèque Mazarine, one of the oldest libraries in Paris. There he met the scholar Léon Cahun. Cahun introduced him to medieval stories and languages from distant countries. He also introduced him to his nephew, the writer Marcel Schwob. In 1900, Wilhelm fell in love with Linda Molina da Silva, the young sister of a friend. He sent her poems, but she did not answer them. In May 1901, Apollinaire's life changed. A rich woman, the Viscountess Elinor de Milhau, employed him as the private teacher of her nine-year-old daughter, Gabrielle. In August 1901, the whole household travelled by car to Germany. They went to the Rhineland, the area around the river Rhine. They first lived near Honnef and later in a country house called "Neu-Glück", near Oberpleis. Apollinaire spent a full year discovering German life. He saw vineyards, ruined castles above the river, forests of fir trees, village festivals, and Christmas markets. He also learned the old legends of the Lorelei. During the first months of 1902, the viscountess took the household on a long journey through Germany. Apollinaire saw the carnival in Cologne and visited Berlin, Dresden, and Munich. In March, he travelled alone to Prague and Vienna. Prague made a particularly strong impression on him. He later used the city in one of his best short stories, "Le Passant de Prague" ("The Wanderer of Prague"). The story is based on the legend of the Wandering Jew. This year in Germany gave him the "Rhénanes", or "Rhineland poems". They form one of the most beautiful groups of poems in Alcools. In poems such as "Nuit rhénane", "Mai", and "La Loreley", German folk songs, drinking songs, and river legends are mixed with the poet's own sadness. In September 1901, Apollinaire also published his first poems. They appeared in a small Paris magazine called La Grande France. One of them later became the poem called "Clair de lune" in Alcools. While he was in Germany, Apollinaire fell deeply in love. The governess in the Milhau household was Annie Playden, a young Englishwoman from south London. A governess was a woman employed to teach and care for children. Annie was blonde, pretty, and shy. She came from a very strict religious family. At first, she seemed to return Apollinaire's love. Later, she became frightened by the strength of his feelings and moved away from him. In August 1902, Apollinaire left his job and returned to Paris. Annie's cold behaviour had deeply hurt him. However, he did not give up. In November 1903, he travelled to London and tried to win her back. He returned again in May 1904. He found Landor Road, the grey street of small brick houses where Annie's family lived. He walked with her through the foggy streets of London. When he returned to Paris at the end of May, he was still hopeful. The visit had not ended in a complete break. At the beginning of 1905, however, Annie left Europe for the United States. She later said that one reason for leaving was to escape from Apollinaire. He then understood that he had lost her. Annie worked in the United States as a governess and never read Apollinaire's books. Researchers found her in America only in the 1950s. They told her, to her great surprise, that she had become one of the most famous loved women in French poetry. The memory of Annie appears throughout Alcools. She is the distant woman in "La Chanson du mal-aimé" ("The Song of the Badly-Loved"). This long poem tells of a young man who follows a woman through London but is refused by her. Apollinaire wrote most of the poem in 1903. It was not published until 1 May 1909, in the Mercure de France. Annie is also the young woman who leaves her country in "L'Émigrant de Landor Road". She appears again in the short and sad poem "Annie", which is set in Texas. Pascal Pia, one of Apollinaire's biographers, wrote that Annie Playden's shadow lies over a whole part of Alcools. Through this experience, Apollinaire learned an idea that became central to his poetry: for him, love would almost always be a love that had been lost. Apollinaire returned to Paris in August 1902. He lived with his mother again and looked for work. He wrote for a small weekly newspaper about European affairs called L'Européen. In June 1903, he began working as a clerk in a bank. He later worked in several other banks and financial offices until 1907. During the day, he copied numbers. At night, he wrote. La Revue blanche, an important literary magazine, published his first short stories. These were strange and learned tales about heretics, false gods, and wandering souls. Heretics are people who reject the official teachings of a religion. For the first time, he signed these works with the name "Guillaume Apollinaire". In 1903, he began attending the evening meetings of the magazine La Plume. Many young poets of Paris met there. He became friends with the poet André Salmon, with Alfred Jarry, the wild writer of Ubu Roi, and with Jean Mollet. Mollet later became his loyal, unpaid secretary. In November 1903, Apollinaire started a small magazine with Salmon, Mollet, and the poet Nicolas Deniker. It was called Le Festin d'Ésope, or "Aesop's Feast". Only nine issues appeared. In this magazine, Apollinaire published his first long prose work one chapter at a time. It was called L'Enchanteur pourrissant, or "The Rotting Enchanter". It is a dream-like dialogue about the wizard Merlin, who is buried alive by the fairy who loves him. Even this very small magazine taught Apollinaire an important lesson. Modern poetry needed its own magazines and other places where it could appear freely, away from the large newspapers that were controlled by business. One evening in February 1905, Apollinaire was waiting for the last train home in a bar near the Saint-Lazare railway station. Jean Mollet brought a young Spanish painter to his table. The painter was almost unknown and very poor. His name was Pablo Picasso. Writers about their lives often describe this meeting as an important turning point for both men. The next day, Picasso introduced Apollinaire to his closest friend, the poet Max Jacob. The three men understood one another immediately. Picasso lived on the hill of Montmartre in a strange wooden building filled with artists' studios. Max Jacob called it the "Bateau-Lavoir", or "washing-boat", because it looked like the boats on the river Seine where women washed clothes. Apollinaire returned to Montmartre again and again. He saw the sad blue pictures of Picasso's "blue period" and the circus performers of his "rose period". In the spring of 1905, Apollinaire wrote his first two articles about Picasso. One appeared in La Revue immoraliste, a small magazine that he had recently started with Mollet and Salmon. The other appeared in La Plume. These were among the first important articles written about Picasso. Apollinaire had found another kind of work: he would explain modern painting to the public. A famous group of friends grew around Picasso and Apollinaire. It became known as the "bande à Picasso", or "Picasso's gang". Its members included Max Jacob, André Salmon, and later many other artists and writers. They were poor, humorous, and hard-working. They were also completely sure that they were changing art forever. In April 1907, when he was twenty-six years old, Apollinaire finally left his mother's home. He rented his first flat near Montmartre. One month later, Picasso returned from the small shop of the art dealer Clovis Sagot. With a very serious expression, he told Apollinaire that he had found a future wife for him there. Apollinaire quickly went to the shop and met the young painter Marie Laurencin. She was twenty-three years old, clever, gifted, and often ironic. She painted soft grey-and-pink pictures of young women, deer, and flowers. Apollinaire and Marie loved one another for five difficult years. They argued, separated, and then came together again. Apollinaire's mother believed that Marie was not rich enough for her son. After 1911, Marie's mother no longer wanted Apollinaire to visit her daughter. By the end of 1911, their love was slowly ending, and Apollinaire knew it. This feeling helped him write "Le Pont Mirabeau", or "The Mirabeau Bridge". The poem was published in February 1912 and is perhaps his best-loved poem. In it, the river Seine flows under a bridge in Paris and carries love away, while the poet remains behind. In June 1912, after another serious quarrel, Marie left Apollinaire for the last time. Their friends tried to bring them together again, but they failed. Apollinaire became deeply depressed, and this sadness lasted throughout the summer. He left Auteuil, the area where he and Marie had lived near one another. At the end of the year, he rented a flat at 202 boulevard Saint-Germain. It remained his home for the rest of his life. In June 1914, Marie married the German painter Otto von Wätjen. A few weeks later, the war made France and Germany enemy countries. From 1910, Apollinaire earned his living as a journalist. He wrote a daily art column for the newspaper L'Intransigeant. From 1911, he also wrote a famous column of news and stories called "La Vie anecdotique" for the Mercure de France. He reviewed almost every important art exhibition in Paris. Most critics laughed at the new painters, but Apollinaire defended them. These artists included Henri Matisse, André Derain, Georges Braque, Robert Delaunay, Marcel Duchamp, the young Marc Chagall, the dream-like painter Giorgio de Chirico, and above all Picasso and the Cubists. His support for the newest art had a cost. In March 1914, the director of L'Intransigeant became tired of Apollinaire's constant praise for modern painters and took the art column away from him. Apollinaire then moved to another newspaper, Paris-Journal. He also admired painters whom almost nobody else respected. The old painter Henri Rousseau was known as "le Douanier", or "the customs officer". He painted jungles and dreams in a simple, childlike style. Official critics laughed at him, but Apollinaire understood his importance. Rousseau painted a large double portrait of Apollinaire and Marie Laurencin called The Muse Inspiring the Poet in 1909. To make the portrait accurate, he measured Apollinaire's face and body with a ruler. In November 1908, Picasso organized a famous banquet in Rousseau's honour at the Bateau-Lavoir. A banquet is a large formal meal. Poets and painters crowded into the studio. They sang songs in Rousseau's honour, and the old painter sat in the place of honour under paper lanterns. The year 1908 was an important turning point for Apollinaire. In May, he wrote to his old school friend Toussaint Luca and described his aim in one sentence. He wanted "un lyrisme neuf et humaniste à la fois": a form of poetry that was completely new but still deeply human. Within a few months, he published a strange prose poem called "Onirocritique", or "Dream-criticism". In it, an enchanter walks through a dream world where flames become flowers. He also gave a public talk about young poets. He wrote two introductions about modern painting, in which the flame became a symbol of art. He also published two long poems that he always considered among his deepest works: "Le Brasier", or "The Brazier", and "Les Fiançailles", or "The Betrothal". In these poems, the poet throws his old self into the fire. Like the Phoenix, the legendary bird that burns and is then born again, he returns from the flames with new powers. Scholars often see 1908 as the passage between the young Apollinaire, who was still close to Symbolism, and the fully modern poet. One figure appears behind all these works: the enchanter. Since his summer in Stavelot in 1899, Apollinaire had continued to write and rewrite his book about Merlin, L'Enchanteur pourrissant. When the book finally appeared in 1909, "Onirocritique" became its final chapter. A short animal poem from the same year shows his fear of time passing. He wrote: Dieu ! Je vais avoir vingt-huit ans / Et mal vécus, à mon envie ("God! I am going to be twenty-eight, and I have not lived as well as I wished"). That summer, while spending a holiday on the coast of the North Sea, he made an important decision. He would leave his bank job and earn his living only through writing. Apollinaire's first books appeared slowly and in very small numbers. They were also beautiful objects made together with artists. L'Enchanteur pourrissant, his book about Merlin, was printed in November 1909. The young art dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler published only about one hundred copies. The book included dark woodcuts by André Derain. Woodcuts are pictures made from designs cut into wood. The work is often described as one of the first important modern "painters' books", in which writing and art are designed together. L'Hérésiarque et Cie, or "The Heresiarch and Co.", appeared in October 1910. It brought together twenty-three of Apollinaire's best short stories. They tell of false prophets, miracles, crimes, and wandering people, often with dark humour. In December 1910, the book received several votes for the Prix Goncourt, the most famous French prize for literature. The prize was finally given to Louis Pergaud. Apollinaire believed for the rest of his life that the prize had been unfairly taken from him. Le Bestiaire ou Cortège d'Orphée, or "The Bestiary, or Procession of Orpheus", appeared in March 1911. It is a group of very short poems about animals, usually only four to six lines long. The animals include the dromedary, the mouse, the carp, and the dove. A woodcut by Raoul Dufy appeared beside each poem. Only 120 copies were printed. Behind its jokes about animals, the small book is really about Orpheus, the first poet of Greek legend, and about poetry itself. Apollinaire also enjoyed literary jokes. In 1909, he invented a young woman poet called "Louise Lalanne". He wrote poems and articles under her name for the magazine Les Marges. Critics praised this new and fresh female voice. Some of the poems were actually written by Marie Laurencin. Apollinaire also wrote many works simply to earn money, both under his own name and under false names. These included introductions to old erotic books, popular novels, and hundreds of newspaper articles. He knew both the popular and the serious sides of literature. He later used material from both worlds in his poetry. In August 1911, the Mona Lisa, the most famous painting in the world, was stolen from the Louvre museum in Paris. Newspapers wrote about the theft every day, and the affair had serious effects on Apollinaire's life. The story behind it was unusual. In 1907, a charming but dishonest young Belgian called Géry Pieret had secretly stolen two small ancient Iberian stone statues from the Louvre. He sold them to Picasso. Pieret had once worked as Apollinaire's secretary. Picasso kept the statues. Some art historians believe that they helped him move toward Cubism. In 1911, Pieret returned to Paris and stole another statue. After the Mona Lisa disappeared, he sold this statue to a newspaper. He wanted to show how badly the Louvre protected its works of art. The police began looking for the newspaper's unknown thief. Apollinaire became frightened and helped Pieret leave France by train. Then Apollinaire and a very frightened Picasso took the two earlier statues to the newspaper so that they could be secretly returned to the museum. It was already too late. On 7 September 1911, the police arrested Apollinaire at his home. A judge accused him of helping the thieves and sent him to the Santé prison in Paris. For the newspapers, it was an exciting story: a foreign poet, known as a leader of strange modern art, was connected with the theft of the Mona Lisa. Picasso was questioned by the judge. At first, he denied everything. According to some accounts, he even denied that Apollinaire was his friend. Apollinaire spent five days and nights in a cell at the Santé prison. He was released on 12 September. In January 1912, the case against him was completely dropped. The real thief of the Mona Lisa was an Italian worker called Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught only in 1913, and the painting was returned to the Louvre. The affair left deep emotional wounds. Apollinaire was still a foreigner and feared that France would force him to leave. He wanted very much to become a French citizen. Some newspapers attacked him with hateful words about his foreign birth. While in prison, he wrote a group of short and painful poems called "À la Santé", or "At the Santé". He later included them in Alcools. In these poems, the prisoner no longer has a name. He is only a number: "le quinze de la Onzième", or "number fifteen of the eleventh division". Even the sky is described as "blue like a chain": (In a pit like a bear / Every morning I walk round and round) The short series recalls the prison poems that Paul Verlaine had written about forty years earlier. Even the critic who later attacked Alcools most strongly admitted that these poems were deeply moving. They had been written at a moment when Apollinaire had forgotten all literary art and felt only pain. In February 1912, Apollinaire and four friends founded a new magazine called Les Soirées de Paris, or "Paris Evenings". The founders included the writer André Billy and René Dalize, Apollinaire's old school friend from Monaco. "Le Pont Mirabeau" appeared in the first issue. In November 1913, after the magazine had stopped for a time, it began again with money from the painter Serge Férat and the baroness Hélène d'Oettingen. Apollinaire now directed the magazine himself and made it the main place for his ideas. The magazine published the new poets. It was also one of the first magazines anywhere to print pictures of Cubist paintings. Many readers cancelled their subscriptions because they disliked the new art. Apollinaire continued without changing direction. These were years of constant movement and invention. In October 1912, Apollinaire stayed in the Jura hills with the painter Francis Picabia and Marcel Duchamp. He read them his newest poem, "Zone". In a public talk during the same month, he announced a new form of Cubism. He called it "Orphism", after Orpheus. It was a kind of painting based on pure colour and light. For Apollinaire, its main artist was Robert Delaunay. In January 1913, he travelled to Berlin to speak at an exhibition of Delaunay's work. For the exhibition, he wrote "Les Fenêtres", or "The Windows". The poem is built like one of Delaunay's paintings, with bright pieces of the world placed next to one another. On 24 December 1913, at the Sorbonne, the language scholar Ferdinand Brunot recorded Apollinaire's voice on a phonograph. The recordings were made for Brunot's new "archives of speech". They still exist. People today can hear Apollinaire reading "Le Pont Mirabeau", "Marie", and "Le Voyageur". In March 1913, Apollinaire published Les Peintres cubistes. Méditations esthétiques, or "The Cubist Painters: Aesthetic Meditations". It was not a cold or difficult book of theory. It was a poet's book about painting. Apollinaire wrote about Picasso, Braque, Jean Metzinger, Albert Gleizes, Marie Laurencin, Juan Gris, Fernand Léger, Picabia, and Duchamp. He explained the main idea of modern art in a clear and bold way. A modern painting did not have to copy nature like a photograph. Music could be true without copying an object, and painting could do the same. The book made Apollinaire, in the eyes of the public, the official voice of Cubism. He followed every new art movement in Europe. In the summer of 1913, he published a manifesto for the Italian Futurists called L'Antitradition futuriste. A manifesto is a public statement of ideas. This wild printed sheet offered roses to the people who invented new things. It also shouted the half-printed insult "MER…DE" at professors, museums, and critics. Some of Apollinaire's friends were shocked. In fact, he was partly joking. He shared the Futurists' love of machines, cities, and games with printed words. However, he did not share their hatred of the past. His own work showed the opposite idea: the newest poetry could carry all the old stories and legends inside it. In April 1913, the publisher Mercure de France published Apollinaire's first major collection of poems, Alcools, or "Alcohols" and "Spirits". He was thirty-two years old. The book contained about fifty poems written during fifteen years. The oldest came from his year in the Rhineland in 1901 and 1902. The newest was "Zone", which he had finished only a few months before the book was printed. The title means strong drink, but it also suggests fire and life. For Apollinaire, the modern world itself was like alcohol. It burned people and made them drunk. Near the end of "Zone", the first poem in the book, the poet drinks his own life like burning brandy. In "Vendémiaire", the final poem, he describes himself as drunk because he has drunk the whole universe. At the front of the book was something very unusual for a poetry collection: a Cubist portrait of Apollinaire drawn by Picasso. The face was made of broken lines and flat shapes. Many readers thought the portrait was a joke. For Apollinaire, it was the perfect image of the collection. It joined order with adventure and tradition with invention. When Apollinaire read the first proofs of Alcools at the end of 1912, he made a bold choice. He removed every comma, every full stop, and every other punctuation mark from the whole book. A few poets, including Stéphane Mallarmé, had already tried this in single poems. The Futurists had also asked poets to do it in their manifestos. However, removing punctuation from a complete poetry collection was still very unusual. It attracted much attention. A critic asked Apollinaire why he had done this. In a letter written in July 1913, he answered that punctuation was useless. He wrote: "le rythme même et la coupe des vers voilà la véritable ponctuation", meaning that the rhythm and the division of the lines were the real punctuation. He also removed other parts of the poems. More than fifty lines disappeared from the manuscript of "Zone" before the book was printed. He also removed names of places and dates that made the poems seem too private. Without punctuation, each line can stand by itself. Words may connect with the line before or with the line after it. One sentence can therefore have two meanings at the same time. The famous beginning of "Le Pont Mirabeau" shows this: (Under the Mirabeau Bridge flows the Seine / And our loves) Do "our loves" flow away with the river, or do the words begin the next sentence? Both readings can be true at the same time. After Alcools, poetry without punctuation became common in many languages. It remains common today. Alcools contains many different voices. It begins with "Zone", the newest poem, and ends with "Vendémiaire", a great song of praise to Paris. The poems between them are not placed in the order in which they were written. The order of the poems is itself part of the art. The scholar Marie-Jeanne Durry noticed that "L'Émigrant de Landor Road", the poem about Annie's departure, is placed at the exact centre of the book. The same number of poems comes before it and after it. For Durry, this quiet arrangement shows that Apollinaire's lost English love remained at the centre of his inner life. "Zone" is a long walk through Paris and through the poet's whole life. It begins in the morning and ends the next morning. Its first line is one of the best-known lines in modern French poetry: À la fin tu es las de ce monde ancien, or "In the end, you are tired of this ancient world". The poem praises aeroplanes, posters, typists, and advertising papers as the true poetry of modern life. It then moves through Apollinaire's memories: his religious childhood, Prague, London, his lost loves, and the poor people leaving their countries at the Saint-Lazare station. It ends at sunrise with two strange short lines: Adieu Adieu / Soleil cou coupé, or "Farewell Farewell / Sun cut throat". The red rising sun is seen as a cut neck. Readers have connected this image with the cut heads and burning suns in his poems of 1908. "Le Pont Mirabeau" is a slow and sad song about the end of his love for Marie Laurencin. Time and love pass like the river. Only the poet remains. "La Chanson du mal-aimé" is his long London poem for Annie Playden. It mixes his own story with Ulysses, the Cossacks of Zaporozhia, and the queens of legend. "Marie" is a song about two women at the same time. The Marie who dances the maclotte, a folk dance from the Ardennes, is Mareye of Stavelot. The Marie whom the poet asks to return is Marie Laurencin. The "Rhénanes" are the German poems. They are filled with night, wine, travelling people, and drowned voices. "Les Colchiques", or "The Autumn Crocuses", compares the eyes of the loved woman to a beautiful but poisonous flower. "Cortège", "Le Brasier", and "Les Fiançailles" are difficult and powerful poems. In them, the poet burns his old self and is born again. Apollinaire believed that "Les Fiançailles", which he dedicated to Picasso, was one of his best works. The shortest poem in the book, "Chantre", or "Singer", has only one line. Old and new appear side by side throughout the collection. Strict classical verse stands next to free verse. Church bells stand next to aeroplanes. Merlin stands next to the Eiffel Tower. This mixture was exactly what Apollinaire wanted. The reviews were divided. Some critics praised the music and beauty of the book. Others mocked it or became angry. The strongest attack came from the poet Georges Duhamel in the Mercure de France in June 1913. He wrote that the collection looked like a second-hand shop. It was, he said, a pile of used objects, some valuable, but none made by the shopkeeper himself. Duhamel also attacked Apollinaire's mixed foreign origins with words that today clearly show hatred of foreigners. Apollinaire was deeply hurt. For a short time, he even thought about challenging Duhamel to a duel. Many years later, Duhamel said that he regretted the review. Younger readers reacted very differently. For many poets born around 1895, Alcools soon became a model and a place to begin. Today, it is one of the most studied works of French poetry. Marie-Jeanne Durry wrote several volumes of university lectures about it, and many books explain the poems one by one. In 1914, Apollinaire began to draw pictures with words. On 15 June 1914, Les Soirées de Paris published "Lettre-Océan", or "Ocean-Letter". It was the first of his visual poems. At first, he called such poems "idéogrammes lyriques", or "lyric ideograms". An ocean-letter was a real form of message at that time. It was sent between ships at sea by the new wireless telegraph. "Lettre-Océan" covers two full pages. Its words form two large wheels with lines like spokes. They look like radio waves spreading from the Eiffel Tower. The reader's eyes can follow the words in several directions. Inside the two wheels are parts of a letter to Apollinaire's brother Albert in Mexico. There are also street cries from Paris, ship sirens, and the calls of a bus driver. All these sounds happen at the same time. The scholar Willard Bohn describes it as a poem that must be seen all at once, like a picture, rather than read only one line after another. The Italian Futurists had experimented with the printed shape of words a few months earlier, and Apollinaire learned from them. However, one month later he published four more picture-poems that were completely his own: "Voyage", "Paysage animé", "La Cravate et la montre", and "Cœur couronne et miroir". These were real drawings made from words. They showed a heart, a crown, a mirror, a necktie, a watch, and a smoking cigar. Apollinaire planned to collect them in a book called Et moi aussi je suis peintre, or "I Too Am a Painter". The war stopped the project. The book was finally published only in 2006. In 1917, Apollinaire invented a new and beautiful name for these poems: calligrammes. The word comes from Greek words meaning "beautiful" and "writing". Many critics complained. They asked whether this was still poetry or only a childish game. Apollinaire answered that he was bringing back a very old tradition, which went back to ancient Greece. He also believed that he was pointing toward a future in which poetry, drawing, and cinema would come together. At the end of July 1914, Apollinaire was in Deauville, on the coast of Normandy. He was writing a light newspaper report with his friend, the artist André Rouveyre. On 31 July, as war came very close, the two men drove through the night back to Paris. France ordered a general mobilization the next day. Within a few days, the First World War had begun. Apollinaire did not have to fight. He was not a French citizen. He was officially a Russian subject who had been born in Rome, so France could not force him to join its army. He chose to fight. On 5 August 1914, he asked to join the army. In September, he also asked to become a French citizen. The army was slow to deal with foreign volunteers. While he waited, Apollinaire went to Nice. On 4 December 1914, he finally signed an agreement to serve "for the duration of the war". On 6 December, he entered the 38th field artillery regiment at Nîmes as an ordinary gunner. The historian Annette Becker notes that his military papers use the word "engagement" three times on two pages. In French, this word means a soldier's free decision to serve. Apollinaire was thirty-four years old. He was older and heavier than most new soldiers, but he trained seriously. He rode horses for six hours a day and learned to use the French 75-mm gun. Half as a joke, he told his friends that being a soldier seemed to be his true profession. In Nice, at the end of September 1914, Apollinaire met Louise de Coligny-Châtillon. She was a divorced young noblewoman whom everyone called "Lou". She was independent, careless, and fascinating. Apollinaire fell violently in love with her. The day after he arrived at the military camp in Nîmes, Lou appeared at the gate. For nine days, they had an intense love affair in a hotel near the railway station. The relationship did not last. Lou loved another man and slowly changed Apollinaire's passion into friendship. They met for the final time in March 1915. For many months, however, Apollinaire sent her letters and poems from the military camp and later from the front. These included love poems, erotic poems, sad poems, and some of his first poems about the war. He often decorated them with small calligrams. The "Poèmes à Lou" were published only long after his death, in 1947 and 1955. They are now considered some of the most intense love poems of the 20th century. On 2 January 1915, Apollinaire was travelling by train from Nice to Marseille. In his compartment was a shy young woman with dark hair called Madeleine Pagès. She was twenty-one years old. Madeleine was a literature teacher travelling home to her family in Oran, in French Algeria. They talked about poetry. Before she left the train, Apollinaire asked for her address and promised to send her one of his books. From the front, in April, he sent her his first postcard. They began writing to one another. The letters were first polite, then loving, and finally passionate. On 10 August 1915, Apollinaire wrote to Madeleine's mother and formally asked permission to marry her. Her mother accepted. He had seen Madeleine only once, for a few hours on a train. He filled the planned marriage with his imagination. He sent her nearly fifty poems and trusted her with his manuscripts. He also told her the full story of his life in long letters. These letters are now very useful to writers who study his life. At the beginning of 1916, Apollinaire spent his first long military leave with Madeleine's family in Oran. It was the only long time they ever spent together. On 4 April 1915, Apollinaire's unit reached the front in Champagne. At first, he served with the artillery, several kilometres behind the front line. He carried ammunition at night under enemy fire, delivered messages on horseback, and watched the German lines for the flashes of guns. He was promoted quickly. He became a corporal and then a sergeant in command of a gun. His friends in Paris were surprised that many of his letters from the war were filled with wonder. The rockets and lights above the trenches seemed to him like a terrible festival. He enjoyed the strange new words used by soldiers. For the first time in his life, he felt completely equal to the men around him. In June 1915, while still near the front, he even made a book. With a typewriter, a copying pad, and violet ink, he and two other soldiers produced Case d'Armons. It contained his newest poems and calligrams. They made only twenty-five copies, a few hundred metres from the enemy lines. It is now one of the rarest books of French poetry. In November 1915, Apollinaire asked to move to the infantry, the soldiers who fought on foot in the trenches. He became a second lieutenant in the 96th infantry regiment. This was a braver choice and a much more dangerous life. He now lived in the mud of the front line, among rats, cold, and dead bodies. His poems became darker and quieter. On 9 March 1916, the official government newspaper announced that Apollinaire had become a French citizen. Eight days later, on 17 March, at about four in the afternoon, he was sitting in a trench at the Bois des Buttes, near Berry-au-Bac. He was reading the new issue of the Mercure de France. A German 150-mm shell exploded above him. A piece of shrapnel passed through his steel helmet and entered his right temple. Shrapnel is a sharp piece of metal from an exploding shell. At first, the wound did not seem very serious. Apollinaire finished reading, walked to the medical station, and was operated on that night in a field ambulance. His condition then became worse. He suffered from dizziness, terrible headaches, and a slow loss of movement in his left arm. He was moved through several hospitals. First came the Hôtel-Dieu in Château-Thierry, then the Val-de-Grâce military hospital in Paris, and then the Italian hospital on the quai d'Orsay. His friend, the painter Serge Férat, worked there as a nurse. On 9 May 1916, at the Villa Molière, a hospital building in Auteuil, the surgeon Dr Baudet performed a trepanation. He opened Apollinaire's skull to reduce the pressure on his brain. By a strange chance, Auteuil was the same part of Paris that Apollinaire had left after losing Marie Laurencin. He later wrote that he returned there only "in the year 1916, to have my skull opened at the Villa Molière". During the operation, the fingers of his paralysed hand began to move again. Apollinaire kept the damaged helmet and the blood-covered copy of the Mercure de France as special objects. On 17 June 1916, he received the Croix de guerre, the French military cross. The official statement praised his calm behaviour and courage. One friend wrote that poets and artists were wounded in the head, as though the enemy understood what it was doing.
