In Tours, royalists asked him to become their candidate. He refused, even though he was neither a republican nor a supporter of the government. None of these plans led to an election campaign. The legitimists wanted to restore the old royal family. Balzac first moved toward them at the very end of 1831. In the spring of 1832, the change became public. He began to write for their new newspaper, Le Rénovateur. His first article for the paper, published in March 1832, protested against a plan to destroy the monument to the murdered duke of Berry. The scholar Bernard Guyon studied Balzac's political change year by year. He argued that it was not a sudden emotional decision. It was a careful and practical choice. Balzac believed that a writer who wanted a political career needed the support of an organized party. The royalist party was weak and needed new talent. Balzac thought that it would give him an important place more quickly than the liberal side, which was already full of ambitious men. His new friend, the marquise de Castries, was the niece of the duke of Fitz-James, an important legitimist leader. Guyon believed that she supported and strengthened Balzac's decision, but that she did not create it. Barbéris points to another fact that makes the situation more complex. During the same months, Balzac continued to sell strong articles attacking the government to La Caricature, a newspaper of the left. In 1832, therefore, two political sides of Balzac existed together: a royalist side and a rebellious side close to the left. Barbéris argues that Balzac's royalism was mainly a position from which he could fight the government. It gave him a way to attack the new power of money. It was very different from the sad royalism of old nobles who only wished to return to the past. Balzac's royalism remained practical rather than emotional. In May and June 1832, Le Rénovateur published his Essai sur la situation du parti royaliste, or "Essay on the Situation of the Royalist Party". He told the royalists that they had to face the problems of the 19th century as modern problems. In September 1832, he wrote another article for the same paper, called "Du Gouvernement moderne", or "On Modern Government". In this article, he went further. The idea that the old royal family had a natural right to rule might seem absurd, he wrote. However, even if legitimacy did not exist, it would have to be invented. He saw it as a useful way to give government strength and stability. Le Rénovateur thought the article was too daring and did not publish it. It first appeared only in 1933. Barbéris reads it as an argument for a strong, well-managed, and open society, written under royalist language. In such a society, Balzac wrote, social classes should not be closed walls. They should be open fields of competition that anyone could enter. In this way, no human energy would be wasted. Balzac never received an opportunity to stand in an election. In June 1832, while staying at Saché, he discussed with his friend Margonne the possibility of becoming a candidate at Chinon. Like his earlier political plans, this idea came to nothing. He never stood for parliament during the July Monarchy. In private, Balzac was less sure of himself than he appeared in public. In June 1832, he wrote openly to his friend Zulma Carraud. He said that he threw himself into political storms and the dry winds of literary fame because he had not been given the simple happiness of being loved. After this period, Balzac placed more of his political ideas inside his novels. The first important example was Le Médecin de campagne (1833). He had partly planned it as a book that could help him win voters. Barbéris gives the book a more personal meaning. The year 1832 had brought Balzac accidents, political failure, and loneliness. Le Médecin de campagne was his way of recovering. Its hero, Doctor Bénassis, improves the life of a poor mountain village. He is the first major character in Balzac's work who builds something useful instead of only suffering or fighting against society. Balzac offered himself as a candidate again in 1848, but once more he was not elected. Balzac wrote Le Père Goriot, or "Old Goriot", very quickly between September 1834 and January 1835. It first appeared in a magazine. The novel takes place in a poor and dirty boarding house in Paris called the Pension Vauquer. Three people who live there are especially important. Old Goriot is a retired maker of pasta who has given everything he owns to his two selfish daughters. Eugène de Rastignac is a poor young student from southern France who wants to rise in society. Vautrin is a strange and powerful man who is really an escaped convict. At the end of the novel, Goriot dies almost alone. Rastignac stands on the heights of the Père Lachaise cemetery and looks down at Paris. He gives his famous challenge to the city: from now on, the struggle is between Paris and himself. However, this challenge is not the last sentence of the novel. Balzac added another sentence and made it stronger in later editions. Rastignac has just declared war on society. His first act in this war is to go to dinner with Madame de Nucingen, one of Goriot's own daughters. Pierre Barbéris studied the manuscript and Balzac's corrections. He believed that this ending contains the main meaning of the novel. Rastignac's revolt does not free him from the corrupt world. It takes him directly to the tables where its rich members eat. While writing the novel, Balzac developed one of the most important ideas of his career: characters would return. The same invented people would appear in different novels at different times in their lives. For example, Rastignac had already appeared as an older man in La Peau de chagrin. In Le Père Goriot, readers saw him as a young student. Vautrin would return in later novels under different names. Balzac was very excited by this idea. According to a story told by his family, he ran to his sister's home and announced that he was becoming a genius. The manuscript shows the exact moment when he made this decision. At first, Balzac called the student "Massiac". While writing, he crossed out this name and replaced it with "Rastignac", the name of a character who already appeared in another work. Rastignac's family was partly based on Balzac's own family. A letter that Rastignac receives from his sister Laure closely follows a real letter written to Balzac by his sister Laurence in October 1819. From this time, Balzac's separate novels slowly became parts of one enormous connected work. The return of characters became one of the main ideas behind La Comédie humaine. Women were central to Balzac's life and to his letters. After Madame de Berny, he became close to the duchess of Abrantès. She was the widow of one of Napoleon's generals and told Balzac many stories about the Empire. In 1832, he was deeply hurt by the marquise de Castries. She was an important noblewoman who had helped move him toward the royalist party. She encouraged his love, allowed him to follow her to Aix-les-Bains and Geneva, and then refused him. Balzac later took revenge through fiction. In La Duchesse de Langeais (1834), a proud noblewoman plays with the love of an honest soldier and suffers terribly as a result. On 28 February 1832, Balzac received a letter from Odessa. It was signed only "L'Étrangère", meaning "the Stranger" or "the Foreign Woman". The writer was Ewelina Hańska, a Polish countess. She lived with her much older husband on a very large estate at Wierzchownia in Ukraine, which was then part of the Russian Empire. She admired Balzac's books. However, she feared that his recent writing was less morally pure than his early Scènes de la vie privée. Balzac answered her, and a very long exchange of letters began. He continued writing to her for the rest of his life. Of these letters, 414 still exist. Together, they are about one quarter as long as the whole of La Comédie humaine. They are among the best sources for understanding his life and the way he worked. Balzac and Ewelina first met in Neuchâtel, Switzerland, in September 1833. They met again in Geneva during the winter. They became lovers on 26 January 1834. They met once more in Vienna in 1835. After that, they did not see one another for eight years and could communicate only by letter. Ewelina was married, rich, careful, and far away. Balzac dreamed that her elderly husband would die and that she would finally be free to marry him. Balzac also had other, less public relationships. He almost certainly had a daughter with Maria Du Fresnay, a young married woman who admired him. The child, Marie, was born in 1834. Balzac continued to know the family and mentioned Marie in his will. Stories also connected him with several other women. However, work filled more of his nights than love did. Fame did not make Balzac's life peaceful. In 1836, he lost a large amount of money on the Chronique de Paris, a newspaper that he had bought and directed. In the following year, he only just avoided being sent to prison for debt. Madame de Berny died in July 1836. Balzac had just completed Le Lys dans la vallée, or "The Lily of the Valley". Its pure and unhappy heroine, Madame de Mortsauf, was partly based on Madame de Berny. In the same year, Balzac tried a new form of publication. His short novel La Vieille Fille, or "The Old Maid", appeared in separate parts, day after day, in a French daily newspaper. It is often called the first French novel to be published in this way. This new form, called the serial novel, changed literature. Balzac helped to develop it, and it soon controlled much of his working life. Many of his later novels had to be written under the pressure of daily publication dates. Balzac never stopped hoping to make a quick fortune. In 1838, he travelled to Sardinia because he believed that ancient Roman silver mines could be opened again. The plan was not foolish. The mines later made money, but another person had already obtained the right to work them. Balzac returned home with even less money. He then spent large sums on Les Jardies, a small country house at Sèvres near Paris. Among his many plans, he imagined growing pineapples there and selling them in Paris. The house itself cost him about 50,000 francs in 1839. To hide from the people to whom he owed money, Balzac sometimes used false names. From October 1840, he rented rooms in the village of Passy near Paris. The house had a hidden back door that allowed him to escape visitors. He lived there for seven years. It is the only one of his homes in Paris that still exists. It is now the Maison de Balzac museum at 47 rue Raynouard. In 1839, Balzac became president of the Société des gens de lettres, a new association of French writers. He worked to protect the rights of authors. He wanted strong laws to protect literary property. Literary property is the idea that a written work belongs to its author. Balzac also fought newspapers that copied and printed books without paying the writers. His public letters about these questions helped prepare the later development of copyright law in France. He also tried to save a notary called Peytel, who had been sentenced to death for murder. Balzac believed that he was innocent and wrote publicly in his defence. His efforts failed. Balzac also wanted to succeed in the theatre, but most of his plays failed. His play Vautrin opened in Paris on 14 March 1840. The famous actor Frédérick Lemaître played the main part. In the fourth act, Lemaître appeared in a wig that made him look like King Louis Philippe. The king's son left the theatre in anger. The government banned the play the next day. Several of Balzac's other plays failed or were refused by theatres. Critics usually consider Le Faiseur, also called Mercadet, to be his best comedy. It tells the story of a brilliant debtor who uses clever tricks against his creditors, the people to whom he owes money. The play became successful only in 1851, after Balzac had died. In 1840, Balzac made another attempt to succeed in journalism. He wrote almost all of three issues of a magazine called the Revue parisienne. The magazine lost money. However, critics still see some of its articles as among the best literary criticism of the 19th century. The most famous example is Balzac's long and generous study of Stendhal's La Chartreuse de Parme. Balzac praised the novel at a time when very few people understood how great Stendhal was. By 1840, Balzac had written many novels and stories. He understood that they formed one great picture of society. He searched for a title for the whole work and chose La Comédie humaine, or "The Human Comedy". The title answers the Divine Comedy of Dante Alighieri. Dante had described a journey through hell, purgatory, and heaven. Balzac would describe a journey through modern society. In October 1841, Balzac signed a contract with a group of publishers led by Furne. They planned to publish a complete and organized edition of his works under the new title. The first volumes appeared in 1842. They opened with the famous "Avant-propos", or foreword, in which Balzac explained the complete plan of his work. By 1848, the Furne edition had grown to seventeen volumes. Balzac continued to correct his personal copy until the end of his life. Scholars call this copy the "Furne corrigé". Modern editions of La Comédie humaine are largely based on it. In November 1841, Ewelina Hańska's husband, Wacław Hański, died in Ukraine. Balzac learned about the death early in 1842. Ewelina was now free to marry. Balzac gave himself one final great aim: he wanted her to become his wife. Ewelina did not agree to marry Balzac immediately. She had a daughter whose future marriage had to be arranged, and she wanted to protect her wealth. She also had doubts about Balzac, who spent money more quickly than he earned it. In 1843, Balzac travelled to Saint Petersburg to meet her after eight years apart. In 1845 and 1846, they travelled together through Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, France, and Italy. In 1846, Ewelina became pregnant. Balzac was very happy and had already chosen the name Victor-Honoré for the child. However, the baby was born dead at the end of the year. People close to Balzac believed that he never fully recovered from this loss. Despite these difficulties, Balzac continued to write. The complete Illusions perdues, or "Lost Illusions", appeared in three parts between 1837 and 1843. The novel tells the story of Lucien de Rubempré, a handsome but weak young poet from the provinces. Paris and the dishonest world of newspapers destroy him. The story continues in Splendeurs et misères des courtisanes, or "The Splendors and Miseries of Courtesans", which Balzac finished in 1847. Lucien enters a darker Paris ruled by police officers, bankers, and hidden powers. Vautrin controls much of this world from the shadows. In 1846 and 1847, Balzac published the two novels known as the Parents pauvres, or "Poor Relations". La Cousine Bette tells the story of a poor and jealous cousin who secretly destroys her rich relatives. Le Cousin Pons tells the story of a gentle old music lover. His valuable collection of art awakens the greed of everyone around him. La Cousine Bette, which was published in parts in a daily newspaper, was the last great popular success of Balzac's life. His health was now becoming very poor. Many years of working at night, drinking coffee, and worrying about money had damaged his heart. In September 1847, he made his first long journey to Wierzchownia, Ewelina's home in Ukraine. He returned to Paris in February 1848 and saw the revolution that ended the July Monarchy. He even watched the crowd enter the Tuileries palace. In the autumn of 1848, he returned to Ukraine. He stayed there for a year and a half and was seriously ill. Doctors found that he had severe heart disease. He also suffered from bronchitis and problems with his eyes. He could hardly write any longer. Balzac and Ewelina finally married on 14 March 1850. The wedding took place in the church of Saint Barbara in Berdychiv, a town in Ukraine. Balzac was already very ill. At the end of April, the couple began the long and painful journey back across Europe. They reached Paris late during the night of 20 to 21 May 1850. Their arrival became like a scene from one of Balzac's darkest stories. He had prepared a splendid house for Ewelina in the rue Fortunée in Paris. It was filled with works of art, flowers, and lights. However, when they arrived during the night, nobody opened the door. The servant who had been left in charge had become mentally ill. He had damaged parts of the house and locked himself inside. A locksmith had to open the door so that the exhausted couple could enter their own home. Balzac lived for less than three more months. His legs became badly swollen, an infection developed, and his sight became weaker. On 18 August 1850, Victor Hugo visited him and found him close to death. Balzac died that night at the age of fifty-one. A famous story says that, while dying, he called for Bianchon, the great doctor from his novels. It was as though the world he had invented had become more real to him than the real world. There is no proof that this story is true. However, as one scholar wrote, it is exactly the kind of thing that Balzac might have done. His funeral took place on 21 August 1850. Balzac was buried in the Père Lachaise Cemetery, on the same heights from which Rastignac had challenged Paris. Victor Hugo gave a famous speech beside the grave. He said that all Balzac's works together formed one single book. It was a living, bright, and deep book in which the whole of modern civilization could be seen moving. Ewelina de Balzac remained in Paris. Over time, she paid all her husband's debts. She protected his papers and arranged for his unfinished books to be completed and published. Le Député d'Arcis appeared in 1854. Charles Rabou completed the unfinished work. Les Paysans, or "The Peasants", was also unfinished and appeared in 1855. Ewelina died in April 1882 and was buried in the same grave as Balzac. Balzac's mother died in 1854. During the 1850s, his sister Laure Surville published the first biography of him. She based it partly on his letters. La Comédie humaine is the name that Balzac gave, from 1841, to his main collection of novels and stories. It contains about ninety finished works. Balzac planned to write many more. A list that he printed in 1845 contains 137 titles. More than one third of these planned works were therefore never written. Even though it was never finished, the collection is very large. It has thousands of pages and about 2,500 named characters. Balzac explained the purpose of the work in his foreword of 1842. He wanted to write the kind of history that ordinary historians often leave out: the history of manners. By "manners", he meant the everyday ways in which people live, feel and behave in a society. The novels cover a period from about the French Revolution of 1789 to Balzac's own time. Most of their stories take place during the Restoration, from 1815 to 1830, and the July Monarchy, from 1830 to 1848. Balzac wrote that French society itself would be the historian and that he would only be its secretary. The "Avant-propos", or foreword, of 1842 is one of the most studied texts about the history of the novel. In it, Balzac explains that his main idea came from a comparison between human society and the animal world. Balzac followed with great interest the debates between important French naturalists. Naturalists were scientists who studied living things. He was especially interested in Georges Cuvier and Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire. Geoffroy believed that all animals were different forms of one basic plan of life. Their surroundings helped to shape them into different species. Balzac used a similar idea to describe society. Just as there are different animal species, he wrote, there are and always will be different social types. For Balzac, a soldier, a shopkeeper, a lawyer, a priest and a rich man with no work were as different from one another as a wolf, a crow and a sheep. An animal is shaped by its surroundings. In the same way, a person is shaped by his or her social surroundings: the home, the town, the job, the social class and the amount of money the person has. This is why Balzac describes houses, streets, clothes and furniture so carefully. For him, these details are not only decoration. They help to form people's lives and characters. The scholars who took part in a large conference about Balzac in 1980 showed how strongly these scientific ideas shaped his whole system. They also showed that the ideas agreed with his political views. They allowed him to describe very great changes in society while he continued to believe that society remained, at a deeper level, one complete whole. Two other statements from the foreword became famous. Balzac said that his list of invented characters would compete with the état civil, the official French record of births, marriages and deaths. He also said that he wrote by the light of two eternal truths: Religion and Monarchy. The section about his ideas later in this article explains this surprising statement. Balzac divided his novels and stories into three large groups. He divided the first group again into six kinds of "scenes": Études de mœurs (Studies of Manners) form the main part of the collection. These novels describe life in France. The group has six parts: Scenes of Private Life, Scenes of Provincial Life, Scenes of Parisian Life, Scenes of Political Life, Scenes of Military Life and Scenes of Country Life. Études philosophiques (Philosophical Studies) try to discover the hidden causes behind life in society. They often include strange, fantastic or religious ideas. Examples include La Peau de chagrin and Louis Lambert. Études analytiques (Analytical Studies) are clever books written more like essays. They examine the main rules of life in society. Examples include the Physiologie du mariage and the Petites Misères de la vie conjugale. Balzac described these three levels as effects, causes and principles. The Studies of Manners show what happens in society. The Philosophical Studies ask why it happens. The Analytical Studies try to explain its general laws. The system looks very clear on paper. In practice, Balzac often wrote quickly and under great pressure. He moved some books from one group to another, and several parts remained very small. However, the plan shows his greatest aim. He did not only want to tell stories. He wanted to explain a whole world. One of the most important features of La Comédie humaine is that many characters return in several books. The scholar Fernand Lotte counted about 2,500 characters in the whole collection. Of these, 573 appear in more than one novel or story. The banker Nucingen appears most often, in thirty-one works. He is followed by the doctor Horace Bianchon, who appears in twenty-nine works, the fashionable Henri de Marsay, who appears in twenty-seven, and Rastignac, who appears in twenty-five. This system has several effects. It joins the different books together and makes them part of one world. It also saves time, because Balzac does not need to introduce a well-known character again. Most importantly, it makes the world of the books seem real. Rastignac first appears as a young man in 1819 in Le Père Goriot. He returns years later in other novels, when he has become rich and hard. Readers feel that he has continued to live between the books, even when Balzac was not writing about him. The writer Félicien Marceau compared this effect to talk in a small town, where every name reminds people of several other stories. Readers can also see the characters change over time. Rastignac begins as a kind and warm-hearted student. Step by step, Paris teaches him to become a cold and successful man. In the later novels, he is a count, a government minister and a millionaire. Vautrin, the escaped prisoner, ends his career as the head of the Paris security police. This ending is dark but also based on real life. Vidocq, the first real head of this police force, had also been a criminal. Doctor Bianchon is honest and hard-working. He is present at about half of the deathbeds in La Comédie humaine. According to a famous story, Balzac even called for Bianchon when he himself was dying. Goriot, however, never returns. Balzac did not later write about the earlier years of Goriot's life. Two novels stand at the centre of this large group of connected stories: Illusions perdues and Splendeurs et misères des courtisanes. Albert Béguin counted 265 characters in these two books. Of these, 147 also appear in other parts of La Comédie humaine. This is a much larger share than in most of Balzac's books. Almost every part of Balzac's world has a connection with these two novels. Béguin called Le Père Goriot the "mother cell" from which the whole connected system developed. He saw Illusions perdues and Splendeurs et misères des courtisanes together as the central turning point of the system. This section gives short descriptions of some of Balzac's best-known works. The table in the section "Selected works" below gives links to the complete French texts on Wikisource. Eugénie Grandet (1833). The story takes place in the quiet town of Saumur. Old Grandet once made wooden barrels, but he has secretly become very rich. His love of gold controls the whole house. His daughter Eugénie falls in love with her poor cousin Charles and gives him her small collection of gold coins. Her father's cold anger and Charles's later betrayal slowly change her. She begins as a fresh young woman and ends as a lonely, generous and unhappy rich woman. The novel is one of literature's most complete studies of greed, or the love of money. Le Père Goriot (1835). This novel is described above. Goriot's blind love for his daughters, Rastignac's lessons in ambition and Vautrin's terrible ideas about society have made it Balzac's most widely read novel. Henry James placed it among the small number of the greatest novels ever written. Le Colonel Chabert (1832). Colonel Chabert was officially reported dead after one of Napoleon's battles. Years later, he returns to Paris. His wife has married another man and does not want Chabert to return. The law does not know what to do with a dead man who is still alive. Critics often describe the work as a short and powerful masterpiece about war, money, marriage and personal identity. La Recherche de l'Absolu (1834). In Flanders, Balthazar Claës destroys his loving family because he cannot stop his chemical experiments. He is searching for the "Absolute", the one basic element behind all matter. In this novel, science becomes a passion as dangerous as greed or gambling. Le Lys dans la vallée (1836). In the peaceful valley of the Indre, near Saché, the young Félix de Vandenesse falls in love with Madame de Mortsauf, a married and deeply moral woman. Their love remains pure, but it destroys her all the same. The novel contains some of Balzac's most personal memories. These include memories of his childhood without enough love and of his relationship with Madame de Berny. César Birotteau (1837). César Birotteau is an honest seller of perfume in Paris. A land deal and the plans of the banker Nucingen ruin him. He spends the rest of his life paying back every franc that he owes. He dies from joy on the day when his good name is restored. Balzac turns the laws of business failure into a powerful story and makes an ordinary shopkeeper into a kind of hero. Illusions perdues (1837 to 1843). Many readers and critics believe that this is Balzac's greatest novel. Lucien de Rubempré is a handsome young poet from the provinces. He comes to Paris because he wants fame, but journalism, pride and debt destroy him. At the same time, his brother-in-law David Séchard is a printer and inventor in the provinces. Other people quietly steal his invention from him. The novel gives a complete picture of the modern world of print. It describes newspapers, publishers, critics, paper-making and the buying and selling of opinions. Splendeurs et misères des courtisanes (1838 to 1847). This novel continues the story of Illusions perdues. Vautrin is now hiding under the clothes and name of a Spanish priest. He tries to rebuild Lucien's fortune. To do this, he uses the love of Esther, a courtesan, and the money of the banker Nucingen. A courtesan was a woman who was paid to spend time with rich men. The story includes police officers, secret agents, prisons and suicide. At the end, Vautrin makes an extraordinary change. The great criminal becomes the head of the police. La Cousine Bette (1846). The story takes place in Paris during the rule of Louis Philippe. Cousin Bette is poor and unmarried. She secretly plans the destruction of the Hulot family. The attractive but dangerous Madame Marneffe helps her. At the same time, the old Baron Hulot destroys his life because he cannot control his desire for women. Modern critics also study the novel for what it says about gender, jealousy and desire. Gender means the roles that society gives to men and women. Le Cousin Pons (1847). Pons is a poor old musician who owns a wonderful collection of paintings and art objects. He does not fully understand how valuable it is. When the people around him discover its value, they gather around the dying man like hungry birds. Many readers consider this one of Balzac's darkest and most moving books. Many other works are also important. Gobseck (1830) is the story of a money-lender who thinks deeply about money and human life. Sarrasine (1830) is a strange story about love, art and a mistake about a person's identity. It became famous again during the 20th century. La Fille aux yeux d'or (1835) is a violent Paris story about desire. Le Chef-d'œuvre inconnu (1831) tells of an old painter who destroys his own masterpiece because he wants to make it perfect. La Femme de trente ans (1832 to 1834) gave the French language a new type of character: the interesting "woman of thirty". Ursule Mirouët (1841) and La Rabouilleuse (1842) are two important novels about family battles over inheritance in the provinces. An inheritance is the money and property that a person leaves after death. Une ténébreuse affaire (1841) is one of the first political detective novels. In Le Médecin de campagne (1833) and Le Curé de village (1839), Balzac presents his ideas about society and religion. Les Paysans was left unfinished and published in 1855. It is his dark study of the struggle between peasants and landowners. Money has a very important place in Balzac's novels. From his own painful experience, he understood that the France created by the Revolution had become a society ruled by money. The old rules based on birth and social rank were becoming weaker. People could become rich very quickly, but they could also lose everything just as quickly. Balzac's novels give many exact figures. They tell readers how much people earn, how much rent they pay, what dowries they receive, and how much they owe. A dowry is money or property that a woman brings into a marriage. The novels also give exact prices and rates of interest. Readers in Balzac's time knew these things well and could check his figures. His numbers were usually correct. Balzac describes every level of the world of money. At the lowest level are money-lenders such as the frightening but intelligent Gobseck. Gobseck believes that gold contains everything that human beings desire. In the middle are shopkeepers and merchants such as César Birotteau. For Birotteau, paying every debt is almost a religious duty. At the highest level stands the powerful banker Nucingen. In La Maison Nucingen, Balzac explains carefully how this "Napoleon of finance" made his fortune. Three times, Nucingen pretended that his bank was close to failure. This frightened the people who had lent him money. He then paid them with shares that were worth less than they appeared to be. Each false crisis made him richer. Modern readers may feel that these pages describe financial scandals from a much later time. One scholar writes that Balzac understood almost everything about capital and credit. In Balzac's work, debt is more than a subject. It makes the stories move forward. The struggle between people who owe money and the people who have lent it appears in many of his plots. Debt also controlled Balzac's own life. From 1828 until his death, he was almost always in debt. In a strange way, this helped to produce his books. He had to write to pay what he owed, and every new debt forced him to write another work. Behind Balzac's picture of society lies a philosophy of life. He believed that every human being receives a limited amount of life energy. He sometimes imagined it as a kind of living fluid. Thought, desire, and strong passion use up this energy. A person who desires too strongly uses up life very quickly. La Peau de chagrin turns this idea into a fable. A magic piece of skin becomes smaller whenever its owner makes a wish. At the same time, the owner's remaining life becomes shorter. Louis Lambert tells the story of a boy with an extraordinary mind. His thought becomes so powerful that it destroys both his body and his mind. All his will passes into the life of the spirit, and he dies because he has thought too much. In many of Balzac's philosophical stories, one idea or passion becomes too strong and destroys the person who follows it. The painter Frenhofer is destroyed by his search for perfect art in Le Chef-d'œuvre inconnu. The chemist Claës destroys himself through his search for the basic secret of matter in La Recherche de l'Absolu. The love of money rules the miser Grandet. Goriot is destroyed by his uncontrolled love for his daughters. Balzac called thought the great destroyer of humanity, and he built many stories around this idea. This helps to explain why so many of Balzac's characters live for only one passion. Critics sometimes call this monomania. Monomania is a state in which one fixed idea rules a person's mind. This single passion gives Balzac's characters much of their power. It also shows one of Balzac's own fears. He knew that he was using up his life in the same way when he worked for eighteen hours a day. The same human energy can also move upward toward religion and mysticism. Balzac read the Swedish thinker Emanuel Swedenborg, who wrote about visions of heaven. Balzac used Swedenborg's ideas rather freely in Louis Lambert, and especially in Séraphîta (1834). Séraphîta is the strange and beautiful story of an angel-like being who lives in the mountains of Norway. Both a man and a woman fall in love with this being. Balzac dreamed that human love and human will could rise, step by step, until they reached the level of angels. However, at the end of Séraphîta, he also accepts that this dream fails. Human beings remain tied to time and to their own weaknesses. Balzac's novels often place two different parts of France against one another. The first is la province, the world of towns far from Paris. Life there is slow and closed. Everyone watches everyone else, everybody knows the other families, and hatreds can continue for many years. The other world is Paris. Paris is fast, bright, and cruel. It attracts young people and then uses up their energy. Balzac describes it more than once as a monster that eats people. The whole story of Illusions perdues follows a young man as he moves from the provinces to Paris. However, Balzac does not simply say that one of these worlds is good and the other is bad. His provincial towns contain monsters such as Grandet and the Rogron cousins, who make the young Pierrette suffer. They also contain people of great goodness. Paris destroys Lucien, but it also contains the Cénacle. The Cénacle is a group of poor, honest, and gifted young men who support one another. Balzac is interested in the whole system. He shows how people, money, and ambition move from the provinces to Paris, and sometimes return. In both places, readers can follow the rise of the bourgeoisie, or middle class, and the slow fall of the old nobility. One subject appears throughout La Comédie humaine: the place of young people in a society that does not know what to do with them. The critic Pierre Barbéris wrote a long study about Balzac and the mal du siècle. This French expression means the "sickness of the century". It was often used for the sadness felt by the Romantic generation. Barbéris explained this sadness through history. He did not see it as only a general feeling of unhappiness.

Charles Pierre Baudelaire (; 9 April 1821 – 31 August 1867) was a French poet, art critic, and translator. He was born and died in Paris. He is also known for translating the stories of the American writer Edgar Allan Poe into French. His translations helped to make Poe famous in France. Baudelaire's most famous book is Les Fleurs du Mal ("The Flowers of Evil"), first published in 1857. It is a collection of poems written in verse. A smaller collection called Les Épaves ("The Wrecks") followed in 1866. After Baudelaire's death, a collection of his poems in prose was also published. It first appeared under the title Petits Poèmes en prose, but today it is usually called Le Spleen de Paris. Baudelaire also wrote important essays about painting, literature, and music. Baudelaire has an important place in the history of modern poetry. He took many ideas and feelings from the Romantic writers who came before him, but he changed them into something new. His work had a major influence on later French poetry. Younger poets such as Verlaine, Mallarmé, and Rimbaud saw him as a master. In a famous letter written in 1871, Rimbaud called him "the first seer, king of poets, a true God". His life was short and difficult, and many parts of his work are closely connected with his personal experience. His father died when he was five years old. His mother later married an army officer, Jacques Aupick. At first the boy got on with his stepfather, but their relationship later became very difficult. As a young man, he received the money left by his father and quickly spent about half of it. A court then placed the rest under the control of a lawyer. He also had a long and troubled relationship with the actress Jeanne Duval. In 1857, a court decided that Les Fleurs du Mal was an offence against public morals. Baudelaire had to pay a fine, and six poems were banned. He later tried to enter the Académie française, but he failed. He moved to Belgium in 1864. In March 1866, a sudden illness paralysed the right side of his body and left him almost unable to speak. Baudelaire helped to create the image of himself as a poète maudit, or "cursed poet". However, his poetry is carefully constructed and shows close control of language and form. The judgment of 1857 was cancelled by the highest French court only in 1949, almost one hundred years later. By that time, Les Fleurs du Mal had become widely studied and had strongly influenced modern poetry. Charles-Pierre Baudelaire was born on 9 April 1821 at 13 rue Hautefeuille in Paris. His parents were very different from each other. His father, Joseph-François Baudelaire, was sixty-one years old when Charles was born. As a young man, he had become a Catholic priest, but he later left the Church. He worked as a private teacher for the two sons of the count of Choiseul-Praslin, a noble family. For his young pupils, he wrote a small Latin schoolbook and illustrated it himself with watercolour pictures. During the Revolution, when the boys' parents were put in prison, he continued to care for the children and tried to help the family. Later, he held several jobs in the offices of the French Senate. He liked the manners and culture of the 18th century. He loved painting and painted as an amateur. Joseph-François already had a son from his first marriage, Claude-Alphonse, born in 1805. In September 1819, he married Caroline Dufaÿs, who had been born in London in 1793. Her father was a French soldier who had left France during the Revolution. He died in 1795 during a failed landing in Brittany by royalist troops, soldiers who were loyal to the king. Her mother brought her back to France in 1800 but died soon after the journey. Caroline was seven years old. She was then brought up by the family of the lawyer Pierre Pérignon. Her husband was thirty-four years older than she was. Baudelaire's father died on 10 February 1827, when Charles was five years old. The boy kept only a soft and uncertain memory of him, but his love of pictures probably came from his father. After his father's death, Charles and his mother spent the end of the summer of 1827 together in a small house at Neuilly, near Paris. They then lived quietly together in the city for several more months. Baudelaire remembered this short time throughout his life as a lost period of happiness. One of his poems, "Je n'ai pas oublié, voisine de la ville...", keeps the image of the "white house, small but quiet". Much later, in a long letter of 6 May 1861, he reminded his mother of that early time. There had been in his childhood, he wrote, "a period of passionate love" for her. She had been "at once an idol and a comrade". This happy period ended on 8 November 1828, when Caroline married Jacques Aupick, an army officer who later had a successful career. Aupick had been born in 1789. His father was an Irish soldier who served in the French army and died from wounds received in battle. His mother was probably English. Aupick lost both parents when he was a small child and was brought up by a judge in the small northern town of Gravelines. He worked hard and slowly rose to higher positions in the army. He became a general and later the head of the École polytechnique, a famous military school in Paris. He later served as French ambassador in Constantinople and Madrid, and finally became a senator. At first, Charles and his stepfather had a good relationship. It became difficult when Charles made it clear that he wanted to become a writer and nothing else. For many years, books described Aupick as a cruel ruler of the family. The scholar Claude Pichois later gave a more balanced picture. Aupick was an honest and hard-working man, but he could not understand a boy with such sensitive feelings. Baudelaire later remembered his mother's second marriage as a painful break in his childhood. It ended the time of what he called "unbroken tenderness". In his mind, the general came to represent a hard society ruled by money, duty, and success. In 1832, the family moved to Lyon, where the army had sent Aupick. Charles was sent to a boarding school. He remembered these years as dark and closed: a black city, fog, and locked doors. In 1836, Aupick was called back to Paris, and Charles entered the famous Lycée Louis-le-Grand, again as a boarder. He was a gifted but uneven student. He did very well in Latin verse. In 1837, he won the second prize for Latin verse in the concours général. This was a national competition between the best pupils in France. He read a great number of books, but his independent behaviour often annoyed his teachers. In April 1839, the school expelled him. Another pupil had passed him a note during a lesson, and Charles swallowed the paper instead of giving it to the teacher. He finished the school year as a day pupil at another Paris school, the Collège Saint-Louis. In August 1839, he passed the baccalauréat, the French final school examination. These eight years in boarding schools felt like years in prison to him. They gave him a strong knowledge of Latin and of the classical writers, and this learning can be seen throughout his work. At the same time, they left him with a deep and lasting feeling of loneliness. After leaving school, Baudelaire registered as a law student, but he rarely attended classes. He told his older brother that he wanted only one thing: to become independent as soon as possible and live by writing. He spent his time with young poets in the Latin Quarter, including Gustave Le Vavasseur and Ernest Prarond. During this period, he had a relationship with a poor woman called Sara who worked as a prostitute. He also caught a venereal disease, an infection passed on during sex. His biographers usually identify it as syphilis, though the exact diagnosis has been questioned. There was no cure at that time. The illness may have harmed his health throughout his life and helped cause his early death. His mother and General Aupick were worried by his free way of life and by his growing debts. In June 1841, they placed him on a ship called the Paquebot des Mers du Sud, which sailed from Bordeaux for Calcutta. The voyage did not reach its planned destination. A violent storm near the Cape of Good Hope badly damaged the ship. It stopped for repairs at Mauritius, then sailed on to the island of Bourbon, now called La Réunion. There Baudelaire refused to travel any further, and the ship left for Calcutta without him. He came home on another ship, the Alcide, and reached France in February 1842. Aupick was angry, but the voyage became very important for Baudelaire's poetry. The sea, ports, tropical smells, bright light, and distant islands appeared again and again in his work. Poems such as "L'Albatros", "Parfum exotique", and "La Chevelure" were partly based on these memories. When Baudelaire returned to Paris, he turned twenty-one on 9 April 1842. A few weeks later, he received the money left by his father. It was about 100,000 francs, a large amount at the time. He rented rooms on the île Saint-Louis, and in 1843 he moved into the beautiful old hôtel Pimodan, now called the hôtel de Lauzun. There he lived as a "dandy", a man who tries to make his clothes, manners, and whole life into a work of art. He bought expensive clothes, old furniture, paintings, and rare books. A group of artists met in the same house to use hashish. The writer Théophile Gautier took part, and he gave the group its name, the "Club des Hachichins". The meetings took place in the apartment of the painter Fernand Boissard. A doctor named Moreau de Tours also took part. He studied mental illness and used the meetings for his medical research. Baudelaire himself came only rarely because hashish did not interest him much. The novelist Balzac attended one meeting. Baudelaire later told the story in Les Paradis artificiels: Balzac examined the drug, smelled it, and handed it back without touching it. At the hôtel Pimodan, Baudelaire probably met Gautier for the first time, but their real friendship began only in the 1850s. His close companions during these years were the poet Théodore de Banville and the writer Champfleury. He also met Nadar, who later became a famous photographer. Around 1842, he met Jeanne Duval, a woman of colour who had played small parts in a Paris theatre. Almost nothing about her life is known for certain, not even her real family name. In 1859, she told a hospital that she had been born in Saint-Domingue, now Haiti. For almost twenty years, she was his lover. They separated and came back together many times. Nadar saw her for the last time in 1870; she was walking with crutches. Several well-known love poems in Les Fleurs du Mal, including "La Chevelure" and "Le Balcon", are connected with her. In only two years, Baudelaire spent about 44,500 francs, almost half of his fortune. His worried mother went to court. On 21 September 1844, the court decided that a lawyer, Narcisse-Désiré Ancelle, would control the money that remained. From that time, the poet received a small yearly allowance: 2,400 francs at first, about 200 francs each month. Baudelaire felt deeply humiliated. He was twenty-three years old but was treated like a child and had to explain how he spent every franc. The decision made his relationship with his mother more bitter and kept him poor for the rest of his life. He lived with debts, moved again and again from one furnished room to another, and wrote endless letters about money. In the spring of 1855, he told his mother that he had been forced to move six times in a single month. Over his whole life, Claude Pichois counted at least thirty different homes in Paris. He often had to write quickly for newspapers simply to earn enough money to live. Over time, however, he and Ancelle slowly began to trust each other. During his years in Belgium, Baudelaire sent the lawyer some of his most honest and personal letters. Baudelaire first became known to the public not as a poet but as an art critic. In May 1845, he published his first work, the Salon de 1845. He signed it "Baudelaire-Dufaÿs", adding his mother's family name to his own. The book was still close to a simple list of paintings, but its judgments were already strong. Baudelaire said that Eugène Delacroix was the best painter in the exhibition. The little book found very few readers, and Baudelaire himself was soon unhappy with it. A few weeks later, on 30 June 1845, Baudelaire tried to kill himself with a knife in a Paris café. In a farewell letter to Ancelle, he wrote: "I am killing myself because I am useless to others, and dangerous to myself." He also wrote, more strangely: "I am killing myself because I believe that I am immortal, and because I hope." In the same letter, he left almost everything he owned to Jeanne Duval. The wound was real, and for several days he could not leave Jeanne's rooms. He then lived for a while with his mother and the general. But he could not accept the rules of their house, and he soon returned to his free and disordered life. The following year, the Salon de 1846 was a much more important work. It was no longer a list but a complete book of ideas about art. It begins with an unusual address, "To the bourgeois", and asks serious questions. What makes a good critic? What is Romantic art? What is colour? The chapter on colour is one of the most original parts of the book. Baudelaire describes nature as a great concert of colours, in which every tone lives in harmony with the others. For him, colour works like music. To support this idea, he quotes a page by the German writer E. T. A. Hoffmann about the hidden links between colours, sounds, and perfumes. The famous poem "Correspondances" later developed the same idea. Baudelaire again said that Delacroix was better than the painters of the Ingres school and the fashionable painters of the time. He strongly attacked Horace Vernet, a painter famous for pictures of military glory. Some readers have understood this attack as an indirect attack on General Aupick. The most important part of the book is its final chapter, "On the Heroism of Modern Life". Here Baudelaire first explained an idea that became central to his thinking about art. Every period of history has its own kind of beauty. The black coats, crowded streets, and ordinary people of the modern city also have their own beauty and heroism. Artists must learn to see them. During the same years, Baudelaire wrote short pieces for newspapers such as Le Corsaire-Satan. In 1847, he published his only short story, La Fanfarlo. Its hero, Samuel Cramer, is an ironic portrait of the young dandy that Baudelaire had once been. He may have first seen the actress Marie Daubrun, "the woman with the green eyes", on a Paris stage in 1847. The first clear signs of a close relationship, however, date only from 1854. She inspired a second group of love poems, including "L'Invitation au voyage" and "Le Poison". Another important woman was Apollonie Sabatier, called "la Présidente", who welcomed painters and writers into her home. Baudelaire had probably first met her during the 1840s in the circle of the hôtel Pimodan, but their special relationship began in the early 1850s. Between December 1852 and May 1854, he sent her seven letters with poems. He wrote them in a disguised hand and did not sign them. Most of these poems, such as "Réversibilité" and "Le Flambeau vivant", show a more spiritual and ideal kind of love. They form the third great group of love poems in Les Fleurs du Mal. He revealed that he was the author only on 18 August 1857, two days before the trial of his book. He asked for her help and listed "the monsters" for her: the president, the judges, and the prosecutor Pinard, marked "fearsome". Their love story ended at the end of that same month, but she remained a loyal friend. In February 1848, the Revolution of 1848 began in Paris, and Baudelaire took part in it. He was seen in the street fighting carrying a gun. According to one witness, he shouted that General Aupick should be shot. His political anger and his anger against his family had become closely connected. With Champfleury and Toubin, he started a small newspaper called Le Salut public, but only two issues appeared. For several weeks, he then worked for another paper, La Tribune nationale. In June 1848, when the workers of Paris rose again, he is said to have fought on their side. In October, he even went to Châteauroux, in central France, to run a small conservative newspaper, but his ideas shocked its staff and owners. The bloody fighting of June and the coup d'état of 2 December 1851, when Louis-Napoléon took power by force, ended his hopes for political change. "The Second of December took all politics out of my body," he wrote to Ancelle in 1852. If he had voted, he joked in the same letter, he could only have voted for himself. After this, his view of life became much darker. From the writer Joseph de Maistre, he took the Christian idea of original sin, the belief that human beings are born with evil already inside them. This became an important part of his thinking. However, the memory of 1848 never completely left his poetry. Old women, rag-pickers, workers, and other poor and broken people of the Paris streets appear again and again in his poems about the city. In 1847, Baudelaire discovered the work of Edgar Allan Poe in French newspapers. The first story he read was "The Black Cat", in a translation by Isabelle Meunier. Poe's work made a very strong impression on him. Years later, he explained this feeling in a letter to the critic Théophile Thoré. He had translated Poe so patiently, he wrote, "because he resembled me". When he first opened one of Poe's books, he had found, "with terror and delight", subjects that he himself had dreamed about. He had even found whole sentences that he had thought, but that Poe had written twenty years before. Baudelaire saw Poe as a brother. They shared the idea that art should be carefully and consciously made, and both were interested in strange and disturbing subjects. Baudelaire also saw a similar fate in Poe's life: a writer destroyed by a society that cared mainly about money. Baudelaire's first translation of Poe, the story "Mesmeric Revelation", appeared in 1848. For the next seventeen years, he gave a large part of his energy to translating Poe and making French readers admire him. He taught himself enough English for this work and questioned Americans who lived in Paris. In 1852, he published his first long essay about Poe's life and work. His translations appeared one after another through the publisher Michel Lévy: Histoires extraordinaires in 1856, Nouvelles Histoires extraordinaires in 1857, Les Aventures d'Arthur Gordon Pym in 1858, Eurêka in November 1863 (the printed date is 1864), and Histoires grotesques et sérieuses in 1865. Even the title Histoires extraordinaires was not Poe's own title. Baudelaire created it for French readers. The first printing of 6,000 copies sold quickly. This work helped Baudelaire in three ways. It gave him his most regular income, more than all his own books together. It also gave him the respectable position of a serious working writer. Finally, translating Poe helped him develop his own art. Poe's ideas about short works and carefully planned effects made Baudelaire even more interested in tight form and careful work. Baudelaire's picture of Poe as a great mind destroyed by a society ruled by money was also a picture of himself. By defending the American writer, Baudelaire was also attacking his own age. The book published in 1857 was the result of about fifteen years of work. As early as 1845, Baudelaire announced a future book called Les Lesbiennes. In 1848 and 1851, he used the title Les Limbes. The final title, Les Fleurs du Mal, perhaps suggested by the writer Hippolyte Babou, appeared in 1855. That year, the respected Revue des deux mondes published eighteen of the poems under this title. This publication introduced the poems to a larger group of readers. These poems later formed the centre of the book. Baudelaire was never satisfied with his work and continued to delay the complete book. In the end, his friend Auguste Poulet-Malassis, a young printer from Alençon, published it. Poulet-Malassis remained loyal to Baudelaire until the end and lost money because of this loyalty. On 27 April 1857, General Aupick died. His widow moved to Honfleur, where she lived in a small house above the sea. Baudelaire called it the "toy house". He later spent several useful periods of work there. On 25 June 1857, Les Fleurs du Mal went on sale. About 1,100 copies were printed for sale. About twenty more, printed on fine Holland paper, went to friends such as Delacroix, Gautier, and the poet's mother. The book contained one hundred poems divided into five sections. Fifty-two of them appeared there for the first time; the others had already been published in reviews. It opens with "Au lecteur", or "To the Reader", a poem placed before the numbered series. Its last line became famous: "Hypocrite lecteur, mon semblable, mon frère !" ("Hypocrite reader, my equal, my brother!"). On 5 July, Gustave Bourdin attacked the book violently in the newspaper Le Figaro. Two days later, the government asked the courts to act. Baudelaire did not give in. On 9 July, he told his mother that the book was clothed in "a cold and sinister beauty" and had been made "with fury and patience". It would live, he wrote, in the memory of educated readers beside the best poems of Hugo, Gautier, and even Byron. In the days that followed, the police began taking copies from Paris shops. On 11 July, Baudelaire sent his publisher a hurried note: "Quick, hide the whole edition, and hide it well." He himself had already hidden fifty copies. The authorities brought the author and his publishers before the sixth court of the Seine. They were accused of offending public and religious morals. The trial took place on 20 August 1857. The prosecutor was Ernest Pinard, the same man who had prosecuted Flaubert's Madame Bovary in January. In that earlier case, Flaubert had been found not guilty. Pinard handled Baudelaire's case carefully. He almost abandoned the religious part of the accusation and concentrated on the poems about the body and sexual desire. Baudelaire's lawyer, Gustave Chaix d'Est-Ange, failed to save the book. The court gave its judgment on the same day. It found no offence against religion, but it found an offence against public morals. Baudelaire had to pay a fine of 300 francs, and each publisher had to pay 100 francs. The court ordered six poems to be removed: "Lesbos", the first poem called "Femmes damnées", "Le Léthé", "À celle qui est trop gaie", "Les Bijoux", and "Les Métamorphoses du vampire". The judges said that the poems showed the body in a coarse and direct way that offended accepted ideas of modesty. The poems were therefore punished not mainly for their ideas, but for the open way in which they represented the body and sexual desire. At that time, "realism" in literature was a major subject of public debate. Baudelaire had hoped that the trial would show the public that he had done nothing wrong, and the judgment affected him deeply. He said again and again that the court had misunderstood the book. In notes prepared for his lawyer, he argued that Les Fleurs du Mal had to be judged as a complete work. When read as a whole, he said, its moral meaning was clear: it showed horror at evil. To describe evil with horror was not the same as praising it. He did not appeal against the judgment. At the end of 1857, he wrote to the Empress, and in January 1858 his fine was reduced to fifty francs. Some writers supported him. Four favourable reviews, by Thierry, Dulamon, Asselineau, and Barbey d'Aurevilly, were printed together in a small booklet for the judges because most newspapers had refused to publish them. Flaubert and Custine sent Baudelaire warm messages, while Sainte-Beuve gave him careful private support. From his island of exile, Victor Hugo wrote that the poems "shine and dazzle like stars". In October 1859, Victor Hugo sent Baudelaire an open letter. Baudelaire had asked for it as a preface to his small book on Gautier. In this letter, Hugo thanked him for two poems dedicated to him and made a famous judgment. Baudelaire, he wrote, had created "a new shiver", or un frisson nouveau, in art. Hugo also politely explained that their ideas about art were different. He himself had never believed in art for art's sake, he wrote, but always in art for progress. The six poems remained banned until 31 May 1949. On that date, under a law passed in 1946, the highest French court cancelled the judgment of 1857. The trial did not stop Baudelaire's work. Instead, it pushed him to give the book a new form. During the following years, he wrote some of his greatest poems, including "Le Voyage", "Le Cygne", "Les Sept Vieillards", and "Les Petites Vieilles". "Le Voyage", the longest poem in the book, was probably written at Honfleur, in his mother's house, at the start of 1859. The last three were dedicated to Victor Hugo. He also prepared a second edition of Les Fleurs du Mal. It was published in the first days of February 1861, and 1,500 copies were printed. The six banned poems were removed, and thirty-two new poems were added. Nearly all of the new poems had already appeared in reviews. Only one, "La Fin de la journée", was printed here for the first time. Baudelaire had wanted a symbolic picture at the front of the book. The engraver Félix Bracquemond could not produce one that satisfied him, so the edition carried an engraved portrait of the poet instead. The new edition also contained a new section called "Tableaux parisiens", or "Paris Pictures". Scholars usually use this 1861 edition today because it was the last one published under Baudelaire's own control. Government lawyers examined it but did not take any action. Other books appeared during the same period. Les Paradis artificiels (1860) is a two-part study of hashish and opium. Its second part is a French version, with Baudelaire's own comments, of Thomas De Quincey's book about opium. In February 1860, after hearing Wagner's music in Paris, Baudelaire sent the composer a letter full of admiration. Richard Wagner et Tannhäuser à Paris (1861) strongly defended the composer after Paris audiences had laughed at his work. In Wagner's music, Baudelaire found support for his own idea of "correspondences", or links between the senses and the arts. He also wrote essays about living writers such as Hugo, Gautier, and Banville. In 1859, he published the Salon de 1859. In this long essay, he defended imagination. He called it "the queen of the faculties". He argued against the idea that art should only copy the real world exactly. Photography, he wrote, should remain only "the servant of the sciences and the arts". In 1863, Le Figaro finally published Le Peintre de la vie moderne, or "The Painter of Modern Life", about the artist Constantin Guys. Guys drew quick scenes of daily life for newspapers. His drawings had given Baudelaire back his pleasure in art after French painting in 1859 had disappointed him. The essay was mostly written by 1860. It became Baudelaire's most important explanation of what "modern" art should be. In December 1861, Baudelaire took a step that surprised his friends. He became a candidate for a seat in the Académie française, first for the seat of Eugène Scribe and then for that of the churchman Lacordaire. His friends were surprised by the decision. It was partly meant to shock people and partly an attempt to appear respectable to his mother. However, Baudelaire was also serious. He believed that the Académie, the most important French literary institution, should respect pure poetry and should also recognise the writer who had been condemned in 1857. Candidates had to visit members of the Académie and ask for their support. These visits did not go well for Baudelaire. Only the old poet Alfred de Vigny welcomed him warmly, and Vigny advised him to withdraw. During the campaign, Sainte-Beuve published an article that praised him but also made fun of him. He called Baudelaire a "nice boy" who had built a "strange kiosk" at the extreme point of "the romantic Kamchatka". Kamchatka is a distant, cold land at the eastern end of Russia. The joke placed Baudelaire at the far edge of literature. Baudelaire withdrew in February 1862. These years of intense work were also years in which his health became worse. From January 1860, Baudelaire suffered his first attacks affecting his brain. In April 1862, his half-brother Alphonse died. His illness was a form of paralysis similar to the one that later struck the poet. Jeanne Duval, partly paralysed since 1859, lived in a care home that he paid for. Poulet-Malassis, deeply in debt, went to prison in 1862 and lost his business. In 1863, he moved to Belgium to escape further legal action. Baudelaire's own money problems also became worse. On 1 November 1863, he sold Michel Lévy the full rights to his five Poe volumes. The price was only 2,000 francs. After this sale, he lost his most regular source of money. In January 1862, Baudelaire noted a strange warning in his private papers. He had felt pass over him "the wind of the wing of imbecility", a failing of the mind. He believed that his death was approaching. During this period, he gave most of his attention to the major work of his last years: the short prose poems. They appeared in groups in newspapers, mainly from 1861 onward. In 1862, La Presse published twenty of them with Baudelaire's opening letter to Arsène Houssaye. His death stopped the collection at fifty poems. On 24 April 1864, Baudelaire arrived in Brussels. He had two hopes. First, he planned to earn money by giving public lectures at the Cercle artistique et littéraire, a private cultural club. Second, he hoped to sign a contract for his complete works with Lacroix and Verboeckhoven, the publishing house that had published Hugo's Les Misérables. The first lecture, about Delacroix, went well and was even praised in the Brussels press. But the next lectures, about Gautier, opium, and hashish, attracted smaller and smaller audiences. There were five lectures in all. Baudelaire had agreed by word of mouth to receive one hundred francs for each one. Instead of five hundred francs, the club sent him only one hundred, with a letter of apology. Lacroix and Verboeckhoven were invited to every lecture but never came. Baudelaire had planned to remain for two months, but he stayed for two years at the hôtel du Grand-Miroir. During this time, he was poor, disappointed, and increasingly bitter. He then began a new writing project: a violent book against Belgium. He collected notes under several changing titles, including Pauvre Belgique !, but he never completed the work. He also wrote a group of sharp satirical poems called the Amoenitates Belgicae. Scholars have argued that his hatred was directed at more than Belgium. Its real target may have been the whole modern world of money and business, as well as Baudelaire's anger at his own failure. He himself said that the Belgian book would be only the first step towards another work called Pauvre France !. The Belgian years also produced Les Épaves in 1866, a small book of twenty-three poems secretly printed in Brussels by Poulet-Malassis. Only 260 copies were made, with the false address "Amsterdam" on the title page. The artist Félicien Rops drew a strange picture for the front. The book included the six banned poems, so the copies meant for France had to cross the border in secret. In May 1868, after the poet's death, a court in Lille even ordered the destruction of Les Épaves. Baudelaire's health was now very poor. Around 15 March 1866, he visited the church of Saint-Loup in Namur with Poulet-Malassis and Félicien Rops. While he was looking at the carved confessionals, he suddenly felt dizzy and fell on the stone floor. He claimed that his foot had slipped, and his friends pretended to believe him. During the following days, his condition became worse. By the end of March, the right side of his body was paralysed, and he had lost the power of speech. He could say almost nothing except a short curse, "crénom". However, part of his mind remained clear, and he recognised the friends who came to visit him. At first, he was cared for in a religious hospital in Brussels. His mother travelled quickly from Honfleur to be with him. In July 1866, Baudelaire was brought back to Paris and placed in a care home in the rue du Dôme. There Mme Paul Meurice played Wagner's music for him on the piano. He remained in this condition for more than a year. Baudelaire died quietly on the morning of 31 August 1867, at the age of forty-six, with his mother at his side. On that same day, a Paris review, the Revue nationale et étrangère, printed one of his last prose poems. On 2 September, he was buried in Montparnasse Cemetery in the same grave as General Aupick. About one hundred people came to the church of Saint-Honoré d'Eylau, and fewer still walked to the grave because many Parisians were away for the summer. Banville and Asselineau spoke there. Among those present were the painter Manet and the young poet Verlaine. His mother died in 1871 and was buried in the same grave. In 1902, a large memorial designed by José de Charmoy was built in the same cemetery. After Baudelaire's death, his writings were collected and arranged. The rights to all his works were sold at auction on 4 December 1867. His friend Asselineau bought them for the publisher Michel Lévy for only 1,750 francs. Between 1868 and 1870, Lévy published the Œuvres complètes, or "Complete Works", in seven volumes, edited by Asselineau and Banville. Three of the seven volumes contained the Poe translations. A third edition of Les Fleurs du Mal, published in 1868 with a preface by Gautier, included new poems, but scholars no longer follow its order. Two volumes, Curiosités esthétiques and L'Art romantique, collected his essays about art and literature. The Petits Poèmes en prose appeared in 1869. His private notebooks, including Fusées and Mon cœur mis à nu, his writings about Belgium, and his letters appeared slowly over many years. Editors continued this work from Eugène Crépet's edition of 1887 to the major scholarly editions of the 20th century. Yves-Gérard Le Dantec prepared the first Pléiade edition of the complete works. Claude Pichois revised it in 1961 and later replaced it with his own two-volume edition of 1975 and 1976. Baudelaire always said that his book was a construction, not a simple collection. "The only praise I ask for this book is that people see that it is not a mere album, and that it has a beginning and an end," he wrote to Vigny in 1861. All the new poems of 1861, he added in the same letter, had been made to fit into this chosen frame. Many critics read the order of the poems as a journey of the soul. The 1861 edition has one hundred and twenty-six poems in six sections. Between the two editions, Baudelaire also moved the wine poems to an earlier place, so that each stage prepares the next. "Spleen et Idéal" ("Spleen and the Ideal") is by far the longest, and it lays the base of everything. Man is pulled in two directions: upward, toward beauty and the love of the spirit; downward, toward "spleen", empty time and death. The section moves through the condition of the poet, the theory of beauty and the three love cycles. Then it falls into spleen, marked by four poems that all carry that name. The "Tableaux parisiens", new in 1861, take the drama into the modern city. Here are the crowds, the old men and women, the poor, and the ghosts of a Paris torn up by Haussmann's building works. "Le Vin" ("Wine") and the section called "Fleurs du Mal" (without "Les": that is the name Baudelaire gave it) pass through the false ways out: drink and forbidden pleasure. "Révolte" ("Revolt") pushes the war with religion as far as a prayer to Satan. "La Mort" ("Death") opens onto the last voyage. The book ends with the last line of "Le Voyage": "Au fond de l'Inconnu pour trouver du nouveau !" ("to the bottom of the Unknown to find something new"). The Italian scholar Mario Richter notes that this last poem no longer says "I" but "we". For him, the final departure toward the unknown is a journey made together. Barbey d'Aurevilly had already pointed this out in 1857, when he spoke of a "secret architecture". Baudelaire himself teased his readers about it. In a draft preface, he played with the idea of explaining "why and how I made this book". Such a study, he wrote, might amuse minds in love with "deep rhetoric", the deeper way in which a book is built. But he refused: an artist does not show the public the machinery of his tricks. In 2001, Mario Richter went looking for this deep rhetoric. His two volumes give the first complete reading of the 1861 book. He follows the poems one by one, in order, like a single story. He notes, for example, that the poem numbers run on across the borders of the sections. He also shows that many key words in the book keep two meanings at the same time. For him, this planned double sense is the deep rhetoric itself. It is also why the poems must be read slowly and in order. In Richter's reading, this structure makes the book a kind of drama of human life. The opening address gives its religious frame. Man is a fallen being, in the hands of the Devil. His worst vice is not crime or lust but Ennui: boredom, a soft monster that dreams of scaffolds while smoking its water pipe. The "Mal" of the title has more than one meaning. It is the deep evil in human nature, the evil men do, and the pain and misery of the poor man's life. The poet's task is to change this dark material into something else. A famous line from a draft epilogue for the 1861 edition says it: "You gave me your mud and I turned it into gold." Spleen is one of the central ideas of the book. In Baudelaire the English word means far more than sadness. It is a deep sadness, boredom and disgust with life, felt almost in the body. It joins a deep fear and the painful feeling that time cannot be escaped. The four "Spleen" poems have given the language some of its most famous pictures. The low, heavy sky presses down like a lid. The falling rain looks like the bars of a huge prison. Anguish plants its black flag in the bowed head. On the other side, the "Ideal" is not a safe religious answer. It is a reaching out with no certain end. Beauty, art, perfumes, music and love give short, bright signs of it. The contrast between spleen and the ideal runs through much of the book. The short poem "Correspondances" became a key text for the poets who came after. Nature in it is a temple where man walks through "forests of symbols". Smells, colors and sounds answer one another, so that a smell can be "green" or a sound "sweet". Behind this stand two ideas. The things of the senses are signs of a higher spiritual world: an old religious idea, taken from the thinker Swedenborg. And the different senses open into one another. From this poem comes the picture of the poet as a reader of signs. In an essay of 1861 on Victor Hugo, Baudelaire himself defined the poet as "a translator, a decoder" of these signs. This idea of the poet as a translator is important in Baudelaire's work. Later poets, such as Rimbaud and Mallarmé, took up this idea. Women and love fill almost a third of the book. They are pulled between two poles: worship and hatred, spirit and cruelty. The Jeanne Duval cycle is dark, warm and sometimes bitter. The Sabatier cycle turns the loved one into a being of light. The Marie Daubrun cycle is soft like autumn, with its invitation to a voyage to a country that looks like the loved woman. Around them stand the unnamed women of the streets and the poor, like the thin, coughing African woman of "Le Cygne". There are also the "Femmes damnées", through whom desire opens onto pity and punishment. In his notebooks Baudelaire often says hard and unjust things about women. In many of his poems, love is closely connected with guilt, suffering and evil. The city, finally, is the most clearly new thing of 1861. Baudelaire knew Paris as few writers did. Apart from the Lyon years, the voyage of 1841, some stays at Honfleur, and the last years in Belgium, he rarely left it. With the "Tableaux parisiens", he made the modern city one of the central subjects of French poetry. It is not street color, which Romantic writers had done before him. It is the inner experience of the city: the crowd, the shock, the meeting that is over in a second ("À une passante"). It is the pain of memory in a changing city ("Le Cygne": "Paris is changing, but nothing in my sadness has moved!"). It is the strange seen in broad daylight ("Les Sept Vieillards"). Mario Richter compares the section to a picture gallery, where framed views of Paris hang in careful order. Walter Benjamin later made these poems the key documents of his study of Paris as the capital of the 19th century. The old gods of Greek and Roman myth also live on in the book, a mark of Baudelaire's classical schooling. Sisyphus appears in "Le Guignon", Venus in "Un voyage à Cythère", and the Muses in two early poems. Baudelaire mixes these ancient figures freely with Christian images such as Satan and the angels, and he changes their stories to build a personal mythology. The clearest example opens "Le Cygne". Andromache, the exiled widow of the Trojan hero Hector, becomes there the sister of all the lost and displaced people of modern Paris. The surprise of Les Fleurs du Mal is that completely new feelings are expressed in old, strictly kept forms. Baudelaire invented no new verse forms. He used the traditional French twelve-syllable line and the fourteen-line sonnet (almost half the book) with great care, and gave them new effects. He defended the sonnet in a letter of 1860: because the form constrains, he wrote, the idea springs out more intensely. A piece of sky seen through a small window, he added, gives a deeper idea of the infinite than a whole mountain view. What is his own is more secret. Rich and surprising rhymes. The noble word placed next to the low word: a dead animal in the sun, described like a loved body. Capital letters that turn ideas into persons: Ennui, Anguish, Hope. And above all a music that takes hold of the reader like a spell. Paul Valéry put this "charm", in the old sense of a magic song, at the center of his study. The line "Sois sage, ô ma Douleur, et tiens-toi plus tranquille" ("Be good, my Sorrow, and keep more still") is the example everyone gives. Baudelaire himself thought of poetry in this way. In his essay on Gautier of 1859, he wrote that skill with language is a kind of magic (sorcellerie évocatoire): the poet's words call things up before the reader's eyes.
