He therefore used traditional poetic forms to express new subjects and feelings. The other half of his poetry is the book of fifty prose poems. He had a hundred in mind, but death cut the work short. His first two prose poems had appeared as early as 1855, so the project accompanied him for more than ten years. Baudelaire left a handwritten list of the fifty titles. His friends Asselineau and Banville probably followed it when they published the book in 1869 as Petits Poèmes en prose. That title, however, was not really his own. In his letters, the words "petits poèmes en prose" describe a kind of writing, not the name of a book. The only title he clearly used in his last years was Le Spleen de Paris. Other names had passed through his papers. Six early pieces appeared in 1857 as "Poèmes nocturnes" ("Night Poems"). Around 1861, he also thought of Le Promeneur solitaire ("The Lonely Walker") and Le Rôdeur parisien ("The Paris Prowler"). The title Le Spleen de Paris first appeared in print in February 1864, in Le Figaro. This is the title that readers use today. Baudelaire did not invent the form itself; he points to the Gaspard de la Nuit of Aloysius Bertrand. But he made it into something new. Bertrand had cut small, delicate pictures of old times. Baudelaire wanted something else. In his opening letter to Arsène Houssaye he describes "the miracle of a poetic prose, musical without rhythm and without rhyme, supple enough and abrupt enough to fit the movements of the soul, the waves of dream, the jumps of conscience". And this dream, he adds, is born above all of great cities and the crossing of their countless relations. The same letter offers the book to the reader in pieces. It has no head and no tail, Baudelaire says: we can cut it anywhere, and each part can live alone. The prose poems did not always find an easy audience. In 1864, the director of Le Figaro stopped printing the prose poems, telling Baudelaire that they bored everybody. The book takes up some material from the verse book; some texts are the prose brothers of verse poems, like "L'Invitation au voyage". But the tone is new: ironic, cutting, sometimes brutal. The poet comes down into the street. In one text his halo falls into the mud of the road, and he is glad of it ("Perte d'auréole"). In the famous "Enivrez-vous", he tells the reader to be always drunk, "on wine, on poetry or on virtue". Another well-known piece bears an English title, "Any where out of the world" ("N'importe où hors du monde"). He meets the poor, the traveling players, the widows. In one poem, the narrator attacks a glass-seller. In another, he beats an old beggar in an attempt to give him back his self-respect. His prose poems do more than make prose sound poetic. They test what poetry can become in the modern city, among crowds, money and sudden change. Le Spleen de Paris had a strong influence on later prose poetry, including Rimbaud's Illuminations. Baudelaire is generally seen as one of the greatest art critics of the 19th century. His thought is found in the Salons of 1845, 1846 and 1859, and in his essays on caricature, where he treated Daumier and Goya as serious artists and built a theory of laughter. In his essay on laughter (1855), laughter is born of pride and of man's fallen state: it is "satanic", and for that very reason deeply human. He also reviewed the great art exhibition of 1855. There he wrote that "the beautiful is always strange": true beauty always contains a surprising element that no rule can fully explain. The high point is Le Peintre de la vie moderne (1863), together with his essay on Delacroix (1863). Three ideas give it shape. First, true criticism is not cold. It must be "partial, passionate, political", written from one chosen point of view, but the point of view that opens the most horizons. The best review of a painting might even be a poem. Second, imagination is "the queen of the faculties". The true artist draws from nature as from a dictionary and copies nothing. Against the school of the exact copy Baudelaire fought a long war; photography, in his Salon de 1859, should remain only "the servant of the sciences and the arts". Third, the theory of "modernity". Beauty has two halves: one eternal and unchanging, the other belonging to the present day, to fashion and the feeling of the moment. Modernity, he says, is the passing, fleeting half of art; the other half is eternal and never changes. Baudelaire even excused himself for this strange new word: no better one existed, he said, for the idea he wanted to express. The painter of modern life must take from fashion whatever poetry it may contain, and draw the eternal out of the passing. Such an artist looks at the world like a child, or like a person just recovering from a long illness, for whom everything seems new. Genius, Baudelaire writes in the same essay, is simply "childhood recovered at will". Baudelaire gave this account through one artist, Constantin Guys. Guys refused to be named, so the essay calls him only "M. G.". Baudelaire even promises to pretend, together with the reader, that M. G. does not exist. The essay gave one of the most influential nineteenth-century accounts of modern art and modern life. Writers before him, such as Stendhal, had already said that beauty changes with each age. Baudelaire gave the idea its most powerful form. Memory holds this theory together. As early as 1846, Baudelaire wrote that art is a way of helping memory hold on to beauty. The true artist does not copy the model standing in front of him. He draws from memory, keeps the main lines, and drops the small details. In this way, the work also speaks to the memory of the viewer. Guys worked exactly like this: he watched the city all day and drew at night, from memory. The scholar J. A. Hiddleston has shown that this idea runs through the whole of Baudelaire's writing on art. Baudelaire's quarrel with photography had a personal side. In 1859, for the first time, photography was shown in the same building as the Salon, the official art exhibition. It had, however, a separate entrance. In his review, Baudelaire attacked the new industry with anger. He called it "the refuge of every failed painter". He mocked a public that rushed "like a single Narcissus" to stare at its own image on the metal. Yet photography filled his life. Nadar was one of his oldest friends, and Baudelaire sat for him, for Étienne Carjat and, in Brussels, for Charles Neyt. In letters to Nadar, he even joked about his Salon of 1859. He said he was writing it with only the catalogue and one quick visit to the exhibition. And at the end of 1865, ill and alone in Brussels, he asked his mother to have a photograph of herself made for him. The same essay paints the flâneur: the man who walks through the city and watches, whose true home is the crowd, "a mirror as vast as the crowd itself". It also contains a praise of make-up that turns the Romantic worship of nature upside down. Nature, for him, is marked by original sin, the old fault of man; everything beautiful and noble is therefore the fruit of reason and design. As a music critic, Baudelaire gave with his Wagner essay of 1861 one of the first great French studies of that composer. He linked Wagner's music to his own idea of "correspondences". Among the young painters, Édouard Manet was his close friend in the 1860s. Manet's painting La Musique aux Tuileries shows Baudelaire in the crowd. From Baudelaire, Manet received both warm support and one famous two-edged sentence: "You are only the first in the decline of your art." Published in 1860, Les Paradis artificiels ("The Artificial Heavens") joins an essay on hashish to a free French adaptation of Thomas De Quincey's book about opium. The book does not praise drugs. Baudelaire examines their effects and their moral dangers. Hashish is described with the care of a scientist, but judged as a false shortcut for the spirit. It gives the feeling of higher power without the work, and in the end it kills the will. The man who takes it wants to be equal to God without paying the price. The artist must reach his higher world through work and discipline. This judgment agrees with the religious base of his thought. Baudelaire himself also used opium. From the late 1840s, he used laudanum, a liquid form of opium sold by chemists. He took it first against stomach pains. How dependent he became is still discussed. So is how much the drug shaped his life. In 2004, the British writer Frank Hilton defended the strongest view. For him, opium addiction was the hidden cause of many of Baudelaire's troubles: the endless delays, the unpaid debts, the plans that were never finished. Other scholars answer that his drug use has been exaggerated, and that Les Paradis artificiels cannot be read as a simple report of personal habit. The papers found after his death were later published and are still widely read. They were published as Fusées and Mon cœur mis à nu ("My Heart Laid Bare", a title taken from an idea of Poe's). Working notes, sharp sayings, plans, prayers, self-examinations and cries of anger follow one another without order. Here are some of his most famous statements. In every man, at every hour, there are two pulls at the same time: one toward God, one toward Satan. Beauty is something burning and sad. Here too are the moving work rules of his last years, written by a man who felt his will leaving him. These pages, with the unfinished Belgian book, contain many of his private thoughts about religion, work, politics, art and his own character. They have fed both the Catholic reading of him (Claudel) and the reading of the left. Benjamin and his heirs saw in Baudelaire the anger of a writer forced by the new market to sell himself. For Baudelaire, the "dandy" was much more than a man who dressed well, although Baudelaire himself had treated clothing and manners as works of art when he was young. In Le Peintre de la vie moderne, the dandy becomes a moral and almost religious figure. Baudelaire calls him "the last flash of heroism in times of decline" and "a setting sun". The dandy represents a new kind of upper class, based not on birth or money but on strength of mind, self-control, and refusal of everything ordinary or vulgar. The life of the dandy is a hard discipline, close to the self-control taught by the Stoics. He must never appear surprised, weak, or deeply moved. In his notebook Mon cœur mis à nu, Baudelaire writes that the dandy must try to be sublime, above all common life, at every moment: he must "live and sleep in front of a mirror". This means that he must always watch and shape himself. The idea came partly from Brummell and from Barbey d'Aurevilly. It is also connected with Baudelaire's belief that art should resist nature instead of simply following it. The scholar Bernard Howells has linked this figure with Baudelaire's view of history. Baudelaire did not believe in progress. For him, dandies appear in unstable times, when the old world of birth and rank is falling, and the new world of money and equality has not yet fully won. In his last notebooks, Baudelaire even copied out two pages of sayings by the American thinker Ralph Waldo Emerson. He had read Emerson's book The Conduct of Life around 1860, and he used these sayings as rules to strengthen his will. His idea of the dandy later influenced writers such as Villiers, Huysmans, and Oscar Wilde. Christian ideas are deeply present in Baudelaire's work. How far he personally accepted Christian belief is a question on which critics disagree. Some describe him as a Christian who had lost his way but still thought inside the frame of that belief. The central idea he kept is original sin, which he took especially from Joseph de Maistre. Among his private notes, under the heading Hygiène ("Hygiene"), he even wrote: "De Maistre and Edgar Poe taught me how to reason." According to this idea, evil is already present in human nature. Baudelaire therefore rejected the belief that society automatically becomes better with time. He thought that this easy faith in progress belonged to lazy minds. True civilization, he wrote, is not in gas or steam machines: it lies in reducing "the traces of original sin". This helps to explain the two opposite movements in Les Fleurs du Mal: one toward God and the other toward Satan. Readers have understood the satanic side of the book in very different ways. The prosecution argued that some poems attacked religious morals, but the judges rejected this charge. The court condemned the book only for its offence against public morals. Literary historians often see it as part of the dark Romantic style of the time. Some Catholic critics of the 20th century saw it as a reversed form of faith. In their view, a person does not fight so strongly against something in which he has no belief at all. Baudelaire himself wrote to his lawyer Ancelle in February 1866 that he had put into this "terrible book" all his heart, all his tenderness, all his religion, though "in disguise", and all his hatred. In public, he went on, he would swear the exact opposite: the book was only pure art. "And I will lie like a tooth-puller." Elsewhere, he wrote that evil is done naturally and without effort, while good is always the result of work and art. Beauty also has this double nature. In "Hymne à la Beauté", he asks whether Beauty comes down from heaven or rises from the abyss. The poem answers that it does not matter, if her eyes open the door of an unknown Infinite. Baudelaire saw himself as part of Romanticism. In 1846, he explained that Romanticism was not mainly a choice of subjects. It was a way of feeling based on inner depth, the life of the spirit, colour, and a desire for the infinite. He used many Romantic subjects, including sadness, revolt, distant countries, and the figure of Satan. However, he treated them in a new way. He preferred controlled form to long emotional speeches, cool irony to open tears, the modern city to the countryside, and a dark view of human nature to easy hope. His relationship with the older Romantic writers was complex. He admired Hugo when he was young, but later his public praise was mixed with private doubts. He also owed much to the young Sainte-Beuve, whose Poésies de Joseph Delorme had been important to him during his school years. His respect for Gautier remained deep. He dedicated Les Fleurs du Mal to Gautier, calling him "the perfect magician of French letters". The dedication offers him the poems as "these sickly flowers". Baudelaire also had links with the new Parnassian school. Like the Parnassians, he cared about exact, finished, and carefully shaped poetry. In March 1866, their collection published his Nouvelles Fleurs du Mal, a group of fifteen poems. However, he did not share their ideal of poetry kept cool and far from the writer's own life. Critics often note that even his essays on other artists speak, indirectly, of himself. For this reason, historians of literature often place him at a meeting point between several movements. He is seen as the last great Romantic, a close relative of the Parnassians, and a father of the Symbolists. Through Le Spleen de Paris, he also opened new paths for prose poetry and for forms of modern writing that went beyond any single literary school. At first the book was known above all through the trial, which gave it a doubtful kind of fame. The unsold copies went quickly. But the established critics long saw Baudelaire as a strange, gifted man, perhaps a joker playing with the public. Sainte-Beuve never gave him the public review he was waiting for. But from the 1860s a new generation took him for a master. In 1865 Verlaine published a warm study of him, and Mallarmé did the same. Baudelaire was half pleased and half annoyed at having imitators. "To tell the truth, they give me a terrible fright," he wrote in March 1866 to Jules Troubat, the secretary of Sainte-Beuve. "I like nothing so much as being alone." After his death his influence kept growing. In 1869, his loyal friend Asselineau published the first book about his life. There was Mallarmé's poem in his memory, and the collection of homage poems of 1896. Les Fleurs du Mal became an important model for the new poetic movements. Rimbaud, in 1871, called him the first "seer", the king of poets. But he added that Baudelaire's form was too narrow, and that new visions would need new forms. Verlaine, Laforgue and Huysmans followed. In Huysmans' novel À rebours, the hero des Esseintes loves Baudelaire above all other writers. Between 1865 and 1900, his influence on younger poets became more and more important. His fame also spread to other countries. Swinburne praised him in England as early as 1862, and later wrote the memorial poem "Ave atque Vale". Stefan George translated him into German.

Baroness Karen Christentze von Blixen-Finecke (born Dinesen; 17 April 1885 – 7 September 1962) was a Danish author who wrote works in Danish and English. She is also known under her pen names Isak Dinesen, used in English-speaking countries, Tania Blixen, used in German-speaking countries, Osceola, and Pierre Andrézel.

Gustave Flaubert ( in French; 12 December 1821 – 8 May 1880) was a French writer. He is best known for his novels. Many people consider him one of the most important French writers of the 19th century. He was born in Rouen, in Normandy, and lived most of his life at Croisset, a small place on the river Seine near Rouen. He died there at the age of fifty-eight. His first published novel, Madame Bovary (1857), is his most famous book. It tells the story of a doctor's wife in a small town who is unhappy with her life and dreams of love and luxury. In 1857, the French state took Flaubert to court because it said that the novel offended public morals. Flaubert was found not guilty, and the trial helped to make the book famous. He then wrote Salammbô (1862), a novel about ancient Carthage. L'Éducation sentimentale ("Sentimental Education", 1869) tells the story of a young man in Paris before and during the Revolution of 1848. La Tentation de saint Antoine ("The Temptation of Saint Anthony", 1874) is a long dream-like work written mainly as a dialogue. Trois Contes ("Three Tales", 1877) is a collection of three short stories. His last novel, Bouvard et Pécuchet, was unfinished when he died. It was published in 1881. Flaubert worked very slowly and carefully. He sometimes spent a whole week writing a single page. He searched for what he called le mot juste, the exact word that best fitted each sentence. He also believed that a writer should not directly show personal feelings or opinions in a story. He said that the author should be like God in the universe, "present everywhere and visible nowhere". His careful style and his ideas about writing strongly influenced the modern novel. His work influenced writers such as Guy de Maupassant, Émile Zola, Henry James, Marcel Proust, James Joyce and Franz Kafka. Flaubert's letters are also an important part of his writing. He wrote thousands of them, especially to the poet Louise Colet, who was his lover, and to the novelist George Sand, who became a close friend. In these letters, he often explained his ideas about writing and art. From the age of twenty-two, he also had attacks of an illness that most modern researchers identify as epilepsy. He lived quietly at Croisset for much of his life and gave most of his time to writing. Flaubert's father, Achille-Cléophas Flaubert, was born in 1784 in the Aube region, south-east of Paris. His family had been animal doctors for several generations. He studied medicine in Paris, where he was the best student of his year. He worked under Guillaume Dupuytren, one of the most famous surgeons in France. A surgeon is a doctor who does operations. Dupuytren sent him to the Hôtel-Dieu, the main hospital of Rouen. In 1812, he married Caroline Fleuriot, and in 1818 he became the chief surgeon of the hospital. Dr Flaubert became a well-known and respected doctor. A Paris medical directory of 1826 called him one of the leading doctors in France. He treated poor patients for free. He also had liberal political opinions at a time when the French state and the Catholic Church worked closely together. His son later gave many of his qualities to Dr Larivière, the great doctor who appears near the end of Madame Bovary. Dr Flaubert also became rich. He paid a high tax, which gave him the right to vote at a time when only a small number of Frenchmen could do so. When he died in 1846, he left about 800,000 francs, mostly in land and houses. This property included the house at Croisset. The money later allowed Gustave to live without a job and give all his time to literature. Flaubert's mother, Anne-Justine-Caroline Fleuriot, had a sad childhood. Her mother died when she was born. Her father was a "health officer", a man who practised medicine without being a full doctor. He died when she was nine. She was then brought up by Dr Laumonier, the chief surgeon of the Hôtel-Dieu, and his wife. She was eighteen when she married Dr Flaubert. The couple had six children, but three died very young. Three survived: Achille, born in 1813, who became a doctor like his father; Gustave, born in 1821; and Caroline, born in 1824. Gustave Flaubert was born on 12 December 1821 in his father's apartment at the Hôtel-Dieu in Rouen. The family lived in a wing of the hospital that is now a museum about the Flaubert family and the history of medicine. Patients waited for the doctor downstairs. Upstairs was a billiard room, which Gustave and his sister later turned into a theatre. Above it were the children's rooms. "I was born in a hospital and I lived there for a quarter of a century," he later wrote. Gustave therefore grew up among sick people, dying people and dead bodies. From the family garden, Gustave could see the room where his father cut open dead bodies to teach his students. Gustave and Caroline climbed on a trellis to watch through the windows. Their father sometimes saw them and told them to go away. Many readers think these early experiences help explain two parts of Flaubert's work. One is its sadness. The other is his habit of observing human beings closely and without showing much feeling, almost like a scientist. Gustave was very close to his sister Caroline, who was three years younger. From the age of ten, he wrote and acted in plays with her in the billiard room. Later, when he travelled, he wrote her long and loving letters. His older brother Achille was eight years older and soon left for Paris to study medicine, so the two brothers were never close. His mother taught him to read. The family's servant, Julie, first taught him to love stories. He had two important childhood friends. The first was Ernest Chevalier, whose grandfather lived opposite the hospital and told the boys stories about the adventures of Don Quixote. The second was Alfred Le Poittevin, who was five years older. The two families were very close: Alfred's father was Gustave's godfather, and Gustave's father was Alfred's godfather. Le Poittevin gave Gustave books to read and made him dream about the East. Much later, Flaubert dedicated La Tentation de saint Antoine to the memory of this friend. Gustave wanted to write from a very early age. At the age of nine, he told Ernest Chevalier in a letter that a woman who visited his father always said stupid things and that he would write them down. The critic Jonathan Culler later saw this letter as a sign of Flaubert's future interests. Flaubert collected foolish remarks for the rest of his life, and many of them appeared in his later books. As a boy, he also invented an imaginary character with his friends and his sister. They called him "the Garçon" (the Boy). The Garçon was a loud, vulgar and self-satisfied bourgeois who laughed at everything. The children spoke about him as if he were a real person. Some writers have seen the Garçon as an early version of the pharmacist Homais in Madame Bovary. The theatre in the billiard room lasted about five years, from 1829 to 1834, but Flaubert loved acting all his life. He imitated people so well that his father forbade him to imitate some of them because he thought it affected his son too strongly. "Whatever people say," Flaubert wrote in 1846, "the essence of my nature is the clown." In February 1832, Gustave entered the Collège royal de Rouen, the main school of the city. From May of that year, he was a boarder, which means that he lived at the school. The school was old and famous: the playwright Pierre Corneille had studied there in the 17th century. Only about two per cent of French children went to such schools. Board and lessons cost about 700 francs a year, more than a teacher's yearly salary. Gustave was not a very good pupil at first. He was bored and later remembered the school as a place of dull lessons and long hours of study. However, he read a great deal and began to write. His first stories date from 1835 and 1836. In 1837, a small Rouen magazine printed two of his texts. He wrote horror stories, historical tales and a story called Rêve d'enfer ("Dream of Hell", 1837). In 1838, he wrote Mémoires d'un fou ("Memoirs of a Madman"), which tells the story of his first love in a Romantic style. That love was based on a real experience. During the summer of 1836, at the seaside town of Trouville, Gustave, then fourteen, met Élisa Schlésinger. She was twenty-six years old, beautiful, quiet and religious. She had a baby daughter and lived with the music publisher Maurice Schlésinger. She later married him. Gustave never told her how he felt, and no love affair took place. However, he remembered her all his life. Thirty years later, Élisa became the model for Marie Arnoux, the woman the hero of L'Éducation sentimentale loves without hope. Élisa lived until 1888 and survived Flaubert by eight years. At Trouville, Gustave also met an English family, the Colliers. Their daughters Gertrude and Henriette remained his friends for the rest of his life. In his last year at school, in December 1839, Gustave was expelled. A popular philosophy teacher had been replaced by a man the pupils disliked. Gustave led a protest by the whole class. He wrote a letter to the headmaster which twelve of his classmates signed. They included Louis Bouilhet, who later became his closest friend, and Émile Hamard, who later married his sister. The school expelled Gustave and two other pupils. He prepared for the baccalauréat, the final school examination, alone at home. He passed it in August 1840. His father was pleased and gave him a reward: a long journey from 22 August to 1 November 1840 through the south of France and the island of Corsica. Gustave did not travel alone. His companion was Dr Jules Cloquet, a friend of his father and an easy-going Paris doctor who became an excellent guide for the young man. Gustave loved the Mediterranean, its light and its warmth. He wrote a travel book about the journey, Pyrénées–Corse. In Marseille, on the way home, he spent a night with Eulalie Foucaud, a woman who ran a hotel with her mother. It was his first sexual relationship. He wrote to her for a few months afterwards and used the memory in his story Novembre ("November", 1842). By the age of eighteen, Gustave was a tall and handsome young man with broad shoulders, a deep voice, large gestures and a loud laugh. He did not want a profession, but his father expected him to have one. In November 1841, he registered as a law student in Paris. He hated the subject. He copied textbooks without understanding them and was afraid of becoming a lawyer or a public prosecutor. He preferred to visit the studio of the sculptor James Pradier, where he met artists and writers. In November 1843, he met the great poet Victor Hugo there. In March 1843, he made a new friend, Maxime Du Camp, a rich young man who wanted to become a writer and loved travelling. At the same time, Flaubert began a first novel called L'Éducation sentimentale. It has the same title as his famous novel of 1869, but it is a different work. He passed his first law examination in December 1842, but failed the second one in August 1843. Du Camp, who was present, later wrote that Flaubert's mind was so full of art and poetry that it could not take in the dry rules of law. He failed again at the end of the year. In January 1844, Gustave was returning from Deauville, where his father had bought land. He was driving a small carriage with his brother Achille. Suddenly, he fell to the floor of the carriage as if he had been struck by lightning. For ten minutes, his brother thought he was dead. Achille carried him into a house beside the road and bled him at once. Back in Rouen, doctors bled him again "in three places at once". He had a second attack in February. The treatments of the time were painful and useless. They included a strict diet, no tobacco, repeated bleeding, leeches and orange-flower water. During one bleeding, hot water was poured on his hand to make the blood flow. It burned him badly. The attacks returned from time to time for many years. Du Camp described them: Flaubert became very pale, hurried to lie down, and shook all over. Afterwards, he slept deeply and felt stiff and sore for several days. Doctors today generally think that he had a form of epilepsy. Philippe Hecketsweiler, a doctor who studied Flaubert's illnesses in 2022, concluded that the attacks began with strange visions. Some then led to loss of consciousness and violent shaking. Over his life, Flaubert had thousands of attacks, most of them small. His family kept the illness secret. People outside the family learned about it only after his death. The philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre did not believe that Flaubert had epilepsy. In his very long book about Flaubert, L'Idiot de la famille ("The Family Idiot"), he argued that the illness was a nervous crisis. For Sartre, it was the only way in which the young man could escape from the profession that his father wanted for him. Whatever the illness was, its effect was the same. Dr Flaubert gave up the idea of making his son a lawyer. Gustave left law school, went home, and became a writer. Flaubert himself later gave a similar explanation of his illness. If his brain had been stronger, he told Louise Colet, boredom and the law would not have made him ill. In the same year, 1844, his father bought a house at Croisset. The land he had owned at Deauville had been taken by the state for the new railway from Rouen to Le Havre. The house at Croisset was a large 18th-century country house, about four kilometres from Rouen on the right bank of the Seine, in the commune of Canteleu. It had a park, tall trees and a wide view of the river and its sailing boats. The family moved there in June 1844. Flaubert wrote all his major books in this house. In its garden, a path lined with lime trees became what he called his gueuloir, or "shouting place". There he read his sentences aloud at the top of his voice to test how they sounded. People on passing boats were sometimes surprised to hear him. On 3 March 1845, Caroline married Émile Hamard. Gustave felt that he was losing her. When Ernest Chevalier asked what he thought of the marriage, he answered with only two letters: "AH!" The young couple went to Italy and Switzerland for their honeymoon, and the whole family went with them. Gustave disliked travelling in a group, but the journey gave him one of the most important experiences of his life. In Genoa, in the Balbi palace, he saw a painting of The Temptation of Saint Anthony attributed to Pieter Brueghel the Younger. The picture shows the old hermit surrounded by monsters and strange visions. Flaubert could not forget it. During the next thirty years, he wrote three versions of a book on the same subject. Then came a year of disasters. In January 1846, Dr Flaubert developed a deep abscess in his thigh. His son Achille operated on him, but it was too late. He died of blood poisoning on 15 January. Six days later, Caroline gave birth to a daughter, also called Caroline. Two months later, in March, Caroline Hamard died of childbed fever, an infection that often followed childbirth at that time. She was twenty-one years old. Gustave described her funeral in a letter. The grave was too narrow, and the gravediggers had to force the coffin down with a spade and crowbars. Flaubert now organised the life of the remaining family. He helped his brother Achille obtain their father's position at the hospital. Achille lived in their father's apartment at the Hôtel-Dieu. Gustave and his mother lived at Croisset for most of the year and spent the winter in an apartment in Rouen. They took in the baby Caroline because her father, Hamard, was not able to care for her. For the next twenty-six years, Gustave lived with his mother and helped to raise his niece. He never married. His mother, who had never been very religious, lost her faith after these two deaths. On 28 July 1846, Flaubert went to Pradier's studio in Paris. He wanted the sculptor to make a bust of his dead sister and also wanted to discuss a statue of his father for the city of Rouen. Among the guests in the studio, he saw a beautiful woman with long fair hair. She was the poet Louise Colet, who was thirty-five years old. She had already published several books and had won prizes from the Académie française. She was married to a musician, Hippolyte Colet, and had been the lover of the philosopher Victor Cousin. Paris knew her as "the Muse". The attraction between Flaubert and Colet was immediate. Flaubert visited her the next day, and within a few days they became lovers. He returned to Croisset on 4 August. That night, he wrote her his first letter. This was the beginning of one of the most famous exchanges of love letters in French literature. The new railway between Paris and Rouen made communication very fast. A letter posted in Rouen before eleven in the morning could reach Paris that same afternoon. From the first two years of the affair, 104 of Flaubert's letters survive, but only one of Colet's. He probably burned her letters, or someone destroyed them after his death. The affair was unusual from the beginning. Flaubert loved Louise, and his early letters are full of desire. However, he refused to change his life for her. He stayed at Croisset with his mother and his work. During two years, after their first days together, the lovers met only four times. There were three short meetings in Paris and one day at an inn in Mantes, a town halfway between Paris and Rouen. Louise wanted them to live together. She protested, cried and became angry. He answered that love was not the first thing in his life "but the second". The first was the great work that he hoped to write. In August 1848, the affair ended. Louise came to Rouen in June 1851, soon after Flaubert returned from the East, and the affair began again. This second period lasted until 1855. During these years, Flaubert was writing Madame Bovary. His letters to Louise became a kind of diary of his work and contain many of his ideas about art. He sent her his last letter on 6 March 1855. Louise answered him in another way. In 1859, she published a novel called Lui ("Him"), in which Flaubert appears as a cold and selfish man. The critic Albert Thibaudet later suggested why the affair had lasted for several years. It was made almost entirely of letters. Face to face, he said, Flaubert would not have been able to live with Louise for two months. Two friends were now at the centre of Flaubert's life. The first was Louis Bouilhet, a poet and former schoolmate, who was as poor as Flaubert was rich. He came to Croisset every Sunday, read what Gustave had written, and told him directly what was good and what was bad. Flaubert trusted his judgment more than anyone else's. The second was Maxime Du Camp, his friend from his student years. From May to August 1847, Flaubert and Du Camp walked through Anjou, Brittany and Normandy with bags on their backs. They wrote a travel book together, Par les champs et par les grèves ("Over Fields and Shores"). They took turns: Flaubert wrote one chapter, then Du Camp wrote the next. The book was published only after Flaubert's death. In February 1848, a revolution in Paris drove out King Louis-Philippe and made France a republic. Flaubert was in Paris with Bouilhet and Du Camp and saw some of the fighting himself. Twenty years later, he used these memories in L'Éducation sentimentale. Back at Croisset, he had to serve in the National Guard, the citizens' militia. However, he had little faith in politics. He watched the new Republic and the bloody days of June 1848, when the army defeated a rising of Paris workers, with distance and irony. On 3 April 1848, Alfred Le Poittevin died at the age of thirty-one. Flaubert stayed beside the body for two nights, read Montaigne, and wrapped his friend in his shroud himself. He described these hours in a letter to Du Camp. In May 1848, Flaubert began to write La Tentation de saint Antoine, the book inspired by the painting he had seen in Genoa. He worked on it for sixteen months and finished it on 12 September 1849. It was a very long work, closer to a play than to a novel. The book shows one night of visions. The old hermit Anthony is tempted by the Devil, the Queen of Sheba, the gods of many religions and the sciences. Flaubert believed that it was his masterpiece. He read the whole book aloud to Bouilhet and Du Camp at Croisset. The reading lasted four days. After each part, he asked them: "Well?" They did not want to answer. At the end, they told him what they really thought: the book was a failure. They believed that its strong feelings, endless visions and lack of a clear story hid his real talent. They advised him to choose an ordinary subject from everyday life, in the manner of Balzac. Du Camp later told a famous story. According to him, Bouilhet suggested a piece of local news. A health officer named Delamare, in a village near Rouen, had been ruined by his wife's lovers and debts, and she had poisoned herself. The story is at least partly a legend. Delphine Delamare, the second wife of Eugène Delamare, a health officer at Ry, did die at twenty-six, and her husband died a year later. However, Delamare died only a few months after Flaubert left for the East. The case therefore cannot have been suggested in exactly this form in 1849. What is certain is that Flaubert chose the subject in the summer of 1851. Du Camp's memory of the scene was probably changed by his knowledge of the later novel. Flaubert put the Temptation aside, but he never gave it up. A few weeks later, he left for the East with Du Camp. His mother paid for the journey, a large gift for a son who had never earned any money. The two friends left Croisset on 22 October 1849 and sailed from Marseille in November. They spent eight months in Egypt. They visited Alexandria and Cairo, climbed the Great Pyramid, and sailed up the Nile as far as the second cataract in Nubia. Du Camp took photographs of the temples, among the first photographs ever made in Egypt. Flaubert wrote notes and long letters to Bouilhet and his mother. The best-known episode of the journey took place at Esna on 6 March 1850. A servant led the travellers to the house of Kuchuk Hanem, a famous dancer who also sold sex. The servant was followed by a pet sheep with yellow spots painted on its wool and a black velvet covering on its nose. Kuchuk Hanem danced for them, and Flaubert spent the night with her. He described her in his notes with the same care that he gave to temples and landscapes. He wrote about her clothes, jewels, tattoo, a bad tooth and the bedbugs on the wall. On the journey back down the Nile, he visited her again and felt an "infinite sadness". Louise Colet later told him that the bedbugs disgusted her. He answered that they were the most enchanting detail for him because he wanted some bitterness in everything. The historian Michel Winock has written openly about the sexual side of the journey. The two friends visited many prostitutes, and Flaubert wrote about these visits to Bouilhet in a crude and proud tone that was common among young men of his time. However, Flaubert sometimes preferred simply to observe. In the prostitutes' street at Kena, he walked up and down while women in blue, yellow and red dresses called to him. He was strongly impressed by the scene. He then left without touching any of them because he did not want another experience to change the picture in his mind. From Egypt, the travellers continued to Palestine, Lebanon, Rhodes, Asia Minor and Constantinople. They then travelled to Greece and finally to Italy, where Flaubert's mother joined him. The journey also left him with a lasting illness. In Beirut, in 1850, he caught syphilis, a serious disease passed on during sex. He joked about it in a letter to Bouilhet, but there was no cure at the time. For years afterwards, he took mercury, the usual treatment, which was itself poisonous. He returned to Croisset in June 1851. Francis Steegmuller, who translated the travel notes into English, argued that the journey changed Flaubert. In his view, the Romantic who left for Egypt returned as a Realist ready to write Madame Bovary. Flaubert later became angry with Du Camp, who published his own account of the journey in 1854 without paying much attention to his friend's feelings. Flaubert began Madame Bovary in September 1851, three months after his return. He worked on it for almost five years. His letters to Louise Colet describe this long struggle. He had decided to write the opposite of the Temptation. Instead of a noble and fantastic subject, he chose an ordinary provincial story. Instead of a book filled with the author's own feelings, he wanted a book in which the author could not be seen. In January 1852, he wrote that he wanted to create "a book about nothing". Such a book would depend on nothing outside itself. Its style alone would hold it together. This required a new way of writing. The author would not comment on the story or tell the reader how to judge the characters. Style would have to suggest what earlier novelists had explained directly. "Impersonality is the sign of strength," he wrote. At the same time, he searched for the exact word, removed repetitions and sounds he disliked, and read every page aloud in his gueuloir. The work went very slowly. He sometimes needed a week to write one page and a month to write one chapter. He complained that his characters disgusted him and that the book was a burden that was killing him. The novel was finished in the spring of 1856. Maxime Du Camp was now one of the editors of the Revue de Paris, a literary magazine. The magazine published the novel in six parts, from 1 October to 15 December 1856. The editors were afraid of the government, which closely watched the press under the Second Empire. They cut the scene in which Emma and her lover Léon travel around Rouen in a closed cab. Flaubert protested and demanded that the magazine print a note saying that the cuts were not his. When the editors asked for more cuts before the final part, he asked a lawyer, Jules Sénard, for advice. The magazine printed Flaubert's own note to the reader, saying that the text should be considered as fragments rather than as the complete work. The cuts did not protect the book. The state prosecutor's office decided to act against Flaubert, the manager of the magazine, Laurent-Pichat, and the printer, Pillet. They were accused of offending public and religious morals. The trial took place on 29 January 1857 before a criminal court in Paris, the sixth correctional chamber of the court of the Seine. For his judges, Flaubert prepared a document in which he placed the sentences that had been attacked beside similar passages from great writers of the past. The prosecutor was Ernest Pinard. He summarised the novel and said that a better title would have been "Story of the Adulteries of a Provincial Woman". He called the book "lascivious", meaning full of sexual desire, from beginning to end. What shocked him was not adultery itself but the way the heroine seemed to sing "a hymn to adultery". He admitted that Flaubert had talent and argued that this talent made the book even more dangerous. Six months later, Pinard prosecuted Charles Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du Mal. In that case, he won. Flaubert's lawyer, Jules Sénard, knew the family well. In 1848, he had presided over the National Assembly. He defended Emma Bovary almost as if she were a real person and showed how unhappy her story was. He reminded the court that Flaubert was the son of the respected Dr Flaubert of Rouen. Sénard argued that the novel was moral because it showed the terrible results of Emma's actions. He quoted the poet Lamartine, who had said that Emma's punishment was even too severe for her crime. Flaubert proudly wrote to his brother that the lawyer had "flattened" the prosecution with quotations from religious writers and that the courtroom had been full. The judgment came on 7 February 1857. All three accused men were found not guilty. However, the court strongly criticised Flaubert. Literature, it said, should improve the mind and morals rather than show vice. Flaubert was relieved but angry. He wrote to a reader that his heroine had been "dragged like the lowest lost woman into the dock with the criminals" and that he remained "a suspicious author". He dedicated the book to Sénard. The trial made the novel famous. The publisher Michel Lévy printed it in two volumes in April 1857. He had paid Flaubert only 800 francs for the rights for five years. The first printing sold out quickly, and reprints brought the total to about 30,000 copies. Flaubert soon felt that the publisher had treated him unfairly. Lévy made a large profit, while Flaubert never knew exactly how many copies had been sold. Critics were divided. Sainte-Beuve, the most powerful critic in France, praised the novel in the Moniteur. He saw in it the signs of a new generation: science, observation, maturity, strength and some hardness. Flaubert answered that the book was, for him, "an affair of pure art" and nothing more. In October 1857, Baudelaire wrote an admiring article in L'Artiste. Victor Hugo, writing from exile, told Flaubert that he was one of the leading minds of his generation. Other critics attacked the coldness and "realism" of the book, although Flaubert always rejected that word. An English translation was even prepared under Flaubert's direction by Juliet Herbert, the English governess of his niece. He called it a masterpiece, but it was never published and has disappeared. Flaubert did not rest after Madame Bovary. In September 1857, he began a new novel, which he first called Carthage and later Salammbô. After the dull world of Yonville, he wanted to write about colour, violence and the ancient world, which had interested him since his school days. He wrote that few people would understand how sad a person had to be to try to bring Carthage back to life. He described the book as a desert into which his dislike of modern life had driven him. The subject came from the Greek historian Polybius: the war of the mercenaries against Carthage between 241 and 238 BC. Mercenaries are soldiers who fight for money. After the first war between Carthage and Rome, Carthage did not pay its foreign soldiers, and they rose against the city. Flaubert read hundreds of books about the ancient world. He also wanted to see the places himself. From 16 April to 6 June 1858, he travelled to Tunisia and Algeria and walked over the ruins of Carthage. When he returned home, he threw away everything he had written and began again. The book took four more years. He finished it in April 1862. Michel Lévy paid him 10,000 francs for the book and promised the same amount for his next novel. The publisher allowed newspapers to believe that he had paid 30,000 francs, a very large sum. The Goncourt brothers, two writer friends who kept a famous diary, were shocked by the supposed price. Salammbô was published on 24 November 1862. It was successful with the public and quickly influenced fashion. Flaubert hoped that the Empress Eugénie would wear a Salammbô costume at a court ball, but she was told that it showed too much of the body. At the ball at the Tuileries palace on 9 February 1863, the Countess of Castiglione, who had been the emperor's mistress, appeared dressed as Salammbô instead. The first edition sold out in two months, and a second appeared on 10 January 1863. Critics, however, were divided. Sainte-Beuve wrote three long articles about the book in Le Constitutionnel in December 1862. He respected Flaubert but did not like the novel. He found it cruel, strange and too full of learned detail. Flaubert answered him in a long letter. He was much harsher with Guillaume Froehner, a German archaeologist who worked in Paris. On 31 December 1862, Froehner published an article in the Revue contemporaine listing mistakes that he believed he had found in the novel. He even made fun of the spelling of the heroine's name. Flaubert's reply appeared in L'Opinion nationale on 24 January 1863. He answered every point, gave his sources, and explained that the two "m"s in Salammbô were there on purpose so that the name would be pronounced correctly. His letter was sharp and well informed, and the argument ended in his favour. Other critics repeated some of the ideas used by the prosecutor Pinard. One critic in the Revue des Deux Mondes found the same moral coldness in Salammbô as in Madame Bovary. He described the heroine as suffering from hysteria and as a religious dreamer. In 1855, while finishing Madame Bovary, Flaubert had rented an apartment in Paris on the boulevard du Temple. After Salammbô, he spent more and more of each winter in the capital. People had called him "the hermit of Croisset". Now he dressed in a black suit and white gloves and went to the salon of Princess Mathilde, a cousin of the emperor Napoleon III. He was invited to the Tuileries palace in March 1864 and to the imperial court at Compiègne in November of the same year. Even there, according to Du Camp, he defended Victor Hugo, who was living in exile and was one of the emperor's strongest enemies. On 15 August 1866, Flaubert received the cross of the Légion d'honneur. From the end of 1862, he took part in the "Magny dinners", held every two weeks in a private room of a Paris restaurant. The guests were writers and thinkers, including Sainte-Beuve, Théophile Gautier, Hippolyte Taine, Ernest Renan and the Goncourt brothers. Flaubert came to the second dinner, on 6 December 1862, and attended whenever he was in Paris. The conversation was free and often coarse. In February 1863, the Russian novelist Ivan Turgenev came to a Magny dinner for the first time. He and Flaubert became close friends. Jules de Goncourt called Turgenev a "gentle giant". Turgenev visited Croisset in November 1868. Another important friendship of these years was with George Sand. She was seventeen years older than Flaubert and was famous both for her novels and for her independent way of life. She had praised Salammbô in an article, and they began to write to each other in 1863. She joined the Magny dinners in 1866, the only woman among the men. She stayed at Croisset in April and November of that year and again in 1868. Flaubert called her "dear master" and spent Christmas 1869 at her house at Nohant. Their letters form a long and friendly argument between two very different ideas about life and art. Sand believed in progress, in ordinary people and in the writer's duty to show personal feeling. Flaubert did not share these beliefs. Two women were also important in his private life. Flaubert had raised his niece Caroline almost like a daughter. On 6 April 1864, she married Ernest Commanville, a timber merchant. There was also Juliet Herbert, the English governess who had taught Caroline. Flaubert kept his relationship with her so secret that little is known about it. He visited England in 1866 and 1871, probably to see her. In September 1864, Flaubert began the novel that he called the "moral history of the men of my generation". It tells the story of Frédéric Moreau, a young man from the provinces who comes to Paris in 1840. He falls in love with a married woman, Madame Arnoux, and wastes much of his life in dreams and plans that he never fully carries out. Behind his story, the novel shows French society in the years before and during the Revolution of 1848. Flaubert wanted every detail in the book to be accurate. He read large numbers of newspapers and political books from the 1840s. He questioned George Sand, Du Camp, Maurice Schlésinger and other people who had seen the events of 1848. He also used the history of the revolution written by Marie d'Agoult under the name Daniel Stern. Some sentences in the novel come almost directly from her book. He went to Paris to discover what people could eat at a fashionable café in 1847 and how a funeral was organised. He wrote to Turgenev that he was looking for "the most stupid information one could imagine". He finished the book on 16 May 1869. Two months later, on 18 July, Louis Bouilhet died. He had not been able to read the last two chapters. Flaubert had lost his best friend and his first reader. He gave the manuscript to Du Camp, who checked it for three weeks and found 251 problems of grammar and style. Flaubert accepted most of his suggestions but rejected 87 of them. He argued that style and grammar were two different things and that the main law for a writer was harmony. On 13 October, Sainte-Beuve also died. L'Éducation sentimentale was published by Michel Lévy on 17 November 1869. Most reviews were negative. Critics found the book flat, vulgar and cruel. The Catholic writer Barbey d'Aurevilly accused Flaubert of laughing at every ideal and of suggesting that no heroes were left in the world. The feminist journalist Amélie Bosquet, an old friend, attacked the novel from another direction because it made fun of the women's movement. Only a few friends, such as George Sand and Théodore de Banville, defended the book. Flaubert never understood why it had failed with critics and readers. He was tired, sad and lonely. On 19 July 1870, France declared war on Prussia. The French armies were defeated in a few weeks. On 4 September, the Empire fell and a republic was proclaimed. Flaubert, who had usually shown little interest in politics, became very angry. He said that he wanted "to eat Prussians". He became a lieutenant in the National Guard company of Croisset. He trained his men and went to Rouen to learn how to be a soldier. At the same time, he hid the manuscript of his Temptation of Saint Anthony in the garden. Relatives who were escaping from the war filled the house. In December 1870, Prussian soldiers reached Rouen. In the middle of the month, seven soldiers and three officers were placed at Croisset, together with six horses that had to be fed. Flaubert and his mother left the house and took shelter in Rouen. He wrote to his niece that it was painful to hear the soldiers drag their swords along the path and to have their horses breathe in his face. The Prussians left Croisset after forty-five days, but more came in February 1871. Flaubert stopped wearing the ribbon of the Légion d'honneur because he felt that the words "honour" and "French" no longer went together. In March 1871, the people of Paris rose against the new government and created the Paris Commune. The government defeated it in May with great bloodshed. Flaubert watched these events with horror and despair. He told a friend that he was seeing "the end of the Latin world". From then on, his letters often expressed anger against his time, universal voting rights, the press, the bourgeoisie and crowds. He wrote that he wanted to recognise only "wise men and fools, the innocent and the guilty". On 8 November 1871, Élisa Schlésinger, the love of his youth and now a widow, visited him at Croisset. On 6 April 1872, his mother died. Flaubert was fifty years old. He wrote that she had been the person he loved most. A few months later, he sent Élisa one of his most moving letters. He called her "my old friend, my old tenderness" and invited her to sleep in his mother's room. Of all the people he remembered from his youth, he told her, her face appeared most clearly. Caroline inherited Croisset, but her uncle was allowed to continue living there. On 20 June, two months after his mother's death, he finished the third and final version of La Tentation de saint Antoine. In October, Théophile Gautier died. Flaubert felt that the friends of his youth were disappearing one after another. In 1873, Flaubert changed publishers. Georges Charpentier, a young man who admired his work, became the publisher of his later books. In the same year, Flaubert sent his first letter to the young Guy de Maupassant. Maupassant was the son of Laure Le Poittevin, the sister of Flaubert's dead friend Alfred. Flaubert took him under his protection, read his early writing, and taught him how to improve it. A later story claimed that Flaubert was Maupassant's real father. There is no evidence for this. Their connection was literary, not biological. Flaubert wrote letters of recommendation for the young man, told him to continue asking publishers until they listened to him, and even sent him to his own doctors. Flaubert had always loved the theatre. In 1873, he finished a play by Bouilhet, Le Sexe faible, and wrote a political comedy of his own, Le Candidat ("The Candidate"). The manager of the Vaudeville theatre, Carvalho, liked it and decided to stage it before Bouilhet's play. It opened on 11 March 1874 and failed completely. Edmond de Goncourt wrote that the audience slowly became cold and silent. They expected great speeches and clever lines but did not get them. After four performances, Flaubert removed the play from the stage. He said that he would not allow his actors to be booed. He felt like a criminal when he saw the leading actor leave the stage in tears. At the end of the same month, Charpentier published La Tentation de saint Antoine. This third version was much shorter than the two earlier ones and had a different structure. The two thousand copies of the first printing sold within three weeks, and Flaubert won back some readers who had disliked L'Éducation sentimentale. Almost all the reviews, however, were hostile. Flaubert found comfort in the praise of poets and friends. Villiers de l'Isle-Adam called it a "total work". Banville announced the birth of the modern epic. Daudet said that he knew some passages by heart. Renan, whose opinion Flaubert had especially wanted, sent a polite but uncertain letter. He said that Flaubert had used a club to drive away his bourgeois readers and should now return to subjects that interested everyone. In August 1874, Flaubert began to write Bouvard et Pécuchet, a novel that he had been preparing for years. Then came a serious financial problem. In the spring of 1875, the business of his nephew Ernest Commanville failed. Flaubert had invested part of his money in it and had allowed Commanville to manage his finances. To save the family from bankruptcy, he sold his farm at Deauville for 200,000 francs and immediately paid 50,000 francs to the main creditor. He gave up his apartment on the rue Murillo and moved to a smaller one on the rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré. "My nephew had devoured half my fortune," he told George Sand, and he had used what remained to pay his nephew's debts. From then on, he had little money and worried about it. He even asked friends to find him a paid job in a library. Unable to continue Bouvard et Pécuchet, he wrote three shorter works. In September 1875, while staying with the scientist Georges Pouchet at Concarneau in Brittany, he began La Légende de saint Julien l'Hospitalier. In February 1876, he began Un cœur simple ("A Simple Heart"), the story of a servant woman. He wrote it partly to please George Sand, who had asked him to write a story with more feeling. However, Sand died on 7 June 1876, before she could read it. Louise Colet had also died earlier that year, on 8 March. Hérodias was finished in February 1877. Charpentier published the three stories together as Trois Contes on 24 April 1877. Friends and critics praised the book, but it did not sell well. In his last years, Flaubert lived mostly at Croisset, alone with his servant and his greyhound Julio. He talked to the dog and admired its calm nature. The name may have been a memory of Juliet Herbert. In Paris, on Sundays, he received friends such as Turgenev, Edmond de Goncourt, Alphonse Daudet, Émile Zola and the young Maupassant, who considered himself Flaubert's pupil. Flaubert called Maupassant "my disciple" and his "adoptive son". In January 1880, he read the proofs of Maupassant's story Boule de Suif and wrote to his niece that it was a masterpiece. The writer Paul Morand later said that without Flaubert, Maupassant might never have written it. Flaubert continued to work on Bouvard et Pécuchet. He read hundreds of books about farming, chemistry, medicine, history, philosophy and religion so that the two main characters could try these subjects and fail at them. His health was poor. On 27 January 1879, he fell on the ice and broke a bone in his leg. His brother Achille offered him three thousand francs a year. His friends did more. In 1879, the minister of education, Jules Ferry, made him assistant librarian of the Bibliothèque Mazarine in Paris. The post paid three thousand francs a year, and Flaubert did not have to work there. He accepted the money but felt ashamed. Living on public money, he said, was not something to laugh about. On 8 May 1880, at Croisset, Flaubert collapsed and died. He was fifty-eight years old. His servant later told Maupassant what had happened. Flaubert felt an attack coming and said that it was fortunate because it would have been a problem if it had happened the next day on the train. He said that everything around him looked yellow. He rubbed his temples with eau de Cologne and lay down on the sofa. He spoke a few words about Rouen and some friends. Then he fell back, with his face dark and his hands closed tightly. His friend Dr Pouchet thought that he had died during an epileptic attack. Another doctor thought that he had suffered bleeding in the brain. He had been working on the tenth and final chapter of Bouvard et Pécuchet. In a drawer, he left 2,515 francs. The funeral took place on Tuesday, 11 May. Among the mourners were Goncourt, Turgenev, Daudet, Zola, Maupassant, Théodore de Banville, Joris-Karl Huysmans, François Coppée and José-Maria de Hérédia. After a mass at the church of Canteleu, the funeral procession walked to the Cimetière monumental in Rouen. Witnesses counted about 150 people. Apart from the mayor, almost no official from the city of Rouen came. Flaubert had always presented himself as an enemy of the bourgeoisie. According to one journalist, bourgeois Rouen had not forgotten this. He was buried next to his father and mother, not far from the grave of Louis Bouilhet. There was no formal speech because Flaubert had always refused the idea. His friend Lapierre said only a few words and ended in tears. One story was often repeated after the funeral. Some journalists asked a Rouen cab driver whether he knew the dead man. Of course, he answered: it was Monsieur Flaubert, the doctor's brother. They then asked whether he knew Flaubert's daughter, Madame Salammbô. Yes, said the driver, and she must be very sad. Bouvard et Pécuchet was published in March 1881. In the months after Flaubert's death, Caroline Commanville sold the house at Croisset to an industrial company. The house was pulled down, the trees were cut, and a factory making alcohol from maize was built on the land. Only the small pavilion in the garden survives. The manuscripts went to Caroline. In 1914, she gave the manuscripts of Madame Bovary to the library of Rouen. Charpentier began to publish Flaubert's letters in 1884, starting with his letters to George Sand and a study by Maupassant. Caroline then published four volumes of letters between 1887 and 1893, but she removed many of her uncle's more coarse words. René Descharmes published a fuller edition in 1921. Between 1910 and 1954, the publisher Conard printed Flaubert's complete works in twenty-six volumes, thirteen of them containing letters. The fifth and final volume of his letters in the Bibliothèque de la Pléiade appeared in 2007. Rouen built a monument to Bouilhet in 1882 and later created a museum about Flaubert in the wing of the Hôtel-Dieu where he was born. The full title of the novel is Madame Bovary. Mœurs de province ("Madame Bovary. Provincial Manners"). It begins in a schoolroom in Rouen, where a clumsy new boy, Charles Bovary, is laughed at by the other pupils. Charles becomes a health officer, a country doctor without a full medical degree, and marries Emma Rouault, the daughter of a farmer. Emma was educated in a convent, where she secretly read romantic novels. She dreams of passion, luxury and Paris. Her husband is kind but dull, and life in the small town of Yonville makes her deeply unhappy. She takes two lovers, first the rich landowner Rodolphe and then the young clerk Léon. Both relationships end badly. She borrows more and more money from the merchant Lheureux to pay for her clothes and her dreams. When she can no longer pay her debts, she swallows arsenic and dies slowly and painfully. Charles later dies of grief. The pharmacist Homais is a vain and talkative man who believes strongly in science and progress. The final words of the novel tell the reader that he has just received the cross of the Légion d'honneur. Around Emma, Flaubert shows the life of a small town in Normandy: the priest, the tax collector, the innkeeper, and the agricultural show with its prizes and speeches. He also describes a failed operation on a club foot which damages Charles's reputation. The novel gives a wide picture of what Flaubert saw as the bourgeois world, a world filled with ready-made ideas and empty words. However, the book is not simply a satire. The reader can share Emma's boredom and hopes while also seeing her from the outside. This double point of view is an important part of the novel. Jean Starobinski has shown how the point of view can move from the narrator to a character. Charles visits the farm and watches dust moving on the floor. The reader then begins to see and feel the scene through Charles. His lowered eyes show his shyness without the narrator having to explain it. Flaubert is famous for a method called style indirect libre, or free indirect style. The narrator gives a character's thoughts or words without adding expressions such as "she thought" or "he said". The voice of the narrator and the voice of the character can therefore seem to mix together. Sometimes the reader cannot be completely certain whose words or ideas are being expressed. This uncertainty is an important part of the novel's irony. The narrator does not disappear completely. In some places, he still makes judgments, for example by calling a girl's songs silly or by making a general comment about human nature. Another important feature is Flaubert's use of the imperfect tense, the French tense often used for actions that continued or happened repeatedly in the past. Proust spoke of Flaubert's "eternal imperfect". For Albert Thibaudet, this tense creates the feeling of ordinary life continuing day after day. Emma speaks and thinks in clichés, phrases that have been repeated so often that they have lost much of their meaning. Her language comes from the novels and songs she has read. Léon and Rodolphe use much the same kind of language. Emma cannot escape from it, even when she sometimes notices how empty it is. Charles, however, cannot speak this language at all. For this reason, Emma never understands that he loves her much more deeply than her lovers do. Victor Brombert has studied the way the images in the novel are connected. The chapter about Emma's education already uses many images of being shut in: the convent, the closed room and the quiet afternoon. It also uses images of escape, such as windows, roads and the wish to be somewhere else. Emma tells Léon that when people read, "one moves motionless through countries one imagines one sees". For Brombert, this sentence expresses an important part of her tragedy. Brombert also warns against reading the novel as only a satire. He finds a deep feeling of pity and sadness in it, which is difficult to explain if the book is seen only as an attack on Romantic dreams and the bourgeois world. Diana Knight also argues that the novel does not simply make fun of Emma. However, Emma cannot accept imagination as imagination. She wants her dreams to become real, and this helps to destroy her. Flaubert is said to have answered a woman who asked him where he had found Emma: "Madame Bovary is me." The sentence became famous, but there is no written record that Flaubert said it. To another reader, he wrote almost the opposite. He said that the book was "totally invented" and that he had put none of his own feelings or life into it. Salammbô takes place in Carthage in the third century BC. It begins with a feast in the gardens of the general Hamilcar, where unpaid mercenary soldiers become drunk and destroy things. Salammbô, Hamilcar's daughter and a priestess of the moon goddess Tanit, appears on the steps of the palace. Mâtho, a Libyan soldier, falls in love with her immediately. The mercenaries rise against Carthage. Mâtho steals the sacred veil of Tanit, the zaïmph, from the temple. Salammbô goes to his tent to take it back and gives herself to him. The war is long and violent. The Carthaginians sacrifice their children to the god Moloch. The mercenaries are trapped in a mountain pass and die of hunger. At the end, Mâtho is tortured to death before the people of Carthage, and Salammbô dies at the same moment. The last sentence of the novel says that Hamilcar's daughter died because she had touched the veil of Tanit. Françoise Gaillard has described the sacrifice of the children to Moloch as a "sacrifice without the sacred". The god continues to receive victims, but his hunger is never satisfied. Flaubert wanted to make the ancient world seem alive in every detail: the clothes, weapons, food, religions and smells of the streets. He used the work of Polybius and hundreds of scholarly books, and he travelled to Tunisia to see the places himself. The result is a strange and violent novel, full of colour and cruelty. Sainte-Beuve, who did not like it, asked whether all this learning was useful and whether the book contained too many horrors. Other readers have admired the novel for the same qualities. Victor Brombert called it "an epic of immobility". He argued that beneath all the movement and noise, the novel is always moving towards stone, statues and death. For him, this mixture of movement and stillness was one of Flaubert's deepest interests. The novel soon interested composers. Flaubert himself thought about an opera as early as 1862, with Gautier writing the words and Ernest Reyer the music. For a short time, Verdi seemed interested, but Gautier never wrote the text and died in 1872. Mussorgsky began an opera but never finished it. Reyer's Salammbô, with words by Camille Du Locle, was finally performed in Brussels in February 1890 and in Paris on 16 May 1892, ten years after Flaubert's death. It was very successful. A silent film based on the novel was made in Italy in 1911. The title means "sentimental education", or the education of the feelings. The novel follows Frédéric Moreau from 1840 to 1851 and then jumps forward to 1867. On a river boat, Frédéric sees Marie Arnoux, the wife of an art dealer, and falls in love with her. He loves her for the rest of his life but never has a complete relationship with her. He spends his years between Madame Arnoux, whom he loves and respects; Rosanette, a woman supported by rich men; and Madame Dambreuse, the wife of a rich banker. He almost marries Madame Dambreuse. His friend Deslauriers wants political power. The clerk Sénécal wants a socialist revolution. The shop assistant Dussardier is one of the few honest characters in the novel. Around them, the Revolution of 1848 begins and fails. Dussardier dies on a barricade in December 1851, killed by Sénécal, who has become a policeman. At the end of the novel, Frédéric and Deslauriers are old men. They remember a visit to a brothel when they were boys. They became frightened and ran away without doing anything. "That was the best we ever had," they agree. This ending surprised many readers in 1869 and can still surprise readers today. Flaubert called the book the moral history of the men of his generation. A novel about love becomes a novel about the failure of love, while the story of a generation becomes the story of its failure. Flaubert treats historical events much as he treats his characters. He does not openly take one side. He shows republicans and conservatives, workers and bankers, with the same irony. As with Salammbô, Flaubert collected a very large amount of information for the novel because he wanted its dates and facts to be correct. Jacques Arnoux, a dealer in "industrial art" who moves between art and business, was partly based on Maurice Schlésinger, the husband of Élisa. Brombert reads the novel as a story about pure things being damaged. Frédéric wastes or spoils almost everything he touches. Yet the pure image of Madame Arnoux is never completely destroyed. Brombert therefore argues that, strangely, the loss and failure in the book help to preserve this idea of purity. More recent critics have studied the novel in other ways. Barbara Vinken reads it as a novel about civil war, in which the private conflicts of the characters repeat the divisions of French society. Other critics have studied the scenes at Fontainebleau, where Frédéric and Rosanette walk through the forest and the castle while fighting continues in Paris. They see these scenes as a kind of imaginary museum inside the novel. The book is often described as one of the first modern novels because it does not follow the usual form of a story. The hero fails to achieve most of what he wants, and time passes without leading to a clear final success. The Temptation of Saint Anthony is not a novel. It is written like a play, with speeches and stage directions, but Flaubert did not intend it to be performed. The work shows a single night in the life of Anthony the Great, the Egyptian hermit of the fourth century who is often called the father of Christian monks. Anthony is alone in the desert, hungry and tired, when he begins to see visions. The Queen of Sheba offers him her love. Hilarion, his former pupil, is really the Devil in disguise. He shows Anthony the arguments between early Christian groups, then the gods of different religions dying one after another, and finally the universe described by science. In the final scene, Anthony wishes to become matter itself, and the face of Christ appears in the rising sun. Gisèle Séginger, who edited the work, notes that the painting Flaubert saw in Genoa was by Pieter Brueghel the Younger and that Flaubert described it in his travel notebook. What especially interested him was its grotesque side, the mixture of horror and comedy that Hugo had praised. Flaubert wrote three versions of the work, in 1849, 1856 and 1874. The first was the version that Bouilhet and Du Camp strongly rejected. Parts of the second version were printed in the magazine L'Artiste in 1856 and 1857. The prosecutor later used them against Flaubert during the trial of Madame Bovary. The third and much shorter version was published in 1874. Flaubert dedicated it to the memory of Alfred Le Poittevin, who had first spoken to him about Saint Anthony. The scholar Mary Orr notes that Flaubert's long work on the book was marked by two family deaths: that of his father in 1846 and that of his mother in 1872. For many years, critics found the book difficult and obscure. Orr has argued that it is Flaubert's most serious work about two of the great forces of his century, religion and science. Anthony is not simply the saint of popular religious pictures. He is also a man who questions ideas and refuses to accept a belief before examining it. The religious arguments of fourth-century Alexandria are connected with the arguments of 19th-century France about faith, evolution and the origin of life. Orr suggests that religion and science can begin to look strangely similar in the book. Both have authorities, laws and claims to possess the truth. The ending of the 1874 version was also connected with a scientific argument.

Annelies or Anneliese Marie Frank also known as Anne Frank (12 June 1929about February or March 1945) was a German-born Dutch Jewish girl who kept a diary in which she documented her life in hiding from the Nazis during World War II. Her diary is seen as a classic in war literature and history, and is one of the most widely read books today. Several plays and movies have been made on it. Anne was born in the city of Frankfurt am Main in the Free State of Prussia in Weimar Germany. She lived most of her life in or around Amsterdam, in the Netherlands. She was officially seen as a German until 1935. This was when she lost her nationality because of the anti-Semitic rules of Nazi Germany. She became famous around the world after her death when her diary was printed. In it she described her experiences hiding during the Nazi German occupation of the Netherlands in World War II. Frank family moved from Germany to Holland's capital, Amsterdam in 1933. This was the same year that the Nazis grew powerful in Germany. By the beginning of 1940, because of the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, the Frank family was trapped in Amsterdam. Persecution of Jewish people increased in July 1942, and the family decided to hide. They hid in some secret rooms of her father Otto Frank's office building. After two years, they were betrayed and taken to concentration camps. Anne and her sister, Margot, were later taken to the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp. There, they both died from typhus in 1945. Otto Frank was the only person in his family who survived. He went back to Amsterdam after the war and found that Anne's diary had been saved. He helped print a version of it in 1947. It was translated from Dutch and first printed in English in 1952 as The Diary of a Young Girl. It has been translated into many languages. The diary had been given to Anne on her 13th birthday. In it she wrote of her life from 12 June 1942 until 1 August 1944. Anne Frank was born on 12 June 1929 in Frankfurt, Germany. She was the second daughter of Otto Frank (1889–1980), a German businessman, and Edith Frank-Holländer (1900 – 45). Margot Frank (1926–45) was her older sister. The Franks were Jews, and they lived with many Jewish and non-Jewish citizens. Anne and Margot grew up with Catholic, Protestant, and Jewish friends. The Frank family did not follow all the customs of Judaism. Edith Frank was very religious, though her husband was more interested in studying. He had a large library, and both parents encouraged the children to read. On 13 March 1933, elections were held in Frankfurt, and Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party won.
