Acts of Antisemitism began almost immediately. The Franks were afraid of what might happen to them if they stayed in Germany. Therefore, later that year, Edith and the children went to Aachen. They stayed there with Edith's mother, Rosr.a Hollände Otto remained in Frankfurt, but after getting an offer to start a company in Amsterdam, he moved there to begin the business and to find a place to live with his family. The Franks were included in the 300,000 Jews who ran away from Germany between 1933 and 1939. While in hiding, she would often imagine herself gracefully gliding across the floors of the Secret Annex, finding solace and joy in the imaginary freedom of movement. Roller skating became a symbol of resilience and optimism in Anne's diary, reminding her of the simple pleasures of life outside the Annex. Otto Frank began working at the Opekta Works. Opteka was a company that sold pectin. Otto Frank found an apartment on the Merwedeplein (Merwede Square) in Amsterdam. By February 1934, Edith and the children had arrived in Amsterdam, and Anne and Margot began going to school. Margot went to public school and Anne went to a Montessori school. Margot enjoyed math, while Anne preferred reading and writing. Her friend Hanneli Goslar later remembered that from when she was young, Anne often wrote, though she tried to hide what she wrote and did not like talking about it. Margot and Anne had very different personalities. Margot was polite, quiet, and thoughtful, while Anne was brave, energetic, and friendly. In 1938, Otto Frank started a second company, Pectacon. Pectacon sold herbs, salts and mixed spices that were used to make sausages. Hermann van Pels worked at Pectacon as a helper about spices. He was a Jewish butcher. In 1939, Edith's mother came to live with the Franks. She stayed with them until she died in January 1942. In May 1940, Germany invaded the Netherlands. The government began to hurt Jews by making rules and laws about their freedom. The Frank sisters were both studying well and had many friends. But a new law that Jewish children could only go to a Jewish school made them move to a Jewish school. The companies that Otto Frank worked at still gave him some money, but they became poorer. It was not enough to support their family. For her 13th birthday on 12 June 1942, Anne Frank got a book she had shown her father a few days before. It was actually an autograph book with red-and-white cloth and a small lock on the front, but Anne decided to use it as a diary. She began writing in it almost immediately. Most of her first writings are about normal parts of her life, but she also wrote about some other things. In July 1942, the Zentralstelle für jüdische Auswanderung (Central Office for Jewish Emigration) ordered Margot Frank to come to be taken to a work camp. Otto Frank told his family that they would hide in rooms above and behind the place where his company worked on the Prinsengracht. The Prinsengracht was a street next to one of Amsterdam's canals, where some of his most trusted employees would help them. The notice to Margot made them move a few weeks earlier than they had expected. Anne's father, Otto Frank, was scared that the Nazis would find him and his family which he needed to protect, he then spoke to some of the people who worked in his business. One of them was a young woman of about 33 years old, and was named Miep Gies. He told her he needed help - he was going to turn the top floor of his business into a secret hiding place for himself and his family called "The Secret Annex". Miep and the others would have to help them keep their secret, and bring them food. They hid in their secret hiding place for two whole years, without being discovered by the Nazis. Anne Frank left all her other belongings in Frankfurt. Miep agreed to help. In 1942, the Frank family, together with the Van Pels (And their son Peter) and a dentist named Fritz Pfeffer, moved into the Secret Annex that they had prepared. They planned to stay there until the end of the war. They hoped the war would end soon, but it did not. They spent around two and a half years in their hiding place, never able to go out into the sunshine. During the day, the family had to be very quiet, because the business continued downstairs, and not all the workers knew that the Frank family was in hiding in the upper part of the building. A few months before the Franks went into hiding, Anne was given a diary, for her birthday. She called her diary "Kitty" and wrote in it about all the things that were happening to her and to her family. Anne was only a young girl, but she knew how to write beautifully. She wrote about all the things that young girls think about - how she was getting along with her friends and parents, boys (pretty much Peter), her life and emotions. After a while, Anne had one strong ambition, she aspired to be a writer. She hoped to write a book that everyone would read. After 2 years a thief had come and took not much, but after about two and a half years in hiding, not long before the end of the war, the thief was caught and, in exchange of not going to jail or death, he told the Nazis that a Jewish family - the Franks - were in hiding. Nazi soldiers came into the Frank's secret hiding place. They sent the Franks and the others to a concentration camp. Miep Gies found Anne's diary and put it into a drawer. She wanted to keep it safe until after the war. She hoped that Anne would return, and she would be able give her her diary back to her. However, that was not to be. Anne's father, Otto Frank, lived through the war and came back to Amsterdam in June. Unfortunately, Otto Frank was the only person in the hiding place to survive. Janny Brandes-Brilleslijper, a Holocaust survivor, testified that around January or February 1945, while in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, she discovered Anne was walking emaciated and wrapped in a single blanket. When she asked her where her clothes were, Anne claimed she had thrown them away because lice were crawling all over them. Anne then told Janny to also organize something for her sister Margot because she was gravely ill. She promised Anne to organize some clothing for her and organize something for Margot, and gave Anne some morsels of bread, before she left. Three days later, Janny learned that both Margot and Anne were dead. She then said that Margot fell out of her bed and died almost instantly from shock. One day later, Anne fell into a coma whilst asleep, and died shortly afterwards. Anne's cause of death was most likely typhus fever. Janny and her sister Lientje were given Margot and Anne's bodies and buried them in a mass grave. She also testified that shortly after Margot and Anne's deaths, Bergen-Belsen was liberated by British troops. Bergen-Belsen was liberated by the British on April 15, 1945 (the same year Margot and Anne died). Janny's sister, Lientje, also survived the Holocaust. After World War II ended in Europe (because the Germans did not record Anne's date of death) Lientje was asked when Anne died. Lientje then said that she believed Anne died sometime around March 1945. So Dutch authorities believed that Anne likely died two weeks before the camp was liberated. Later in 1954, the German Red Cross army declared that Margot and Anne died sometime between 1 March 1945 and 31 March 1945. In 2015, the Anne Frank House researchers indicated that Anne died around February 1945. So the Anne Frank House researchers believed that Anne likely died two months before the camp was liberated. When World War II ended, Miep Gies gave Otto Frank Anne's diary and a bundle of notes. Otto Frank then decided to publish her diary to commemorate her. Miep Gies was with Otto Frank when he got the letter telling him that his two daughters were dead. Now she knew that Anne would never return for her diary. She went to the drawer where the diary was kept, and she gave it to Otto Frank. People who were close to Anne read the diary. They told Otto Frank that he should publish it. Anne had wanted to be a famous writer. Now, people would be able to read her book, and they would also learn about the difficult time that the Jews had during the war, and about the wonderful people who helped them. Otto had Anne's diary printed. It became one of the world's most widely-read books. It has been printed in over 60 languages, and people across the world have read and enjoyed this true story. Today, for an admission fee, visitors can see the house in Amsterdam where Anne Frank and her family hid during the war. They can also see Anne's diary.

Federico del Sagrado Corazón de Jesús García Lorca; (5 June 1898 – 19 August 1936) was a Spanish poet, dramatist and theatre director. García Lorca achieved international recognition as an emblematic member of the Generation of '27. He is believed to be one of thousands who were summarily shot by anti-communist death squads during the Spanish Civil War. He was gay. In 2008, a Spanish judge opened an investigation into Lorca's death. The Garcia Lorca family eventually dropped objections to the excavation of a potential gravesite near Alfacar. However, no human remains were found.

André Paul Guillaume Gide (22 November 1869 – 19 February 1951) was a French writer. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1947. Gide was born in Paris into a middle class Protestant family. During a trip to Alegeria, Gide realized that he was gay. His first novel The Notebooks of Andre Walter was published in 1891. Gide met Oscar Wilde in 1894. In October 1895 Gide married his cousin Madeleine. When Gide was 47 15-year-old Marc Allégret became his lover. Gide also opposed colonialism and exploitation of slavery in Africa and was interested in communism and visited Soviet Union, but he expressed critical idea on the totalitarian regime.

Knut Hamsun (August 4, 1859 – February 19, 1952) was a Norwegian author and winner of the Nobel Prize in literature, in 1920. An obituary he wrote for Adolf Hitler was published on 7 May 1945 in Aftenposten (a newspaper). He married Marie Hamsun. Their children include Tore Hamsun. In 1978, Gabriel Langfeldt released a book that listed the entire [written] statement of the court-appointed [medical] experts, from Hamsun's trial; spokesman for the Hamsun family - Leif Hamsun (a grandchild of Knut Hamsun) - said that after Langfeldt revealed my grandparents [privileged interviews with court-appointed experts], there is little that is private anymore. Hamsun voluntarily went to psychoanalysis during 1926 to 1928; the psychoanalyst made notes. Notes from the psychoanalysis of Hamsun, were published in 2017; the photocopied notes were from [Hamsun's appointments] with his psychoanalyst; photocopied notes were part of [a work of] art that was published in Vagant [a magazine].

Eugène Ionesco (born Eugen Ionescu; 26 November 1909 – 28 March 1994) was a Romanian-born French playwright. He wrote in French. He was born in Slatina, Romania. His father was Romanian and his mother was French. He spent most of his childhood in France. As a young man he lived in Bucharest. He settled in France for good in 1942 and became a French citizen in 1957. Ionesco was one of the most important playwrights in French avant-garde theatre (new and experimental theatre) after World War II. His best-known play is La Cantatrice chauve (The Bald Soprano). It was first acted in Paris on 11 May 1950. Since 1957 it has remained on the programme of the small Théâtre de la Huchette in Paris, together with his second play, La Leçon (The Lesson). Other famous plays are Les Chaises (The Chairs), Rhinocéros (Rhinoceros) and Le Roi se meurt (Exit the King). His plays are often called "theatre of the absurd". The English critic (a person who writes about plays) Martin Esslin made this name popular in a 1961 book. Ionesco himself did not like the label. His early plays make fun of everyday talk. The characters speak in ready-made phrases and say nothing. His later plays have a hero called Bérenger. Bérenger is an ordinary man. He is afraid of death, and he refuses to follow the crowd. The most famous of these plays, Rhinocéros, shows a town where everybody slowly turns into a rhinoceros. Ionesco wrote it after seeing his friends in Romania join a fascist movement in the 1930s. All his life he attacked ideologies (systems of political ideas), both on the right and on the left. He was elected to the Académie française in 1970. He also wrote diaries, essays, stories for children and one novel. In his last years he painted. Ionesco died in Paris on 28 March 1994. He is buried in the Montparnasse Cemetery. Ionesco's father, Eugen Ionescu, was a Romanian lawyer. His mother, Thérèse Ipcar, was French. She was the daughter of a French engineer. Her father, Jean Ipcar, was born in Bucharest in 1850 and died in Paris in 1924. Ionesco himself sometimes said that his mother's family was partly Jewish. André Le Gall studied the family papers. He believes that the Ipcars were of French and Greek origin, and that only one of Thérèse's grandmothers may have been Jewish. On his father's side, the family came from Romanian peasants, but Ionesco's grandfather had already left farming. Eugen Ionescu had studied law at the University of Bucharest. He worked as a government official in the provinces. The parents married in Bucharest and then lived in Slatina, a small town in Wallachia on the river Olt. In 1909, Ionesco's father was secretary general of the prefecture, the local government office, of Slatina. Their first child was born in Slatina on 26 November 1909. In the old Orthodox calendar, which Romania still used, the date was 13 November. He was named Eugen, like his father. His French death certificate gives the date of 13 November and his full name as Eugène Dimitri Ionescu, called Ionesco. Later in life, Ionesco often said that he had been born in 1912. Many books still give this wrong date. The family name, Ionescu, was later written in the French form, Ionesco. The marriage of his parents was unhappy. They had violent arguments, and the child never forgot these scenes. He later put them, almost without changing them, into two of his plays, Victimes du devoir (1953) and L'Homme aux valises (1975). In 1911, the family moved to Paris. Ionesco's father wanted to finish his studies in law. A sister, Marilina, was born in Paris in February 1911. A younger brother, Mircea, was born in 1913. He died from meningitis, an illness of the brain, when he was eighteen months old. In 1916, during World War I, Ionesco's father returned alone to Bucharest. He sent no news to his family. For years, his wife and children believed that he was dead. In fact, he had found a good position in Romania. Without telling his wife, he obtained a divorce. He said that she had left the family home. He then married another woman. Thérèse stayed in Paris with the two children. They were poor and lived in a dark flat. Her parents gave them some help. Thérèse went to work in a factory. For a short time, the boy was sent to a children's home near Paris. He suffered because he was away from his mother. The boy was often afraid. Later, he said that he had been obsessed by death from the age of four, when he first understood that one day he would die. He also discovered the puppet theatre in the Luxembourg Gardens. His mother could hardly take him away from the small, jerky figures, which always ended by beating one another. At about the same time, he wrote a "heroic" play in two acts in a school exercise book and a comic story for a film. Both texts are lost. In 1917, the two children were sent to the countryside. For two years, they lived at La Chapelle-Anthenaise, a small village in the Mayenne, in western France. They stayed in an old mill called the Moulin with a farming family. The farmers, Baptiste and Jeannette, and their daughter Marie were kind to them. Marie took the boy everywhere with her, and he became like a little country child. He was happy there, and his fear that his mother would die disappeared. For the rest of his life, he remembered this village as a lost paradise. It became the model for the "radiant city", or city of light, and for all the bright places in his plays. After the war, the children returned to Paris. At about the age of eleven, Ionesco felt that the streets of Paris were like a prison. He found comfort in books. A story by Flaubert, "A Simple Heart", made him want to become a writer. In 1922, Thérèse and her two children left for Bucharest. Ionesco's father had obtained custody of the children, the legal right to keep them, after the divorce. Eugen was thirteen. He had to learn Romanian, a language that he did not know. He and his sister went to live with their father and his new wife, Hélène. Their stepmother did not like them. After one month, she sent Marilina back to her mother, but Eugen stayed. He ate his meals alone in his room. Soon after arriving, he saw his father beat an old Jewish man who rented a house from him. His father wanted to force the man out of a small house behind his own. His father was a hard man. He changed his political ideas whenever the government changed. He supported fascism and later communism whenever this helped him. He did not understand his dreamy son. He blamed him for writing poems, read his private diary, shouted at him, and beat him. At the Saint Sava college, the boy was very good at literature but had little interest in science. His mother had followed the children to Bucharest. She worked as a secretary at the National Bank of Romania. In 1926, when he was seventeen, Eugen left his father's house. His mother's flat was too small, so he lived with one of his aunts and ate his meals with his mother. A grant, money given to a student, from a foundation helped him to live by himself. He passed the baccalauréat, the final school examination, in 1928. In the same year, the great poet Tudor Arghezi published Ionesco's first poems in a small daily paper, Bilete de papagal ("Parrot Notes"). At twenty, he entered the University of Bucharest to study for a degree in French. He earned money by giving French lessons. He wrote a great deal. In 1931, he published a small book of poems in Romanian, Elegii pentru ființe mici ("Elegies for Tiny Beings"). He later called these poems "lamentable". He also wrote articles for many magazines, including a weekly newspaper that fought against fascism. Bucharest was then a lively city for writers. Young writers such as Mircea Eliade, Emil Cioran, Constantin Noica, and Mihail Sebastian began their careers at the same time. In 1934, Ionesco received his diploma as a teacher of French. In the same year, he published a book of criticism called Nu ("No"). In it, he attacked the most famous Romanian writers of the time with humour and irony, which can mean saying the opposite of what one really means. He showed that he could prove one idea and then prove the opposite idea. In this way, he argued that literary criticism had no firm rules. The book won a prize from the Royal Foundations for the first book by a young writer. The jury included Mircea Eliade. However, the Foundations refused to publish such a shocking book, so another publisher, Vremea, published it. The prize caused an angry public debate. The book was translated into French only in 1986. Ionesco did his military service, taught French in three schools, and then worked for the ministry of education. He also became the literary critic of the magazine Facla. On 8 July 1936, he married Rodica Burileanu, a student of philosophy. Their church wedding took place on 12 July. Rodica came from an old Romanian upper-class family. Her father, who had died at the age of forty-four, had run a liberal newspaper. Three months after the wedding, Ionesco's mother died. Rodica stayed with him all his life. In his diaries, he calls her simply "R.". He wrote that she was "my only relative, more than a mother". In July 1986, they celebrated fifty years of marriage. These were dark years in Romania. The country was moving closer to Nazism. The Iron Guard, a fascist movement, wanted a government like Hitler's. King Carol II fought the Guard but slowly became a dictator himself. Ionesco saw his own father support the Iron Guard. He also watched professors, students, and close friends slowly become supporters of it, through a few arguments and through fear. He felt more and more alone. He later described this experience in his diary, and it became the subject of Rhinocéros. Like many Romanian writers and thinkers, Ionesco wanted to leave the country. In 1938, he received a grant from the French Institute of Bucharest to write a doctoral thesis in Paris. Its subject was "Sin and Death in French Poetry since Baudelaire". He never finished the thesis. Ionesco later admitted that it was mainly an excuse to return to France. In Paris, he met the philosopher, or thinker, Emmanuel Mounier and went to meetings of his magazine Esprit. He wrote articles that explained Mounier's ideas to Romanian readers. The war forced Ionesco to return to Romania in 1940. He taught French at the Saint Sava school in Bucharest. He immediately regretted returning. By then, Romania was ruled by the military dictatorship of General Antonescu, who was an ally of Hitler. For almost two years, Ionesco and Rodica tried to obtain passports and visas. With help from friends in important positions, they were finally able to leave for France in 1942. Ionesco became a member of the Romanian legation, a small embassy, at Vichy, the capital of the French government at that time. He was first a press officer. From April 1943, he was cultural secretary, and from June 1944, chief secretary. He received the pay of a Romanian diplomat. His official home was Vichy, but the couple spent much of the war in Marseille, where he also translated texts for a publisher. Ionesco never tried to hide this job. In Marseille, he became friends with writers from the magazine Les Cahiers du Sud and with its editor, Jean Ballard. His only child, Marie-France, was born early at a clinic in Vichy on 26 August 1944. In 1945, the family moved to Paris. They lived at 38 rue Claude-Terrasse until 1960. Ionesco could not find good work. He worked in a warehouse for the paint company Ripolin. He then became a proofreader, a person who corrects printed texts, for a publisher of legal and medical books. Rodica worked as a secretary in a law office. Between 1945 and 1949, he spent much time translating the Romanian writer Urmuz, an earlier writer with a similar kind of strange humour. Ionesco could no longer publish in Romania. The new communist government did not want him, and he openly attacked it. In March 1946, a Romanian magazine, Viața Românească, printed some pages from his diary as a "Letter from Paris". In them, he wrote that nationalism, the belief that one's own nation is better than others, had poisoned all Romanian culture. He added that the fatherland should be the country of the mother, not the country of the father. The army was furious. On 31 May 1946, a military court in Bucharest judged Ionesco while he was absent. It sentenced him to five years in prison for insulting the army and six years for insulting the nation. He never returned to Romania. His father died in Bucharest in 1948. Ionesco was almost forty when he became a playwright, and he had not planned to become one. According to his own story, he decided in 1948 to learn English. He bought an Assimil book, a method for learning a language at home. In its dialogues, Mr and Mrs Smith counted their children and listed the days of the week. They spoke with the calm of people who believed that they were saying very important things. Ionesco copied these sentences. As he copied them, the sentences became strange. The seven days of the week became three, and Tuesday appeared twice. He said that the book had shown him "essential truths". Language can say everything and nothing. It can say one thing and then the opposite without any shame. He told this story in 1958 in a lecture called "The Tragedy of Language". A first version of the play seems to have been written in Romanian under the title Englezește fără profesor ("English Without a Teacher"). He read the play to friends, and they laughed. He then noticed that it was similar to Raymond Queneau's Exercices de style, a book that he read soon afterwards. The publisher Bernard Grasset and the Comédie-Française both refused the play. A young director, Nicolas Bataille, agreed to stage it with his small group of actors. Bataille was twenty-one years old. There were six actors, including Bataille himself and Henri-Jacques Huet, who played the Fire Chief. At first, the play had no final title. Ionesco first called it L'Anglais sans peine ("English Without Toil"), the name of the Assimil book. The final title came from a slip of the tongue, a mistake in speaking. During a rehearsal, which is a practice before a performance, Huet became lost in the strange text. He said "la cantatrice chauve", or "the bald singer", instead of "l'institutrice blonde", or "the blonde teacher". Ionesco kept the mistake. There is no bald singer in the play. The first performance took place on 11 May 1950 at the Théâtre des Noctambules in Paris. It was performed at half past six in the evening because other plays used the theatre later at night. Very few people came. The play closed the following month, after only twenty-five performances. However, some of the few people who came were important. The Surrealists André Breton and Benjamin Péret, the poet Philippe Soupault, Raymond Queneau, and the critic Jacques Lemarchand supported the play. Ionesco later described the event with humour as "a small failure, a mediocre scandal". For several years, Ionesco's plays were performed in tiny theatres on the Left Bank of Paris, for small audiences and little money. La Leçon was first performed in February 1951 at the Théâtre de Poche, directed by Marcel Cuvelier. Les Chaises followed in April 1952 at the Théâtre Lancry, directed by Sylvain Dhomme. Victimes du devoir came in February 1953, directed by Jacques Mauclair. Mauclair became one of the directors who understood Ionesco best. Another was Jean-Marie Serreau, who staged Amédée ou Comment s'en débarrasser at the Théâtre de Babylone in April 1954. In 1951, Ionesco joined the Collège de 'Pataphysique. This was a society of writers who followed Alfred Jarry, the author of Ubu roi. Its members made a science out of nonsense and treated it very seriously. His first plays were published in 1953 by a small publisher, Arcanes. In 1954, the large publisher Gallimard published the first volume of his Théâtre. Jacques ou la Soumission was performed in October 1955 at the Huchette, with the young Jean-Louis Trintignant. In February 1956 came L'Impromptu de l'Alma, in which Ionesco put himself on the stage and made fun of critics. In the same year, Mauclair staged Les Chaises again at the Studio des Champs-Élysées. The famous playwright Jean Anouilh wrote an article in Le Figaro to defend Ionesco. He said that the play was better than Strindberg. This article helped to change the opinion of critics. They no longer saw Ionesco only as a strange comic writer. They began to take his work seriously. By the middle of the 1950s, Ionesco was also becoming known in the English-speaking world. The Lesson was performed in London in 1955, and The Bald Soprano and The New Tenant followed in 1956. In January 1958, the director Tony Richardson staged The Chairs and The Lesson in New York. In 1957, Ionesco became a French citizen. On 16 February 1957, Nicolas Bataille and Marcel Cuvelier brought La Cantatrice chauve and La Leçon together at the Théâtre de la Huchette. This time, the theatre attracted much more attention. Famous people such as Édith Piaf and Sophia Loren were seen in the small theatre. The two plays have remained on the programme there ever since. The same year saw the first Paris performances of L'avenir est dans les œufs and Le Nouveau Locataire. In 1957, Ionesco also published a short story called "Rhinocéros" in the magazine Les Lettres nouvelles. By 1958, Ionesco's plays were being performed in London, where Les Chaises and La Leçon were played with the actress Joan Plowright. The critic Kenneth Tynan had been one of Ionesco's strongest supporters in England. However, on 22 June 1958, in The Observer, Tynan wrote that he was worried by a "cult of Ionesco". He said that Ionesco's plays turned away from real life and politics. Tynan preferred writers such as Arthur Miller and Sartre, who took clear positions on social questions. Ionesco answered in the same newspaper on 29 June. He said that a work of art was not a political message. It was "the expression of an incommunicable reality that one tries to communicate". In other words, art tries to share something that cannot fully be shared. Other writers joined the argument, including the film director Orson Welles and the critic Philip Toynbee. The newspaper did not print Ionesco's final reply. The exchange became famous as the "London controversy". Ionesco later included his answers in Notes et contre-notes. Tueur sans gages (The Killer) was first performed in February 1959 at the Théâtre Récamier. It was the first play to include the character Bérenger. Rhinocéros was written in 1958 from the short story of 1957. The first performance of the complete play was a radio broadcast by the BBC on 20 August 1959. On stage, it was first performed in German at the Schauspielhaus in Düsseldorf in the autumn of 1959. Karl-Heinz Stroux directed it. Stroux presented the play as a tragedy. A German critic wrote that the applause on the first night "did not want to end". The Paris performance followed on Friday 22 January 1960 at the Odéon-Théâtre de France. The great actor and director Jean-Louis Barrault staged the play and played Bérenger. Barrault made the play more like a farce. It was the first Ionesco play to be performed in a theatre paid for by the state. The play was a huge success. On the first night, the theatre was full, with more than twelve hundred people in the audience, including André Malraux, the minister of culture. In May 1960, Orson Welles directed it in London at the Royal Court Theatre, with Laurence Olivier as Bérenger. In New York, the comic actor Zero Mostel played the role. Ionesco was now a famous writer. He was especially popular in Germany. During the 1962 season, he was, together with Shakespeare and Brecht, one of the most frequently performed playwrights there. Later, with the money earned from his plays, Ionesco bought a flat on the boulevard du Montparnasse. He lived there until his death. He knew that Rhinocéros marked a change in his work. He was no longer seen only as a comic writer of the avant-garde. People now saw him as a serious writer interested in human behaviour. In 1961, Ionesco wrote a film story, La Colère (Anger), for one part of the film Les Sept Péchés capitaux (1962), directed by Sylvain Dhomme. It begins with a quiet Sunday morning in a small town, where everyone smiles and gives polite greetings. Then a husband finds a fly in his soup. Anger spreads from flat to flat, from town to town, and from country to country, until the whole planet explodes. The story returns to the idea of the destructive film story that Ionesco had written as a child. In the following years, he wrote a great deal. Le Roi se meurt was first performed in December 1962 at the Théâtre de l'Alliance française. Jacques Mauclair directed the play and played the King. In the same year, Le Piéton de l'air was first performed in Düsseldorf. Ionesco also published two books in 1962: Notes et contre-notes, a collection of his articles and talks about theatre, and La Photo du colonel, a collection of stories. Barrault staged Le Piéton de l'air at the Odéon in February 1963, with Madeleine Renaud. La Soif et la Faim (Hunger and Thirst) was first performed in German at Düsseldorf in December 1964. In February 1966, it entered the Comédie-Française, the national theatre of France. Jean-Marie Serreau directed it, with Robert Hirsch in the leading role. For a French playwright, this was one of the highest forms of official recognition. The audience at the Comédie-Française was not used to avant-garde plays, and some people in the audience protested loudly. In the same year, Ionesco wrote short sketches for an American French course, Leçons de français pour Américains, in the style of La Cantatrice chauve. In 1967 and 1968, he published his first two diaries. In 1969, he received the Grand Prix national du théâtre and the Prince Pierre of Monaco literary prize. He also held his first exhibition of paintings in Geneva. Jeux de massacre (Killing Game), a play about a plague, was first performed in Düsseldorf in January 1970 and in Paris in September 1970, directed by Jorge Lavelli. On 22 January 1970, Ionesco was elected to the Académie française. He took the seat of the writer Jean Paulhan, who had died in 1968. His sponsor was the writer Paul Morand, who was his neighbour in the countryside. He was officially received at the Académie on 25 February 1971 by the writer Jean Delay, who was also a psychiatrist, a doctor who treats illnesses of the mind. In his speech, Ionesco praised Paulhan, whom he had liked very much. He also said that literature comes from "a certain way of looking" that makes reality seem strange. In 1970, he also received the Austrian State Prize for European Literature and the Légion d'honneur. Marie-Claude Hubert writes that these two events, the Comédie-Française in 1966 and the Académie in 1970, confirmed Ionesco's place as a major French playwright. Ionesco continued to write plays, but less quickly than before. Macbett, a free version of Shakespeare's Macbeth, was performed in 1972. In 1973, he published his only novel, Le Solitaire (The Hermit), a sad book written like a serious confession. At the request of Jacques Mauclair, he turned it into a play, Ce formidable bordel!, which was performed in the same year. L'Homme aux valises (The Man with the Luggage, 1975) and Voyages chez les morts (Journeys among the Dead, 1980) are dream plays. They are full of Ionesco's own memories: his father, his stepmother, the flat in the rue Claude-Terrasse, and the mill at La Chapelle-Anthenaise. In 1971, he acted in a television film himself, La Vase, based on one of his stories. He received many honours. On 30 April 1973, he was given the Jerusalem Prize in Israel. In 1974, the University of Warwick in Coventry, England, gave him an honorary doctorate. A year later, he received another honorary doctorate from the University of Tel Aviv. In 1978, a ten-day meeting of scholars about his work was held at Cerisy-la-Salle in Normandy. Politics remained important to him. He wrote angry letters to newspapers whenever he believed that freedom was in danger. He was shocked by the student revolt of May 1968 in Paris because he did not trust mass movements or the behaviour of crowds. He defended dissidents, or opponents of the government, in communist countries. These included Sakharov, Siniavsky and Daniel in the Soviet Union, and Václav Havel in Czechoslovakia. He was angry with left-wing writers in France who took a long time to care about these people. In February 1989, he wrote a text for the European Commission against the dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu. In it, he spoke of a "cultural genocide", meaning the destruction of a people's culture, in Romania. He was too ill to read the text himself. When Ceaușescu fell in December 1989, Ionesco said that he felt "Romanian again". The Romanian Writers' Union made him an honorary member. Prizes, medals, and decorations continued to come from France, Germany, Austria, Monaco, and the United States. They included the T. S. Eliot–Ingersoll Prize in Chicago in 1985 and a Molière, the main French theatre prize, in 1989. During the last fifteen years of his life, painting became very important to him. He worked in a studio in St. Gallen, in Switzerland, a town that he loved. In 1981, he published Le Noir et le Blanc, a book of fifteen lithographs, prints made from drawings on stone, together with a text about his late discovery of painting. Only two hundred copies were printed. Gallimard reprinted it in 1985 under the title Le Blanc et le Noir. His gouaches, paintings made with a kind of water paint, and his lithographs were shown in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Italy, Greece, and Scandinavia. They were shown less often in France. His last work for the stage was the text for an opera, Maximilien Kolbe. It honours a Polish priest who, in a Nazi prison camp, chose to die in place of another prisoner. The music was written by Dominique Probst. The opera was first performed at Rimini in Italy in August 1988, before more than seven thousand people. It was performed again in Arras Cathedral in 1989. His last diary, La Quête intermittente, was printed in December 1987. It begins with a memory of his golden wedding, the fiftieth anniversary of his marriage. His health became worse. In 1984, he spent two days in hospital because of diabetes. On 23 February 1987, the Théâtre de la Huchette celebrated thirty years of La Cantatrice chauve with Ionesco present. In February 1990, he wrote in Le Figaro that the world was "on the edge of an apocalyptic catastrophe" and that there was only one thing to do: pray. He had always regretted that he was not a mystic, a person who feels God directly. During his last years, he could no longer walk without help. Rodica and Marie-France cared for him. His final article for Le Figaro appeared in February 1994. Eugène Ionesco died at his home in Paris on 28 March 1994. He was 84 years old. He was buried on Friday 1 April, which was Good Friday that year, in the Montparnasse Cemetery (Cimetière du Montparnasse). Ionesco called his first play an "anti-play". It takes place in an English living room, on "one English evening". The play begins when an English clock strikes seventeen times. Mr and Mrs Smith talk about their dinner. They also talk about a family in which everybody, both men and women, is called Bobby Watson. Then their guests, Mr and Mrs Martin, arrive. The Martins slowly discover that they live in the same street, in the same house, and in the same room. They therefore decide that they must be husband and wife. The maid, Mary, and a Fire Chief also appear. The Fire Chief tells stories that begin like fables with a lesson, but the lesson never comes. At the end, the four characters shout words and syllables at one another. Then the play begins again from the start, but this time the Martins take the place of the Smiths. Ionesco had first planned a much more violent ending. Angry spectators, placed in the audience by the writer, were to invade the stage. The theatre manager would then call the police, who would shoot them. The play has no real story and no psychology. Its main subject is language itself. The characters speak in platitudes, or empty ready-made phrases that everybody uses. Richard Coe called this "the apotheosis of the platitude": the empty phrase is raised almost to the level of a god. The platitudes pile up page after page, and their great number is what makes them frightening. Ionesco later said that he had looked for the most worn-out clichés so that he could empty words of their meaning and express "absence, the void". He explained that the play is about the petty bourgeois, the narrow-minded middle-class person, "a man of fixed ideas and slogans". This person is a conformist: he always does and thinks what everybody else does. His conformism is shown by the mechanical way in which he speaks. For Rosette Lamont, this attack on language is already political. People who speak in this way do not really talk to one another. Words pass through them "like a dribble of saliva". Ionesco often said that the play was written to make people laugh, and that its comedy is real. However, he also called it "the tragedy of language". The critic who reviewed its first performance in 1950 already placed it in the category of "the absurd", ten years before Martin Esslin made the word famous. La Leçon is a "comic drama" with three characters: a Professor, a young girl who is his Pupil, and a Maid. The Professor begins by teaching arithmetic and then moves to philology, the study of languages. The Pupil has a toothache. The lesson becomes more and more violent, and the Professor kills the girl with a knife. The Maid then tells him that this is the fortieth pupil he has killed that day. Together, they prepare the funeral, and a forty-first pupil rings at the door. In the printed text, the Maid gives the Professor an armband with a swastika, the sign of the Nazis, so that nobody will stop them. Lamont notes that this line reminds the reader of how blind the world can be to mass murder. Harold Bloom says that the play works on stage like a religious ceremony in which a victim is killed, although the ceremony is also a farce, a wild comedy. Language and power are closely connected in the play: the person who controls words also controls the other person. Les Chaises (1952) is a "tragic farce". An Old Man of ninety-five and an Old Woman of ninety-four live in a tower on an island. The Old Man has a message for humanity. He has invited important guests to hear it, including the Emperor. The guests arrive, but they cannot be seen. The Old Woman brings more and more chairs for them until the stage is full of empty chairs. An Orator arrives to give the message. The old couple jump out of the windows into the water. However, the Orator is deaf and unable to speak. He only makes sounds and writes meaningless letters on a blackboard. For Coe, the play shows the emptiness at the centre of things. The invisible crowd and the many chairs fill a life that is itself empty. The play is also about a long marriage and about old age. Nancy Lane thinks that it may be Ionesco's best play because it uses real objects on the stage, the chairs, to show absence and emptiness. Many of Ionesco's plays from the 1950s show objects that multiply and fill the stage. Coe calls this "proliferation", or growth without end. Characters can also multiply: there are three doctors called Bartholomeus in L'Impromptu de l'Alma, two girls called Roberte in Jacques, and countless Bobby Watsons. In Jacques ou la Soumission, written in 1950, a family forces a young man to marry a girl who has three noses. Victimes du devoir (1953) is, in Ionesco's own words, a confession. A policeman forces the hero, Choubert, to search through his memory. The scenes in which a father and mother argue come from Ionesco's own childhood. Coffee cups pile up on the table without end. Ionesco also wrote many short sketches. In Le Maître (The Leader), a very short comic version of Waiting for Godot, the leader for whom everybody has been waiting finally arrives, but he has no head. In Le Tableau (The Picture, 1955), a rich Large Gentleman argues with a poor Painter about the price of a picture and frightens everybody with a pistol. In Les Salutations, three gentlemen greet one another in endless different ways. In Amédée ou Comment s'en débarrasser (1954), a married couple have lived for fifteen years with a dead body in the next room. The body grows all the time. It suffers from "geometrical progression", the "incurable disease of the dead". At the end, its feet reach the door and block every way out. In Le Nouveau Locataire (The New Tenant, 1957), written in a little more than two days in September 1953, a quiet man moves into a flat. Furniture is carried inside until it fills the room, the staircase, and the street, and finally buries him. Marie-Claude Hubert writes that in these plays the object is part of the character. The stage works like a mousetrap that slowly closes. Rhinocéros (1959) is Ionesco's most popular play. It takes place in a small provincial town. Bérenger, a clerk who drinks too much, is sitting at a café with his friend Jean. Jean lectures him about will-power and self-improvement. Suddenly, a rhinoceros runs through the square. Then another one appears. The people argue about whether it was the same animal and whether it had one horn or two. A Logician discusses the question by using false syllogisms, or chains of reasoning. Soon the truth becomes clear: the people of the town are turning into rhinoceroses. In the second act, Jean changes in front of Bérenger. His skin becomes green and rough, and a bump grows on his forehead. Bérenger's fellow workers also change. Botard, who at first refuses to believe that the rhinoceroses exist, finally joins them. Dudard, who accepts almost everything, also leaves. He says that one must "follow one's time". At the end, even Daisy, the woman Bérenger loves, leaves to join the animals. She thinks that they are beautiful. Bérenger is left alone as the last human being. He is afraid and full of doubt. He even wonders whether he himself is the monster. However, he ends the play with the cry: "I will not capitulate!" This means: "I will not give in." Ionesco always said that the play was a fable, a story with a moral, and that the rhinoceroses were first of all Nazi militants. The slow spread of the disease through the town represents the rise of fascism. The play comes from Ionesco's own experience in Romania during the 1930s, when his friends and teachers joined the Iron Guard. The green colour of the animals recalls the green shirts worn by the Romanian fascists, and Jean wears green pyjamas. The characters speak about "the events", the expression that people used at the time for the rise of Hitler. However, the play goes beyond one country or one political party. It shows how any totalitarianism, a system in which the state controls everything, can grow on either the right or the left. It also shows how ordinary people accept such a system one by one, each for a different reason. For Étienne Frois, it is too narrow to read the play only as an attack on Nazism. Its real subject is "rhinoceritis", the disease of conformism, or following the crowd, in all its forms. Bérenger is not a hero in the usual sense. Lamont calls him an "antihero", a hero who does not have the usual qualities of a hero. What makes him human is his doubt. Harold Bloom writes that Bérenger is weak, confused, and frightened, "yet he will not yield". He will probably be killed by the rhinoceroses, "but he will die human". Ionesco later wrote that Rhinocéros could be played as a tragedy, as it was in Düsseldorf, or as a terrible fantastic farce, as Barrault played it in Paris. Bérenger appears in four plays: Tueur sans gages (1959), Rhinocéros (1959), Le Piéton de l'air (1962), and Le Roi se meurt (1962). He is not exactly the same character in each play, but he is always an ordinary man who expresses many of Ionesco's own feelings. Coe writes that with Bérenger, the "Everyman" of 20th-century theatre enters Ionesco's work. "Everyman" is a character who stands for ordinary human beings in general. The plays also become more symbolic: their images stand for ideas. In Tueur sans gages, Bérenger lives in a grey and wet part of a city. An Architect shows him a "radiant city" full of light, which Bérenger has searched for all his life. However, a killer is murdering the people of the radiant city, and nobody does anything. Bérenger decides to find him. At the end, Bérenger meets the Killer, a small man who never speaks and only laughs quietly. Bérenger gives a long speech to try to convince him. He begs him and threatens him, but nothing works. The Killer calmly plays with his knife and slowly comes towards him. The radiant city comes from a real moment of light that Ionesco experienced when he was young. He gave this memory to Bérenger almost word for word. In Le Piéton de l'air (A Stroll in the Air), Bérenger is a French writer who lives in England. He discovers that he can fly. From the sky, he sees a world of horror, and nobody believes what he tells them except his young daughter. The play was first performed in Düsseldorf and later staged by Barrault at the Odéon with Madeleine Renaud. Le Roi se meurt (Exit the King) is Ionesco's play about death itself. King Bérenger the First learns that he will die at the end of the play. His two queens are with him. Marguerite, his first wife, prepares him for death. Marie, his second wife, is young and beautiful. She loves life and cannot accept that he will die. As the King becomes weaker, his kingdom becomes smaller. The seasons stop working properly, the desert comes closer, and the palace cracks and falls into ruin. In the end, only the throne room remains. Marie-Claude Hubert notes that playwrights had almost always avoided showing death itself on the stage. Ionesco boldly made it the whole subject of his play. The play is about one person facing his own death, with all the fear that Ionesco himself had felt since childhood. Ionesco said that he wrote it "to learn to die". It was meant to be a lesson, a spiritual exercise, and a slow journey towards an end that cannot be avoided. The play was successful in many countries. In 1963, Alec Guinness played the King in London. Two months later, the play was staged in Düsseldorf. Forty theatres performed it in a single season. After Le Piéton de l'air, Ionesco wrote more slowly and with greater difficulty. His plays became more literary and more personal. La Soif et la Faim (Hunger and Thirst, 1966) was first called "Life in the Dream". It is written in three "episodes". In the first episode, Jean leaves his wife Marie-Madeleine and their baby daughter to look for an ideal that always escapes him. In the last episode, "The Black Masses of the Good Inn", he reaches a strange place that is a "monastery-barracks-prison". The monks there admit that they are not real monks. They show him a "didactic", or teaching, play. Two prisoners in cages, Tripp and Brechtoll, are starved until each one gives up what he believes. François Mauriac saw this as a parody, or mocking imitation, of the Romantic "hunger and thirst" for another world. Jeux de massacre (Killing Game, 1970) shows a town struck by a plague. Nobody is safe. When the disease finally ends, a fire starts and traps the people who are still alive. Ionesco had also thought of calling the play La Peste ("The Plague") or The Triumph of Death. For the first time, he took ideas from other writers: from Daniel Defoe's Journal of the Plague Year and from Antonin Artaud's essay about the plague. In Macbett (1972), Ionesco took his subject from Shakespeare and used something of the style of Jarry's Ubu. He said that he wanted to write a play about the madness of power. Two lords, Candor and Glamiss, rebel against the greedy Archduke Duncan. Macbett and Banco defend Duncan in a bloody battle. Macbett then takes the throne for himself. The play was performed in 1972 with Jacques Mauclair. In 1989, the Royal Shakespeare Company performed it in England. Ionesco's last plays are dream plays. L'Homme aux valises (1975) and Voyages chez les morts (1980) are made from fragments, like dreams. Their hero, called Jean or the First Man, meets his dead father and mother, his hated stepmother, and people from his childhood. In L'Homme aux valises, the hero has lost his papers. At the consulate, he cannot remember the name of his father, the name of his mother, or even his own age. He says that his profession is "specialist in existence". Voyages chez les morts ends with a long, broken monologue. Ionesco said that with this play he had reached "the frontier of the unsayable". The director Roger Planchon later made a show called Ionesco from these two plays, with the actor Jean Carmet. Ionesco was also a prose writer. His short stories were collected in La Photo du colonel (1962). Several of his plays began as stories in this book. His only novel, Le Solitaire (1973), tells the story of a man who inherits money, stops working, and lives alone. Plazy calls it a moving and desperate book. Ionesco also wrote four short stories for "children under three years old". His essays about the theatre are collected in Notes et contre-notes (1962). The book contains talks, articles, and interviews written since 1950. In it, Ionesco explains how each play was born. He also defines his theatre against three enemies: commercial theatre; Brecht, whom he thought was too didactic, or too much like a teacher; and the old-fashioned psychology of writers such as Anouilh and Giraudoux. Lamont calls the book his "literary philosophy", his way of thinking about writing. His diaries are an important part of his prose work. Journal en miettes (1967) and Présent passé, Passé présent (1968) mix memories from childhood, dreams, and thoughts about death and politics. Découvertes (1969) tries to rebuild his first discovery of the world when he was a baby. Antidotes (1977) and Un homme en question (1979) collect his articles. One of these articles tries to answer the question "Why do I write?". Hugoliade is a mocking life of Victor Hugo. Ionesco wrote it in Romanian in 1935, and it gives special attention to the ridiculous sides of the great poet. It was published in French in 1982. La Quête intermittente (1987) is the diary of an old man. It ends with the words "I hope: Jesus Christ". Painting was an old interest of Ionesco's. When he was young, he wrote about Van Gogh. However, he began to paint seriously only late in life. He worked with gouache and made lithographs. He said that he painted in the manner of a child. He explained that his hand guided him: "it is the hand which is the rhythm". Ionesco did not separate the comic from the tragic. For him the comic was an "intuition of the absurd", and so it was more hopeless than tragedy. And tragedy was funny, because it shows the useless efforts that people make against fate. This is why he gave his plays strange subtitles: La Cantatrice chauve is an "anti-play", La Leçon a "comic drama", Les Chaises a "tragic farce". He often said that his theatre was the opposite of the commercial "boulevard" theatre. The boulevard theatre is entertainment. His own theatre, he wrote, questions the whole destiny of man and what it means to exist. He also refused psychology. His characters are not persons with a past and reasons for what they do. They are puppets, pushed by fear, by desire or by words. Nancy Lane explains that this does not mean that Ionesco saw people as machines. On the contrary, the mechanical characters attack the way modern society turns people into things, which Ionesco saw as its main evil. As he told Claude Bonnefoy, his puppets are "suffering puppets", and "caricature is criticism". Objects are as important as words. Ionesco's stage is full of things that grow, multiply and crush the characters: chairs, coffee cups, furniture, a corpse, eggs, mushrooms. Coe writes that for Ionesco the inner life of man is invaded by things, and that this is the source of his fear and pain. Faust Bradesco, one of his first French critics, called this world "the strange world of Ionesco", a theatre which "imposes itself without defining itself". The scholar Paul Vernois studied what he called the "dynamics" of this theatre in a book of 1972. He showed that the action of the plays moves up and down. Characters rise, like the flying Bérenger or the King who climbs the steps of his throne, or they sink into mud, heaviness and death. He called this "vertical polarization" (the pull between up and down), and saw in it the sign of the destiny of man, "an animal that stands up". Ionesco wrote the preface of the book. He said that he had never felt so well understood. He also rejected the idea that his theatre was about "incommunicability" (people who cannot understand each other). Misunderstandings, he wrote, do not last, and with time everything becomes clear. In 1961 Martin Esslin published The Theatre of the Absurd. The book grouped together Beckett, Adamov, Ionesco and Genet. It had an immediate effect abroad, and a later one in France, where the word "absurd" was linked to the philosophy of Sartre and Camus. Ionesco had already rejected the word in 1953. He wrote that it was a fashionable word, that it would go out of fashion, and that it was already vague enough to mean nothing. Later, Ionesco sometimes accepted it. In old age he even complained that he, and not Beckett, was the true founder of the theatre of the absurd. Ionesco preferred another word, "insolite" (unusual, strange). In 1953 he wrote an article called "The improbable, the unusual, my universe". At the Académie française in 1971 he said that literature is the result of a certain way of looking, which makes reality, dreamed or not, seem unusual. The writers who came before him were the writers of the strange and the grotesque (ugly and comic at the same time): Alfred Jarry and his Ubu, the Romanian writers Caragiale and Urmuz, and Kafka. He said that critics had called him every name. Bradesco wrote in 1967 that no avant-garde author had been more discussed, more dissected and more badly treated. Ionesco's answer was to write a play about it. In L'Impromptu de l'Alma (1956) a playwright called Ionesco is asleep among his books. Three doctors called Bartholomeus explain to him what his plays mean. They stand for the schools of criticism which judged him with fixed ideas, including the followers of Brecht. Ionesco took their words from real articles. Bartholomeus I and II speak like the magazine Théâtre populaire, where Roland Barthes and Bernard Dort wrote. Bartholomeus III speaks like Le Figaro. At the end the author himself begins to talk like a pedant (a person who shows off his knowledge), and the maid tells him to stop. Ionesco's early plays seem to have no politics. Rosette Lamont argues that they are "secretly political" from the start. The mechanical language of the Smiths is the language of conformism, and conformism is the ground where totalitarianism grows. The swastika in La Leçon and the rhinoceroses of 1959 make this open. In the London controversy of 1958, Ionesco refused the idea that a writer must serve a political cause. He said that a play was not a message. The writers praised by Tynan, like Sartre, were for him only the new "boulevard" authors. They repeated what was already in political speeches. Critics who wanted political theatre accused him of "formalism" (caring only about form and not about content). He replied that the most dangerous formalism was the one that reduces living thought to slogans. He wrote that penicillin and the fight against alcoholism were worth more than politics and a change of government. Politics nevertheless became an important part of his writing and of his public life. He had watched fascism win over his friends in Romania. He had watched communism take his country. He opposed both fascism and communism, which he saw as two forms of totalitarianism. In the 1960s and 1970s, when many French writers and thinkers were attracted by communism, he often attacked their ideas. He defended the dissidents of Eastern Europe and called them "the honour of Russia". Richard Coe gave the chapter on his politics the title "The Right-Wing Anarchist". Ionesco himself refused all labels. Above all, he defended individual freedom. Lane sums it up: Ionesco valued the individual and his freedom above everything, and saw modern mass societies as an enemy. His theatre is full of frightening figures of authority, from the Professor of La Leçon to the parents of Jacques, while his heroes are ordinary men. Two experiences of his childhood and youth are at the centre of Ionesco's work. The first is the fear of death. He said that he had been obsessed by death since the age of four. This fear runs through all his plays, from the growing corpse of Amédée to the dying king. The second is the experience of light. At seventeen or eighteen, in a quiet provincial town in June, he suddenly felt that the world had become infinitely more bright. The sky seemed dense, and the light could almost be touched. He felt an enormous joy and thought that he had understood something essential. He later used a Japanese word for this moment, "satori": the sudden light that some Eastern mystics (people who look for a direct experience of God) receive. The light is linked to the memory of La Chapelle-Anthenaise. Vernois also saw the village as a lost paradise, where the young Ionesco had felt safe and happy. The critic Saint Tobi built a whole book on this idea. For him, Ionesco's work is a search for a lost paradise, the paradise of childhood, which looked like a fairy-tale town. The characters lose the light and fall into a heavy, dark world of mud and things. Marie-Claude Hubert says the same. The bright places of the plays, the radiant city or the flight of Bérenger in Le Piéton de l'air, come from this early experience. Ionesco often described himself as a Christian, but he also wrote about his doubts and his difficulty in believing. He once said: "I do not know whether I am a Christian or not." At other times he called himself "a bad Christian, but a Christian all the same". He was shocked by a creation that allows chaos and evil. He regretted all his life that he was not a mystic and could not find peace in prayer. His last public words called on people to pray, because "only God can save men". Plazy sums him up as a clown who tries to climb Jacob's ladder (the ladder to heaven in the Bible), and whose falls make people laugh. By the end of his life, Ionesco was already accepted as a major playwright. In 1959, in Helsinki, he had said that every good avant-garde writer ends up as part of the tradition. This is what happened to him: the "enfant terrible" of 1950 became one of the "immortals" of the Académie française. His complete plays were published in 1990 in the Bibliothèque de la Pléiade, the most respected series of classics in France, edited by Emmanuel Jacquart. La Cantatrice chauve and La Leçon are still on the programme of the Théâtre de la Huchette. When Plazy wrote his biography in 1994, the show had run for thirty-five years. The theatre itself counts more than 19,500 performances of the two plays and more than two million spectators. It describes the show as a world record for a play performed without a break in the same place. The show received the Grand Vermeil Medal of the City of Paris in 1996 and an honorary Molière award in 2000. The plays are performed all over the world. After 1989 they were translated again in the languages of the former communist countries. Richard Coe wrote the first English study in 1960, for readers who knew very little about him. By 1967 it needed rewriting, because Ionesco had more than doubled his published work. Critics have judged him in different ways. Lane notes that critics of the left first praised him and then turned against him, while conservative critics first rejected him and later regretted his early boldness. For her, Rhinocéros and Le Roi se meurt are the two mature plays that have become twentieth-century classics. The three early plays, La Cantatrice chauve, La Leçon and Les Chaises, have stayed fresh, funny and disturbing. Rosette Lamont calls him "a modern classic" and "a twentieth-century Molière". Like Molière, she says, he mocked the bourgeois mind, not as a social class but as a sickness of the mind. She sees his whole work as part of the literature written after the Holocaust. Harold Bloom thinks that Rhinocéros is still his most popular work, but that people often read it in a way that is too simple. Allan Lewis wrote in 1972 that Ionesco had touched something deep in the modern feeling that logic and science are no longer enough. His image has changed. The religious and spiritual side of his work became more important in his later years, and readers have often preferred one Ionesco to the other. In 1994 the novelist François Coupry paid him a strange tribute. His book is a "tragi-comic debate in five acts", in which Faust, Antigone, Don Quixote and other famous characters argue about Ionesco's life and work. Gilles Plazy ends his biography with the image of a clown who always wondered why he was alive, and whose work now matters more than his life. André Le Gall wrote the largest biography in 2009, with the help of the family archives. He presents Ionesco as "a poet of the unusual, and not a singer of the absurd", a mystic dressed up as a joker. The years given are the years of the first performance for the plays, and of the first publication in French for the other books. La Cantatrice chauve (The Bald Soprano, 1950), anti-play. La Leçon (The Lesson, 1951), comic drama. Les Chaises (The Chairs, 1952), tragic farce. Victimes du devoir (Victims of Duty, 1953). Amédée ou Comment s'en débarrasser (Amédée, or How to Get Rid of It, 1954). Jacques ou la Soumission (Jack, or The Submission, 1955). L'Impromptu de l'Alma (Improvisation, or The Shepherd's Chameleon, 1956). Le Nouveau Locataire (The New Tenant, 1957). Tueur sans gages (The Killer, 1959). Rhinocéros (Rhinoceros, 1959). Le Roi se meurt (Exit the King, 1962). Le Piéton de l'air (A Stroll in the Air, 1962). La Soif et la Faim (Hunger and Thirst, 1964). La Colère (Anger, 1962), film scenario. Jeux de massacre (Killing Game, 1970). Macbett (1972). Ce formidable bordel! (A Hell of a Mess, 1973). L'Homme aux valises (The Man with the Luggage, 1975). Voyages chez les morts (Journeys among the Dead, 1980). Nu (No, 1934, in Romanian; French translation Non, 1986), criticism. La Photo du colonel (The Colonel's Photograph, 1962), stories. Notes et contre-notes (Notes and Counter Notes, 1962), essays on the theatre. Journal en miettes (Fragments of a Journal, 1967), diary. Présent passé, Passé présent (Present Past, Past Present, 1968), diary. Découvertes (1969), essay. Le Solitaire (The Hermit, 1973), novel. Antidotes (1977), articles. Un homme en question (1979), articles. Le Noir et le Blanc (1981; reprinted as Le Blanc et le Noir, 1985), lithographs and text. Hugoliade (1982, written in Romanian in 1935). La Quête intermittente (1987), diary. The notes give the author, the year of the book and the page. Full details of every book are in the next section.

Selma Ottilia Lovisa Lagerlöf (; born 20 November 1858, dead 16 March 1940, She was 81 years old. Was a Swedish writer. In 1909, she was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature becoming the first woman to do so. She is mostly known for her children's book Nils Holgerssons underbara resa genom Sverige (The Wonderful Adventures of Nils). She also worked for women's rights.

Luigi Pirandello (Agrigento 28 June 1867 – Rome 10 December 1936) was an Italian playwright, novelist, and short story writer. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1934, for his "bold and brilliant renovation of the drama and the stage". Pirandello's works include novels, hundreds of short stories, and about 40 plays, some of which are written in Sicilian. Pirandello's tragic farces are often seen as forerunners for Theatre of the Absurd. Il Fu Mattia Pascal (The Late Mattia Pascal) I Vecchi e I Giovani (The Old and the Young) Quaderni di Serafino Gubbio (Serafino Gubbio's Journals) Uno, Nessuno e Centomila (One, No one and One Hundred Thousand) Sei Personaggi in Cerca d'Autore (Six Characters in Search of an Author) Ciascuno a Suo Modo (Each In His Own Way) Questa Sera Si Recita a Soggetto (Tonight We Improvise) L'Uomo dal Fiore in Bocca (The Man With The Flower In His Mouth) La Vita che ti Diedi (The Life I Gave You) Il Gioco delle Parti (The Rules of the Game) Il Piacere dell'Onestà (The Pleasure Of Honesty) L'Uomo, La Bestia e La Virtù (The Man, The Beast and The Virtue) Così è (Se Vi Pare) (So It Is (If You Think So))

Johann Christoph Friedrich von Schiller (November 10, 1759 in Marbach, Württemberg – May 9, 1805 in Weimar), usually known as Friedrich Schiller, was a German poet, philosopher, historian, and dramatist. Kabale und Liebe (Intrigue and Love) (1784) Don Carlos, Infant von Spanien (Don Carlos) (1787) Die Jungfrau von Orleans (The Maid of Orleans) (1801) An die Freude or Ode to Joy (1785) which became the basis for the fourth movement of Beethoven's ninth symphony

Johan August Strindberg ( 22 January 1849 in Stockholm- 14 May 1912 in Stockholm) was a Swedish writer and artist. He was born as the fourth child of Carl Oscar Strindberg and Ulrike Eleonora. For the art he was not really interested, but it came later. Later, he began his medical studies at the University in Uppsala, tried to be an actor and worked before his career as a writer and journalist. In the middle of the 19th century he lived in France, Switzerland, Germany, Denmark and England. Beside writing books and something different he was really interested in drawing and natural sciences. 1877 August married Siri von Essen, an actress from the royal drama. With her he had three kids- Karin (1880), Greta (1881) and Hans (1884). After married Frida Strindberg-Uhl he had his inferno-crisis, with full of hallucinations and death thoughts. In 1896, he came back to Stockholm and died at the 14th May 1912 in Stockholm. He was buried in Solna next to his first wife, Finnish actress, Siri von Essen.

Tristan Tzara (;; born Samuel or Samy Rosenstock, also known as S. Samyro; – 25 December 1963) was an artist from Romania and France who was known for starting the Dadaist movement. He was interested in symbolism and was more on the nihilistic side of Dada than others.

Émile Zola (2 April 1840 – 29 September 1902) was a major French writer and the most important naturalist writer. He worked toward political liberalization of France. Zola was nominated for the first and second Nobel Prize in Literature in 1901 and 1902. His death from carbon monoxide poisoning is suspected to have been suicide.

Sir Kingsley William Amis (16 April 1922 – 22 October 1995) was an English novelist, poet, critic, and teacher. He wrote more than twenty novels, three collections of poetry, short stories, radio and television scripts, and books of social and literary criticism. He was the father of the British novelist Martin Amis. Kingsley Amis was born in Clapham, South London, England. He went to school at the City of London School and St. John's College, Oxford. At Oxford, he met Philip Larkin and became friends. Amis served in the Royal Corps of Signals in the Second World War. Amis was a fan of jazz music. He liked the American musicians Sidney Bechet, Henry "Red" Allen and Pee Wee Russell. His first novel Lucky Jim was very successfull. The novel won the Somerset Maugham Award for fiction. Lucky Jim was the first English novel that focused on an ordinary man as anti-hero. As a poet, Amis was a part of The Movement (anti-romantic poetry). As a young man, Kingsley Amis was a member of the Communist Party. He left them when the Soviet Union invaded Hungary in 1956. After that, Amis became anti-communist, and conservative. He talks about his political change in the essay "Why Lucky Jim Turned Right" (1967). Amis was an atheist. Novels such as The Green Man and The Anti-Death League were about the personality of a divine being. They were also about its relationship to death and dying. Amis's novel The Old Devils won the Booker Prize in 1986. He received a knighthood in 1990. Amis was married. The first time in 1948 to Hilary Bardwell and then to novelist Elizabeth Jane Howard in 1965. He divorced Howard in 1983. Amis spent his last years living with his first wife and her third husband. He had two sons and a daughter. His younger son was novelist Martin Amis. Martin wrote about his father's life and decline in his memoir Experience. Amis' interest in science fiction led to New Maps of Hell (1960). It was about how he felt about science fiction in literature. He liked the stories of Frederik Pohl and C.M. Kornbluth. With the Sovietologist Robert Conquest, Amis produced the science fiction series Spectrum I–IV. This series got a lot of its ideas from the 1950s magazine Astounding Science Fiction. He wrote three science fiction novels. The Alteration was an alternate history novel set in a twentieth-century Britain. Russian Hide-and-Seek was an alternate history where Russia had conquered Britain after the Second World War. He also wrote the supernatural-horror novel The Green Man which the BBC adapted for television. Amis wrote books about Ian Fleming's James Bond. He wrote the popular James Bond Dossier. Later, he wrote, The Book of Bond, or, Every Man His Own 007. It was a tongue-in-cheek how-to manual about being a spy like Bond. He wrote it under the name "Lt Col. William 'Bill' Tanner". Tanner was M's Chief of Staff in many of the Bond novels.

Wystan Hugh Auden (21 February 1907 – 29 September 1973) was a Anglo-American poet. He was born in York and moved to Harborne, Birmingham in 1908, then to New York City in 1939. He wrote several famous poems such as Funeral Blues, and As I Walked Out One Evening. He signed his works W. H. Auden. He died in Vienna, Austria and is buried in Kirchstetten. Auden was an Anglican and was gay. He married Erika Mann in 1935 to enable her to escape Nazi Germany. His partner from 1946 until his death was Chester Kallman (1921–1975).

Enid Mary Blyton (11 of August 1897 – 28 November 1968) was an English writer. She was born in Dulwich, South London, England. She was one of the world's most famous children's writers. She wrote a great number of books. Her most famous stories are the Famous Five stories, about a group of four children (Dick, Julian, Anne, and Georgina, who wanted to be called George) and their dog (Timmy) who have many adventures, and her Noddy books for small children. Her parents wanted her to become a pianist, but Enid wanted to be a teacher. Her parents agreed to let her train as a teacher. She began teaching in 1919 in Kent, not far from where she grew up in Beckenham. As a child and teenager her main interest had been writing poems, stories and other items. She had sent many of them to magazines but had never had any published. As she worked as a teacher she began to publish her articles in a magazine called Teachers' World. Her first book, called Child Whispers came out in 1922. It was a book of her poems with illustrations (drawings). She was married soon after. She left teaching and began to have more success with her books. She wrote in and was the editor of magazine for children called Sunny Stories. The magazine came out every two weeks. Some of Enid's most famous books were first printed in this magazine in parts. Enid Blyton is in The Guinness Book of Records as one of the world's biggest selling writers. She is also included because she wrote more books than almost any other writer (about 700). Her books were published in many different languages. She said that she found writing them easy. Her books still sell in large numbers, and used to be owned by her family. A few years ago her family sold them, and now her works belong to a private company. Enid Blyton did a lot of work for charity and had a club for children which helped them to give money to charity. She was married twice and had two daughters. She died of Alzheimer's disease in Hampstead, London. Blyton, Enid 1952. The Story of my Life. Grafton. ISBN 978-0-246-12795-2 Stoney, Barbara 2006. Enid Blyton: the biography. (Kindle ed.) History Press. ISBN 978-0-7524-6957-7

Anthony Burgess (25 February 1917 – 22 November 1993) was an English author. One of these was named A Clockwork Orange. It was about evil. He had the idea for the story after a group of bad young men raped and beat his wife for no reason. Burgess also made songs and music. And he wrote a lot about writers he loved, such as James Joyce, a novelist, and Gerard Manley Hopkins, a poet. Burgess was born in Harpurhey, Manchester, in the north of England. Before he became a writer, he was a soldier, then a teacher. When he was 37 years old, he left his home country to work in Malaysia and Brunei. Later, he lived in the USA, Italy, and France. He was born very poor, the son of a man who made a meagre living out of selling cigarettes to workmen. But when Burgess died, he had grown rich. This was because he worked so hard at his art, which is the art of literature. He wrote at least 1,000 words every day of his life. But he always found time to be kind to other writers. He was friendly to the many people who came to visit with him at his seaside home in Monaco. Burgess died of lung cancer aged 76, in St John's Wood, London. The books by Burgess that people say they like the most are called Earthly Powers, about the Pope; Enderby, about a poet; and Nothing Like the Sun, about William Shakespeare.

Robert Ranke Graves (commonly known as Robert Graves, and in Germany as Robert von Ranke Graves; 24 July 1895 – 7 December 1985) was an English poet, novelist, critic and classicist. He wrote more than 140 works. He wrote poems about Greek myths and historical novels. Many of his novels were set in ancient Rome or were about stories from Greek myths. He also wrote about Greek myths and translated them into English. Graves was born in Wimbledon, now part of London. He was the third of five children. His father was Alfred Perceval Graves (1846–1931). He came from an Irish family. His mother was Amalie von Ranke (1857–1951). She came from a German family. Robert went to many schools when he was young. In 1909 he won a scholarship to Charterhouse, a famous boarding school in Surrey.When the First World War began in August 1914, Graves joined the army right away. He wrote many poems about the war. He became a good friend of another war poet, Siegfried Sassoon. Graves was very badly wounded in the Battle of the Somme. He nearly died and was sent back to a hospital in England. He also had mental problems called by shell shock from the bad experience of battle. His mental problems lasted for several years. In 1918 he married the artist Nancy Nicholson. He went to study at Oxford University in 1919. At Oxford his good friend was T. E. Lawrence. He later wrote a biography of Lawrence called Lawrence and the Arabs. He and Nancy Nicholson split up in the 1920s. He went to live with the poet Laura Riding in Spain They lived in Deià, a small village on the island of Majorca. Graves and Riding lived in America during the Spanish Civil War. Their relationship broke down in 1938. Graves went back to England. He fell in love with Beryl Hodge (1915–2003). Graves wrote many beautiful love poems to Hodge. They moved to Spain in 1946 and lived in Deià with their children. They were married in 1950. Their house in Deià is now a museum. From 1961 to 1966 Graves was Professor of Poetry at Oxford. Robert Graves died at his house in Deià on 7 December 1985. He was 90 years old. He was buried in a churchyard on a hill near his house. Graves had eight children—four with his first wife Nancy and four with his second wife Beryl. I, Claudius, 1934. Claudius the God and his Wife Messalina, 1934 Sergeant Lamb of the Ninth, 1940. The Story of Marie Powell: Wife to Mr. Milton, 1944 Homer's Daughter, 1955.

John Keats (31 October 1795 – 23 February 1821) was an English poet. He is often ranked as one of the five most important poets of the Romantic movement in English literature; the other four are William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Lord Byron, and Percy Bysshe Shelley. Though Keats was the youngest of these poets, he also died before the others: he suffered from tuberculosis and died in Rome at the age of 25. Keats was the son of an inn-keeper Thomas Keats, who died when Keats was nine years old and Frances Keats; and his mother died of tuberculosis in 1810.
